artigo.texto: China’s industry ministry and six other agencies set 2030 as the date for the first large-scale use of all-solid-state batteries, though CATL’s chairman rates the technology four out of nine and calls million-vehicle use before 2030 very unlikely. ProLogium’s Dunkirk plant, the largest new European cell project since Northvolt went bankrupt, is staged at 0.8 GWh in 2028 and will be certified against a Chinese standard. China has set 2030 as the date for the first large-scale use of solid-state batteries. Its biggest battery maker rates the technology four out of nine. A plant in northern France broke ground in February. The plan came from the industry ministry and six other agencies on 28 September and covers 2026 to 2030, as CnEVPost reported. It also targets lithium cells good for 15,000 charge cycles. The ministry acknowledged weaknesses in innovation and imbalances between supply and demand. CATL is promising less than the plan does. Its chairman, Robin Zeng, put all-solid-state at four out of nine in June, on a scale where nine means ready for vehicle production. He called the chance of fitting it to a million cars before 2030 very small. CATL intends limited production in 2027. LG Energy Solution expects the technology to reach smartphones a decade before EVs. Its North America president says large cells are where manufacturers struggle. Europe is further along than that timetable suggests, though not by much, and not on its own technology. ProLogium already makes 6,000 packs a year in Taiwan, which is half a gigawatt hour, at 381 Wh/kg on TUV Rheinland’s measurement. That is roughly 30% above the cells in most electric cars today. The company is now building the same thing in France, with subsidies agreed in 2023 and permits granted the year after. The Dunkirk plant started construction in February beside the Gravelines nuclear station, staged at 0.8 GWh in 2028 and 12 GWh by 2032. Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Mercedes are separately working with Factorial on cells of their own. None of it is close to Chinese volume, and the gap is not narrowing. Chinese and South Korean makers supply 90% of Europe’s batteries, and Northvolt went bankrupt after raising $15bn. Dunkirk is the largest new European cell project since. The standard is Chinese as well. ProLogium’s cells are certified against GB/T 43568-2026, the all-solid-state specification Beijing introduced in July, and were separately tested by UL Solutions. China took 70% of global electric car production under the previous five-year plan. The new one says initial large-scale use rather than mass production, and even that is a target rather than a promise. artigo.texto: A Macau Internacional Troca de Emissões de Carbono Limitada, mais conhecida por MEX, pretende tirar partido das vantagens oferecidas por Macau para promover a negociação de activos ambientais – incluindo de créditos de carbono, certificados de energia verde e outros instrumentos similares – entre a China e os Países de Língua Portuguesa. Meng Meng, Directora-Geral da entidade, revela que a plataforma de negociação operada pela MEX já listou mais de 30 projectos ligados a países lusófonos e de língua espanhola, envolvendo uma redução total de emissões de carbono superior a 14,13 milhões de toneladas Como foi criada a Macau Internacional Troca de Emissões de Carbono Limitada (MEX, na sigla inglesa)? Quais são os seus objectivos estratégicos? A MEX foi criada a 30 de Outubro de 2024. Recorrendo a tecnologias de informação avançadas e padrões de referência no sector, integra produtos e oportunidades relacionados com o clima a nível global, proporcionando à China uma solução específica com características de Macau para se conectar aos mercados internacionais de finanças verdes. A Região Administrativa Especial de Macau (RAEM) é um porto franco, com regras financeiras alinhadas com as normas internacionais. Além disso, a cidade situa-se na confluência de duas importantes estratégias nacionais – o projecto da Grande Baía Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau e a Zona de Cooperação Aprofundada entre Guangdong e Macau em Hengqin. Neste sentido, possui um conjunto de vantagens intrínsecas que lhe permite posicionar-se como um “superconector” no mercado internacional de carbono. A nossa tarefa é transformar gradualmente esse conjunto de vantagens intrínsecas numa realidade concreta. A nível nacional, trabalhamos no sentido de apoiar as metas de “duplo carbono” estabelecidas pelo país [atingir o pico das emissões de dióxido de carbono antes de 2030 e alcançar a neutralidade carbónica antes de 2060], proporcionando um canal mais aberto para que o mercado de carbono da China possa estabelecer ligações com capital, tecnologia e regulamentações internacionais. A nível global, estamos a construir uma plataforma de cooperação no campo da acção climática, ao mesmo tempo que promovemos o alinhamento de padrões com as normas internacionais e a sua implementação prática, divulgando o progresso alcançado pelo mercado de carbono da China. Em paralelo, a MEX encara o comércio de carbono como um motor para alcançar a neutralidade carbónica e desenvolver as finanças verdes. Oferecemos também a diversos sectores-chave em Macau soluções ligadas à neutralidade carbónica, ferramentas associadas a certificados verdes de absorção de carbono e instrumentos de financiamento verde, transformando a transição para a neutralidade carbónica numa vantagem competitiva para as indústrias da RAEM. Qual é o modelo operacional da MEX? A nossa plataforma pode ser entendida como um mercado digital de negociação de activos ambientais. Os produtos listados na MEX incluem créditos de carbono, certificados de energia renovável e outros itens similares. Apoiamos a negociação de certificados verdes internacionais e chineses e somos a única bolsa do género na China a disponibilizar contratos padronizados de créditos de carbono de elevada qualidade com cobertura global. Nas áreas não directamente relacionadas com a negociação de activos, prestamos serviços de dados e estudos, formação, consultoria e outras soluções. Publicamos regularmente relatórios sectoriais para ajudar os participantes no mercado a compreenderem melhor tendências, a identificarem oportunidades e a mitigarem riscos. Além disso, disponibilizamos programas de capacitação que ajudam as empresas a aprofundarem o seu conhecimento sobre os desafios associados à acção climática. Prestamos igualmente serviços personalizados ao longo de toda a cadeia, desde o inventário de emissões de carbono e o planeamento de trajectórias de redução de emissões até à definição de soluções de compensação. Através deste modelo integrado, que combina actividades de negociação e serviços não transaccionais, procuramos criar um ecossistema sustentável de activos ambientais e serviços verdes, permitindo que as empresas que necessitam de soluções nesta área as encontrem na MEX. Quais os principais marcos já alcançados pela MEX? Em primeiro lugar, concretizámos o nosso posicionamento estratégico de utilizar Macau como ponto de apoio para ligar a China ao mercado internacional de carbono. Macau tem vindo, gradualmente, a afirmar-se como um centro activo do mercado de carbono na Ásia. Até Agosto deste ano, o volume acumulado de créditos de carbono negociados através da MEX tinha ultrapassado 1,17 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO2-e). Já o volume de certificados de energia renovável negociados ascendia a 2,07 milhões de certificados. Contamos actualmente com 146 membros registados na nossa plataforma. Logo no dia da nossa inauguração, concluímos as primeiras negociações envolvendo cerca de 870 mil toneladas de créditos de carbono, abrangendo uma dezena de sectores em cinco países. Esperamos que, através da adopção de um conjunto de normas rigorosas e de uma governação sólida, os produtos disponibilizados através da MEX se tornem sinónimo de elevada qualidade. Somos a única instituição de Macau que é membro da Associação Internacional de Comércio de Emissões. Estabelecemos igualmente parcerias com outros membros e organizações internacionais e mantemos uma cooperação aprofundada com diversas instituições académicas e industriais de referência a nível mundial no sector. Estas colaborações, ao promoverem o reconhecimento mútuo de activos, a integração de sistemas e a harmonização de normas, posicionam Macau como um verdadeiro pólo de ligação entre os vários mercados de carbono da Ásia e do mundo. artigo.texto: Amazon abandona NDAs em data centers: o que muda na prática A AWS aboliu os acordos de confidencialidade com governos locais para tentar frear mais de 100 moratórias contra data centers nos EUA. A Amazon Web Services decidiu parar de usar acordos de confidencialidade (NDAs) nas negociações com governos locais para aprovação de novos data centers nos Estados Unidos. O anúncio foi feito por Matt Garman, CEO da AWS, em uma publicação que tenta responder à crescente resistência de comunidades americanas contra a expansão dessas instalações. A medida não é um gesto de boa vontade espontâneo. É uma reação calculada a um movimento que está ganhando corpo: mais de 100 moratórias contra data centers estão sendo discutidas em diferentes localidades dos EUA. O estado de Nova York já aprovou uma suspensão de um ano em licenças para grandes data centers. A Amazon está, na prática, tentando conter um incêndio regulatório antes que ele se espalhe. Por que as comunidades americanas estão rejeitando data centers A raiz do problema é a falta de transparência. A ativista ambiental Erin Brockovich resumiu o padrão que gera revolta: projetos anunciados depois que as licenças já estão garantidas, desenvolvedores que não retornam ligações e autoridades locais que assinaram NDAs antes que os vizinhos soubessem que um projeto estava sendo considerado. Esse ciclo corroeu a confiança pública. Como analisamos na cobertura de tecnologia do portal, a corrida por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial acelerou drasticamente a construção de data centers, mas as empresas trataram a expansão como uma operação sigilosa, e não como um projeto que afeta diretamente a vida de milhares de pessoas. O CEO da Anthropic, Dario Amodei, classificou a situação como “fundamentalmente uma crise de confiança”, em que as pessoas assumem que governos e big techs estão sempre tramando alguma forma de prejudicá-las. É um diagnóstico que vale para todo o setor, não apenas para a Amazon. Os quatro mitos que a Amazon tenta derrubar Garman tentou desmontar quatro críticas recorrentes aos data centers: consumo excessivo de água, aumento nos custos de eletricidade, poluição e ausência de benefícios para as comunidades locais. Sobre a água, a Amazon apontou que o consumo direto de seus data centers representa apenas 0,5% de todo o uso industrial de água nos EUA, volume descrito como “ordens de magnitude menor” do que campos de golfe ou o cultivo de amêndoas. A Nvidia, por sua vez, afirmou recentemente que seu novo sistema de refrigeração elimina “praticamente todo o uso de água” dentro dos data centers. Há um problema nesses números, no entanto. Tanto a Amazon quanto a Nvidia parecem ignorar o consumo mais amplo de água envolvido na geração de eletricidade e na fabricação de chips. Cientistas alertaram que precisam estudar o uso de água e energia dos data centers de forma independente, já que não existem exigências federais ou estaduais sobre como as empresas de tecnologia reportam esses dados. Em outras palavras: as big techs estão pedindo que acreditemos nos números que elas mesmas compilam, sem auditoria externa. Quanto à eletricidade, Garman argumentou que as tarifas só subiram em alguns estados com grande concentração de data centers, enquanto em outros caíram ou cresceram mais lentamente. Ele atribuiu os aumentos à falta de investimento prévio na rede elétrica. Mas um órgão de fiscalização independente apontou recentemente que os data centers foram os principais responsáveis por um aumento de 76% nos preços de energia, em base anual, na maior rede elétrica dos Estados Unidos. Os dados contam uma história diferente da narrativa corporativa. A questão da poluição e o caso Texas O ponto mais delicado talvez seja a poluição. Um data center planejado pela Amazon no Texas tem licença para emitir até 33 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono por ano, volume superior ao de qualquer outra usina de energia do país. Garman contra-argumentou dizendo que os geradores ficam ociosos 99,9% do tempo, funcionando em média apenas 10 horas por ano para testes de manutenção. A resposta, embora tecnicamente válida, não aborda o ponto central da crítica: se os geradores quase nunca funcionam, por que solicitar uma licença tão permissiva? O limite alto na licença cria uma percepção de risco que alimenta a desconfiança, como já discutimos ao analisar o impacto energético da IA. O caso do Texas é emblemático porque ilustra como o setor opera na prática: pede o máximo possível de margem regulatória, argumenta que usará uma fração mínima e espera que a comunidade confie nessa promessa. É uma estratégia que funcionava em um ambiente de baixa fiscalização, mas está sendo desafiada agora. Um bilhão em contribuições é suficiente? Garman também destacou que, nos últimos três anos, a Amazon contribuiu com mais de 1 bilhão de dólares para comunidades onde mantém presença significativa de data centers. É um número expressivo, mas que precisa ser colocado em perspectiva: a AWS gerou cerca de 105 bilhões de dólares em receita apenas em 2024. O investimento comunitário representa menos de 1% desse faturamento. O abandono dos NDAs é um passo concreto, mas provavelmente insuficiente para reverter o sentimento anti-data center. Como observou a escritora Jasmine Sun, quando opositores dos data centers são confrontados com os argumentos das empresas de tecnologia, a resposta costuma ser simples: “Eu não acredito neles.” Para a indústria de tecnologia como um todo, o episódio é um alerta. A expansão da infraestrutura de IA depende de licenças locais, apoio comunitário e redes elétricas que consigam absorver a demanda. Se as moratórias avançarem, Garman avisa que “os EUA podem estar escrevendo seu próprio bilhete perdedor nessa corrida, e as consequências durariam gerações.” O argumento de competitividade global pode funcionar em Washington, mas não convence moradores que veem seus custos de energia subir e caminhões de construção passarem pela porta todos os dias. artigo.texto: Hyundai Motor, Toyota, BYD Intensify Race to Develop 'Dream Battery' Solid-State Technology Automakers are going all-in on developing solid-state batteries, the next-generation power source poised to reshape the electric vehicle landscape. With Hyundai Motor, Toyota, BYD, and other major global automakers simultaneously entering the development race, attention is focused on whether this "game changer" will become a reality. Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a non-flammable solid material. By dramatically reducing fire risk and boosting energy density, they can deliver over 1,000 kilometers of driving range on a single charge—earning them the "dream battery" label. Given that current lithium-ion batteries offer roughly 500–600 kilometers of range, the technology promises nearly double the performance. Manfred Harrer, president of R&D at Hyundai Motor Group, made the company's solid-state battery ambitions clear during a press meeting at the "HMG Tech Talent Forum 2026" held in San Jose, California, over two days starting on the 17th of last month. "We must absolutely participate in the solid-state battery development race," he said. "We will continue investing to secure leadership in this technology, which represents the biggest strategic bet in the automotive industry." Hyundai Motor is pursuing a "battery internalization strategy" in which it develops battery cell specifications and structures in-house while outsourcing mass production to external manufacturers. The rationale: if Hyundai can achieve breakthroughs in solid-state battery development ahead of battery makers, it gains leverage in price negotiations and a favorable position to expand EV sales. Hyundai Motor Group has built a solid-state battery pilot production line at its Uiwang research center in Gyeonggi Province and is targeting commercial mass production around 2030. Global automakers join the fray Hyundai Motor is far from alone in the solid-state battery race. Toyota, which has been cautious about EV development, is collaborating with energy company Idemitsu Kosan and others on solid-state battery research, targeting mass production as early as next year. Honda has also recently entered the fray, partnering with U.S. battery startup QuantumScape. Honda previously unveiled its own solid-state battery pilot line at its research facility in Sakura City, Tochigi Prefecture, in November 2024, and began cell production in January of the following year. The joint research agreement with QuantumScape was signed in June of this year. Nissan is also building a pilot production line at its Yokohama plant, targeting commercialization in fiscal year 2028 (April 2028–March 2029). This means all three major Japanese automakers—Toyota, Honda, and Nissan—now have their own pilot lines and collaboration frameworks in place, accelerating development. Notably, the 2027–2028 timeline cited by Toyota and Idemitsu refers to the commercialization stage, with full-scale mass production to follow—a different benchmark from Hyundai Motor Group's mass production target of around 2030. Chinese players are moving quickly as well. BYD, China's largest EV maker, announced a roadmap to begin pilot production of vehicles equipped with solid-state batteries in the first quarter of next year, enter mass production in 2028, and achieve mainstream adoption after 2030. BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li told local media in Valencia, Spain, last month: "We will unveil the first model featuring solid-state battery technology next year." However, Li did not specify a concrete mass production schedule or a timeline for consumer availability. Industry observers interpret the vehicle she referenced as likely a test vehicle for technology validation rather than a production model. Geely Automobile Holdings announced in its five-year strategy released earlier this year that it would complete in-house solid-state battery development and begin validation within this year. Some Chinese EV makers, including Li Auto, are reportedly already at the sample production stage. Taiwan-based battery maker ProLogium has already entered the mass production phase. On the 2nd of last month, ProLogium announced that its 3.5-generation lithium ceramic battery (LCB) had begun mass production at its gigawatt-scale plant in Taiwan. The large-format cell, with a capacity of 185.4Ah, achieved an energy density of 381Wh/kg by weight and 903Wh/L by volume in German TÜV certification, according to the company. ProLogium classifies this battery as solid-state and has identified data centers, marine, and aerospace applications as target markets beyond EVs. The company plans production bases in France and North America in addition to Taiwan. The solid-state battery timelines announced by major players are summarized below. Caution persists over commercialization timeline Skepticism remains about how quickly the battery market landscape will shift, given the high technical difficulty, demanding manufacturing processes, and the likelihood of elevated prices in the early stages of mass production. Zeng Yuqun, chairman of CATL, the world's largest battery maker, said at the World Economic Forum annual meeting in Dalian, China, in June: "If we divide battery technology maturity into stages 1 through 9, solid-state battery technology is only at stage 4." At the time, projections within China's battery industry suggested that solid-state battery manufacturing costs would exceed three times those of batteries offering 500 kilometers of range. Notably, CATL itself—despite Zeng's stage-4 assessment—is maintaining its plan for small-volume production in 2027. In response to investor inquiries in July, CATL stated it "expects small-scale production in 2027." The company is building a pilot line of approximately 2GWh capacity in Yibin, Sichuan Province, with equipment installation set to begin in the second half of this year. SMM, a battery

artigo.texto: South Korea's Big Three Battery Material Makers Counter China with LFP, LMR, and Solid-State Push — Cathode Supremacy Battle Reignites Chinese battery makers are rapidly encroaching on the global market with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries as their weapon, forcing South Korean cathode material producers to overhaul their product strategies. POSCO Future M, EcoPro BM, and L&F — which had concentrated on high-nickel ternary chemistries — are now racing to close the gap with China by strengthening their LFP response while simultaneously broadening their portfolios to include lithium-manganese-rich (LMR) and solid-state battery materials. According to SNE Research on October 5, global EV battery usage excluding China reached 316.2 GWh in the first seven months of this year, up 25.8% year over year. During the same period, the combined market share of CATL and BYD climbed to 44.6%, up 7.0 percentage points from a year earlier. Chinese companies that once relied heavily on their domestic market are now rapidly seizing the non-China market by expanding supply to global automakers, establishing overseas production bases, and leveraging the price competitiveness of LFP batteries. By contrast, combined battery usage by South Korea's three major cell makers — LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Samsung SDI — in the non-China market fell 8.9% year over year to 86.1 GWh. Their combined share tumbled 10.4 percentage points from 37.6% to 27.2%. While the overall non-China market grew more than 20%, the South Korean trio actually contracted, widening the gap with Chinese rivals. The decline in North American usage was a particularly significant drag on their performance. South Korea's materials industry is strengthening its LFP response beyond its traditional high-nickel focus while preparing LMR and solid-state technologies as next-generation counteroffensive cards. The growing share of entry-level EV models and the explosive growth of the AI data center-driven energy storage system (ESS) market are creating structural demand for low-cost, high-safety materials. Defending with LFP, Counterattacking with LMR POSCO Future M is placing the most aggressive bet on LMR cathode materials. The LMR cathode jointly developed by POSCO Holdings' Future Technology Research Center and global automakers and battery companies has successfully completed pilot production, and the company is now working to secure mass-production technology. LMR reduces the use of expensive nickel and cobalt while increasing manganese content, lowering costs while maintaining high energy density. It also has the advantage of being compatible with existing NCM cathode production facilities, relatively reducing the burden of new factory investment. At the same time, the company is rapidly expanding its LFP footprint in Pohang. It plans to convert part of its existing Pohang NCM cathode lines to LFP and begin supply by the end of this year, while its joint venture CNP New Material Technology is building a dedicated LFP plant with a maximum annual capacity of 50,000 tons at the Pohang Yeongilman Industrial Complex, targeting mass production in 2027. It is a two-track strategy: defending the current market with LFP while targeting the next mid-to-low-priced EV market with LMR. SK Securities analysts Park Hyung-woo and Jung Young-hwan noted, "Precursors and anode materials are expected to become bottlenecks in the LFP landscape next year. POSCO Future M is well positioned to respond flexibly to this." EcoPro BM is raising its commercialization readiness on both the LMR and solid-state fronts. Its LMR cathode has entered the final validation stage targeting mass production for key customers. The company has optimized its processes so that existing ternary cathode production lines can be used as-is, enabling rapid conversion to mass production once orders are confirmed. For solid-state batteries, the company is operating a solid electrolyte pilot line, and its products are undergoing quality verification by major battery makers. The mass-production line design is also complete, with construction to begin once customer demand is confirmed, targeting mass production as early as 2027. Eugene Investment & Securities analyst Han Byung-hwa said, "Next-generation materials including solid-state and LMR have advanced to the stage just before mass production. Once the market recovers from the EV chasm, the company will be able to secure growth engines simultaneously in both existing high-nickel and new battery chemistries." L&F Builds the Broadest Portfolio L&F, based in Daegu, is pursuing the broadest portfolio strategy. Building on its experience as the world's first to mass-produce ultra-high-nickel 95% cathodes, the company has entered LFP mass production and is expanding its next-generation product lineup to include high-voltage mid-nickel, LMR, all-solid-state battery (ASSB), and sodium-ion battery (SIB) cathodes. It unveiled next-generation materials at major exhibitions this year and is in concrete discussions with select customers on mass production of solid-state battery cathodes. Its current primary focus is LFP. The company is pursuing commercialization of LFP cathodes at a level unprecedented in South Korea in the second half of this year, while developing proprietary iron phosphate (FP) technology and a precursor-free manufacturing process to build a supply chain with reduced dependence on China. The plan is to add LMR and solid-state cathodes going forward, transitioning to a structure that addresses everything from high-nickel to mid-to-low-priced and next-generation markets. L&F recently signed a mid-to-long-term LFP cathode supply contract with Samsung SDI worth 1.6067 trillion won (approximately $1.2 billion), followed by a 160 billion won (approximately $119.0 million) supply deal with SK On. artigo.texto: China's First 100MW-Class Compressed CO₂ Energy Storage Project Connects to Grid — A Giant "Power Bank" Rises in the Gobi Desert On October 2, China's first 100MW-class compressed carbon dioxide energy storage project — the China Huadian Xinjiang Mulei compressed CO₂ energy storage project — successfully connected to the grid. The project's commissioning opens a brand-new pathway for large-capacity compressed CO₂ energy storage in the direction of green, zero-carbon, high-efficiency, and cost-effective operation, marking a major breakthrough in China's gas-liquid phase-change energy storage key technologies and engineering integration applications. The project is located on the Gobi Desert in Mulei Kazakh Autonomous County, Xinjiang, covering an area of over 840 mu (approximately 138 acres), with a storage capacity of 100 MW/1,000 MWh. The entire system uses carbon dioxide as a closed-loop working medium, achieving gas-liquid interconversion and two-phase coordination without dependence on geological conditions. It operates at relatively low pressure and temperature levels, offering high reliability and controllable costs. Core technologies and key equipment are fully developed and manufactured in China. According to CCTV News, the project can store 290 million kWh of electricity during grid off-peak periods each year and release 180 million kWh of clean green power during peak periods, capable of continuous power generation for more than 6 hours with minute-level response times. Once fully operational, the project will generate approximately 200 million kWh annually, saving 50,000 tonnes of standard coal and reducing carbon dioxide emissions by roughly 170,000 tonnes per year. Ma Guojiang, head of the China Huadian Mulei compressed CO₂ energy storage project, said that compressed carbon dioxide offers higher energy density, along with multiple advantages including high efficiency, low cost, high safety, and zero pollution. The project's design efficiency is currently the highest among CO₂ power generation units in China. Working Principle: Gas-Liquid Two-Phase Coordinated Storage The compressed CO₂ energy storage and power generation system primarily consists of a gas storage system, liquid storage system, compression system, thermal storage system, heat exchange system, and expansion power generation system. During the storage phase, the system uses surplus electricity from off-peak periods to drive electric motors, compressing CO₂ at ambient temperature and pressure through compressors. This process generates substantial heat, which the project first stores, before condensing the compressed CO₂ into liquid form for storage. Since liquid CO₂ has higher energy density, the system can store more energy. During the discharge phase, the liquid CO₂ is vaporized and expanded to drive generator units for power release, completing the full cycle of "compression — liquefaction — storage — vaporization — expansion — energy release — power generation." Project Configuration and Technological Breakthroughs The project is equipped with 5 gas storage chambers, 141 liquid storage units, and 97 thermal storage units. Compared with traditional storage methods such as pumped hydro, compressed CO₂ energy storage does not depend on specific geological conditions, offers greater siting flexibility, requires lower pressure and temperature ratings, and has competitively priced equipment manufacturing costs. The project was selected for the fourth batch of the National Energy Administration's first-of-its-kind major technical equipment list in the energy sector. As an important exploration direction for new energy storage technologies, compressed CO₂ energy storage holds strategic significance for building China's new power system and supporting carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals. Impact on the Power System Once connected to the grid, the project will significantly strengthen the grid's peak-shaving, valley-filling, and frequency/voltage regulation capabilities. Against the backdrop of a continuously rising share of renewable energy generation, large-scale long-duration storage facilities are crucial for smoothing the volatility of wind and solar output and enhancing power system flexibility and security. The commissioning of the Mulei project provides a new channel for local consumption and cross-time-period dispatch of Xinjiang's abundant wind and solar resources, helping to continuously expand green power supply. From an industry perspective, the engineering validation of compressed CO₂ energy storage technology offers a replicable technical solution for China's long-duration energy storage sector. Compared with electrochemical storage, this approach has differentiated advantages in safety, cycle life, and environmental friendliness, and is expected to see broader demonstration applications and commercial promotion during China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030). artigo.texto: China’s Gotion High-Tech has secured 6GWh of battery storage capacity in Saudi Arabia’s first utility-scale battery storage programme, accounting for around 75% of the total tender. Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) awarded the company three core sites of Al Muwayah, Haden and Al Kahafa, under the G1 project. Each site will provide 500MW/2GWh, giving the project a combined capacity of 2GW/8GWh and a value of around $1.16 billion. The award represents the first international large-scale deployment of Gotion Grid, the company’s utility-scale energy storage system. Gotion says the system has been engineered for extreme environmental conditions, with an operating range from -30°C to 55°C. Its thermal management system is designed for desert conditions and maintains full output during sandstorms, while reducing high-temperature degradation by 40% compared with conventional systems. The ESS has a stated design life of 25 years, compared with an industry average of 15–20 years. The company says this can avoid mid-life equipment replacement, an important consideration for build-own-operate contracts requiring more than 20 years of operation. The system also incorporates an AI-powered battery management system for intelligent dispatch, proactive safety warnings and lifecycle diagnostics. All three Gotion sites can be remotely operated and connected to Saudi Arabia’s 380kV backbone grid. The award adds to the company’s growing presence across the Middle East and North Africa, where it says its regional footprint is around 9GWh. This includes a 1.5GWh BESS in Egypt alongside a planned 3GWh local manufacturing base, and a 1.2GWh project in Morocco with ACWA Power. Globally, the company’s cumulative system-level storage projects exceed 10 GWh, including a 281MW/843MWh solar-storage project under construction in Australia that is expected to enter commercial operation in the first half of 2027. With G1 awarded and G2 underway, the Saudi programme could provide further opportunities as renewable deployment and grid stability requirements increase. Image: Gotion BESS. Credit: Gotion

artigo.texto: Iniciativas incluem incentivos fiscais e uso de energia renovável Nas eleições presidenciais brasileiras, candidatos bem posicionados nas pesquisas têm sido enfáticos sobre a necessidade de atrair a construção de data centers no país. Entre as estratégias discutidas estão incentivos fiscais, a fabricação local de componentes e a exploração do potencial da inteligência artificial. Um data center é uma instalação que armazena e processa informações, sendo os modelos de nuvem e de inteligência artificial os mais comuns. Com a crescente demanda por esses serviços, facilitar a construção dessas infraestruturas ganhou destaque nos planos de governo dos candidatos. ✨ O Brasil possui 218 data centers, ocupando a 12ª posição no ranking mundial, enquanto os EUA contam com mais de 4.700 centros. Candidatos indicam que a atração de data centers é fundamental para o avanço tecnológico e econômico do Brasil, especialmente em comparação com países como os Estados Unidos, onde mais de 64% da população rejeita a expansão desses complexos, temendo os impactos ambientais e sociais. Presidentes e candidatos como Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro e Ronaldo Caiado propõem diferentes abordagens para incentivar a construção de data centers, com foco em benefícios econômicos, sociais e no uso de fontes de energia renováveis. Enquanto isso, protestos contra a expansão do setor nos EUA ressaltam a preocupação com o consumo de energia e água. Daniel Cordeiro, professor da USP, alerta que o Brasil ainda pode evitar os problemas enfrentados por outros países, desde que as políticas de atração sejam bem planejadas e régidas por regulamentações que protejam o meio ambiente e a sociedade. artigo.texto: Elk Grove Village Mayor Craig B. Johnson’s recent defense of data centers presents a fundamentally flawed economic development narrative (“When judging data center incentives, don’t ignore the revenue,” Sept. 30). While he touts short-term revenue, his ledger ignores the long-term, structural costs these facilities impose on local communities. First, using job creation to justify data center subsidies is a sleight of hand. While $1.2 billion in construction permits is impressive, they’re short-term bumps in revenue. This masks the reality that data centers are essentially ghost towns once operational. They consume prime industrial real estate but employ only a small number of permanent staff members, meaning taxpayers are often subsidizing millions of dollars per permanent job. Furthermore, major tech companies rely on specialized, traveling construction crews. The economic multiplier effect largely leaves town when the concrete dries. Second, the mayor’s claim that Class 6B incentives don’t harm homeowners ignores the basic math of Illinois property taxes. When a data center’s assessed value is artificially slashed, the local tax levy doesn’t shrink. The burden simply shifts onto everyone else, driving up residential tax bills for 12 to 24 years. This is compounded when tax increment financing districts are used, such as the one Elk Grove Village created for the Vulcan Construction Materials site in 2022. While the mayor suggests schools stand to benefit, it should be noted TIFs divert new tax revenue to pay for project costs for up to 23 years, meaning schools and municipal services wait decades for the promised windfall. Worse, once operational, these operators frequently deploy aggressive legal teams to appeal their property assessments year after year, forcing municipalities to spend taxpayer dollars defending their own revenue. Finally, while data centers don’t add students to classrooms, they place enormous, invisible strains on our infrastructure. Their construction increases wear and tear on local roads from construction vehicles. Once completed, they are massive consumers of municipal water for cooling and place unprecedented demands on the electrical grid. These upgrades are eventually paid for by everyday ratepayers. Subsidizing heavily automated server farms that hollow out industrial parks, generate negligible employment and strain our grid is not the “pro-growth” policy our region needs. — Donald Guisinger, Strong Towns Oak Forest Will data centers pay fair share? Elk Grove Village Mayor Craig B. Johnson in his op-ed completely ignores the higher cost of water and electricity that his constituents will face subsidizing these monstrosities. Will he demand that data centers pay their fair share for the high volume of water and electricity they use? Or is it too late? — Ken Perez, Wood Dale Department of Justice’s credibility I am hopeful that with the recent focus on the “Broadway Six,” in particular due to the reporting of Tribune reporter Jason Meisner, the public will begin to understand that when prosecutors go unchecked, victims face extreme consequences for which they have very little redress. In recent years, the credibility of the U.S. Department of Justice has fallen to all-time depths as it has been weaponized against those with whom it disagrees, both political and nonpolitical, taking up positions not supported by the facts or even the law. This is on full display in Chicago. U.S. District Judge April Perry is being asked to consider disciplinary action against the U.S. attorney’s office for alleged misconduct in the grand jury investigation and prosecution of the “Broadview Six.” No justice system can function effectively if there are components within it that disregard the rules and mechanisms of checks and balance. The public relies upon this system to keep prosecutors in line, to punish misconduct and to send a message that misconduct cannot be tolerated. Misconduct is anathema to justice. — Michael Segal, U.S. National Title Services, Chicago Celebrate parking meter deal? No. Regarding Chicago’s parking meter deal, what a demonstration of ineptness and buffoonery — this is the 2026 edition of the 2008 disaster. As a Chicago resident and motorist, I have one simple question: Will it cost me less to park? Nothing I’ve read about this deal — a transfer fee, percentages of a future sale and net income, a “city wallet” program and 25- to 50-cent-per-hour surcharges for non-Chicagoans — suggests that it will benefit the great majority of drivers in Chicago. And as for the City Council’s self-congratulation over the deal: same-o, same-o. A final question: Where’s Mayor Brandon Johnson? — John Mjoseth, Chicago I support the arts in the city Thank you for the editorial regarding suburbanite parking in Chicago ( “Chicago may charge suburbanites more to park. How neighborly,” Oct. 1). I am a suburbanite who supports the Joffrey Ballet, the Chicago Architectural Center and the Art Institute with subscriptions to their events. I do attempt to take public transportation when I can, but that is not always feasible, since as the editorial mentions, timing for public transportation is sparse on the weekends. For example, a friend and I have Joffrey season tickets for its Sunday matinees, but trying to coordinate Metra and “L” train times with that is difficult. Although driving into town is stressful, we brave it by going down early to enjoy a great lunch at Italian Village before the show. And yes, we look for cheap parking because we’re already supporting businesses and cultural events. Also, because we are both in our 70s, we cannot park too far from the venue just to find an extremely cheap parking lot; we would then need a taxi to get to the Lyric Opera House. In short, considering our generous monetary contributions to the city of Chicago, asking us to pay more for parking really takes the cake! — Dianne Casuto, Lake Forest Naperville’s welcoming vibe Thank you for say

artigo.texto: Evanston Councilmember Krissie Harris is proposing a formal one-year moratorium on data centers across the city following vocal backlash to a proposal in her Second Ward, telling the RoundTable she wants to complete “due diligence” to understand data centers’ potential impacts before any are approved. Harris’ plan calls for a one-year halt on any city-level zoning approvals and incentives for data centers “pending infrastructure and grid audits,” and will go to the council’s Referrals Committee on Monday, Oct. 12. The measure is co-sponsored by Councilmembers Clare Kelly (1st Ward), Bobby Burns (5th), Parielle Davis (7th) and Matt Rodgers (8th), immediately giving it majority support from the nine-member council. Property owner Reed Beidler submitted a zoning analysis application last month to establish a “computer processing center” at 1265 Hartrey Ave. in the Second Ward. Beidler proposes filling about 20,000 square feet of space in the former factory building and envisions a large organization renting out most of the data center’s processing power alongside other businesses with smaller needs. Like other data center projects around the country, the Evanston proposal drew intense backlash from residents and local organizations, including at Second Ward and City Council meetings last month. Harris said in a phone interview Sunday she hasn’t met with Beidler about his proposal, but that she felt the city could be “bombarded with requests” in the near future and feels an official pause is warranted. “I don’t want it to be one of those [situations] like we say yes because it’s small, looks like it’s … not a big deal, and then it just balloons into this thing that we cannot control,” Harris said. “I want to make sure … we’ve investigated that thoroughly.” While Beidler argued the data center should be approved as a permitted use under existing zoning, city staff disagreed and found it doesn’t fit under any use already listed in the city code, meaning a zoning amendment is necessary for approval. City Manager Luke Stowe called this a “de facto moratorium” during the last council meeting and invited council direction to “pursue an official moratorium,” which Harris is now taking up. previous coverage Harris said she’s particularly concerned about the center’s potential impact on water and power use, sharing that she has a stake in the outcome since she lives just a few blocks away. “If I get more information and we, as a council, feel good about it, we can change that moratorium,” Harris said. “But it gives us, at least, time to just breathe and figure it out.” She also referenced potential state legislation that could impact projects in Evanston and elsewhere. The Illinois General Assembly failed to pass a comprehensive data center bill during its spring session, and Gov. JB Pritzker is pushing hard for lawmakers to take action during the veto session, which will run from Nov. 17 to 19 and Dec. 1 to 3. Asked if the four councilmembers co-sponsoring her proposal feel the same as her, Harris said some are less sure a moratorium is needed but are trusting her judgment, especially since the current proposal is in her ward. “Some people are kind of like, ‘Oh, I don’t know, but I’ll follow your lead on this,’ and so I’m appreciative of my team members saying OK,” Harris said. “I’ve got to be accountable for this, and if it’s going somewhere else [in another ward], I got to trust if somebody says, ‘I need more time to really make a good decision.'” The moratorium will need to be approved by City Council before it can officially take effect. Depending on how much time staff need to develop the proposal into full legislation, it could advance as soon as the council’s next meeting on Oct. 12 or at a future meeting in the coming months. As of Oct. 1, staff are still waiting for Beidler to submit additional information about his proposal before directing him to propose a zoning amendment.

artigo.texto: There's A Big Problem With Building Data Centers Underground Data centers have become the necessary evil we all have to deal with for the sake of rapid AI advancements. However, they're problematic, and most regular people are very much against them for obvious reasons. Data centers are so loud that their noise may carry for a mile, and they may also drive up local utility costs, take up precious land, and waste water reserves. So, why not put them underground? That would theoretically solve most of these issues. If only it were that easy. Though the UAE has considered fortifying its own data centers with guns and burying some underground, that's basically a means-to-an-end solution due to the dangers of Iranian attacks. In normal circumstances, the project would just end up costing more, as you'd need to create a strong shell that can take the weight of all the soil above. That's not even accounting for drilling, insulation, and waterproofing. Then, these facilities wouldn't be easy to scale up because it would require additional blasting or drilling, meaning companies are unlikely to put down the cash for something that will make people happy at an additional cost and loss of scalability. The biggest challenge, though? Maintaining solid air quality. When you're underground, complications with the air can add up quickly. As such, the data center would require some expensive systems to get the same environment that's practically a given above ground, so add the expensive humidity control and ventilation system to an already hefty bill. In the end, it's all much more feasible than making orbital data centers, but far too tricky for companies to seriously consider it. In which case can building underground work? The good thing about underground data centers, theoretically at least, is they'd save operators money on cooling because there's no sunlight. They could also resort to geothermal energy, so it wouldn't waste as much electricity. It truly seems like a magic bullet when you lay it all out — if only the construction costs weren't so high. Well, new AI data centers can be built inside existing underground structures, which automatically solves the brunt of the issues, and we have real-world examples that attest to how well it can work. For instance, there are a few data centers operating out of abandoned mines in the U.S., which makes them super secure by design. The best part is, they're not expensive to build and maintain. Plus, the temperature in the mines, and more importantly, the humidity, are sometimes bordering on perfection. Unfortunately, there aren't that many mines that are both close to a power source and already have the necessary connections, so it's not as if companies can move to the mines in droves, Fallout style. In a perfect world, profits would be secondary to preservation of our natural resources. Ultimately, the reason why there isn't a huge push to find better solutions is that it's simply more expensive than just taking a piece of land and constructing a data center. Plus, the alternatives we have so far are all difficult to pull off. Data centers aren't built in Antarctica because it's too remote and doesn't have a power grid, despite the naturally cool air making it seem like a perfect solution for the AI boom. Until we figure something out, we'll all probably have to contend with effects of new facilities popping up, sadly.

artigo.texto: AI infrastructure is reshaping more than the servers inside data center racks. As GPU-intensive workloads push rack densities higher, Eaton, NVIDIA, Google, Microsoft and others are advancing direct-current power architectures designed to deliver more power with fewer conversion stages and less physical infrastructure. For solution providers, integrators and infrastructure partners, that shift could broaden the scope of AI infrastructure projects. Moving from traditional AC designs toward rack-level 48/50V DC and, eventually, 800 VDC affects not only power distribution but also backup systems, cooling, rack design and serviceability â forcing partners to think about those systems as an interconnected architecture rather than separate infrastructure purchases Why AI is pushing data centers toward DC power The broader demand curve explains why power architecture is receiving so much attention. The International Energy Agency projects global data center electricity consumption will roughly double from 485 TWh in 2025 to approximately 950 TWh in 2030, with consumption from AI-focused data centers growing even faster. Inside the facility, higher density creates another challenge: current. Delivering more power at lower voltages requires greater current, which can mean larger conductors, greater losses, and more heat. Higher-voltage DC distribution can reduce current while eliminating some power-conversion stages between the utility feed and IT equipment. 48V, 50V and 800 VDC architectures take shape The transition is already visible at the rack level. Open Compute Projectâs Open Rack V3 ecosystem uses 48V DC busbar architectures, while Eatonâs upcoming 50V DC system is designed for both conventional 19-inch racks and 21-inch ORV3 racks, with power ratings ranging from 33 kW to 132 kW per rack. Eaton specifically identifies system integrator builds, enterprise and colocation environments, AI/HPC deployments and OCP migration projects among its intended applications. The next step could be significantly larger. NVIDIA, Google and Microsoft are collaborating through OCP to establish 800 VDC as an open architecture for next-generation AI data centers. NVIDIA says moving from todayâs lower-voltage rack architectures toward 800 VDC reduces current, copper requirements and cable bulk while allowing fewer power-conversion stages. More than 80 equipment and infrastructure companies are participating in the ecosystem. Eaton is among them and is developing 800 VDC infrastructure alongside its current ORV3 and 50V DC offerings. DC power creates a broader infrastructure role for partners That does not mean every enterprise data center is about to switch to 800 VDC. In fact, the emerging market is better understood as a continuum. Existing facilities can continue operating AC infrastructure while introducing DC closer to high-density compute. Rack-level 48/50V systems offer another path, while 800 VDC is being positioned for future AI environments with substantially greater density. NVIDIAâs own roadmap explicitly includes hybrid architectures designed to introduce 800 VDC power racks into facilities with existing AC infrastructure. For the channel, architectural knowledge is increasingly important. Partners accustomed to selling servers, UPS systems, racks and power distribution as relatively discrete infrastructure categories may need to approach AI projects more holistically. Power density affects distribution, backup requirements, cooling, physical rack design and serviceability, meaning infrastructure decisions become interconnected earlier in the design process. Eaton similarly argues that power and cooling need to be planned together as AI densities rise. The opportunity, then, isnât simply selling a different power product. It is helping customers determine when existing AC infrastructure remains sufficient, when rack-level DC makes sense, how to design hybrid environments, and when future workloads justify a more fundamental architectural shift. Hyperscalers may be setting the direction today. Channel partners should be watching closely for when their customers begin following it.

The big advantage that the U.S. has over most nations is its access to great wealth and resources, which increases its chances of producing the most sophisticated energy projects. As of late, Lightstar expressed that it is doubling down on Illinois, expanding its community solar and battery-storage footprint across the state. Lightstar continues to advance the United States solar energy sector Lightstar’s approach to project execution means that it is in a position where it is likely to always be in the running to be appointed to spearhead massive projects. Its reputation and previous success also mean that it is in a good position to be selected by countries other than the U.S.A., where it is based. The company’s current commitment is to building sustainable, high-value assets that support local economies and farming legacies for decades to come. Lightstar is doubling down on Illinois, expanding its community solar and battery-storage A recent press release from Lightstar Renewables, a national leader in community solar generation, announced that it is set to continue the expansion of its active Illinois portfolio across three service lines: community solar, agrivoltaic solar, and battery energy storage systems (BESS). Lightstar is known for contributing to Illinois not just in terms of energy facilities but also toward the economic progression of the state. The company develops these projects on private land throughout Illinois, guiding landowners through an origination-to-cooperation process that preserves land ownership, delivers fixed long-term lease income, and keeps land in productive use. Lightstar’s permitted, market-ready project pipeline offers an answer for landowners, municipalities, and clean energy partners looking for companies that develop community solar and battery energy storage in Illinois. Interestingly, Illinois has become one of the most active clean energy markets in the Midwest, driven by the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) and its target of 100% clean energy by 2050. Supportive programs continue to quicken deployment: the Illinois Shines Adjustable Block Program opens its 2026-2027 cycle on June 1, 2026, and the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA) expands community solar while permitting co-location of projects up to 10 MW on a single parcel or adjacent properties. A general overview of Illinois’ clean energy landscape as of 2026 With the year now coming to an end, industry experts are expecting it to be a record-breaking year for Illinois, considering the number of projects that have materialized. In 2026, Illinois enacted statewide energy storage legislation establishing new storage projects, emphasizing demand for reliable, grid-responsive infrastructure. Lightstar actively monitors these programs and evaluates every Illinois project for eligibility. This track record has positioned the company as one of the state’s most determined and experienced community solar and battery storage developers. Gaining an insight into the future of community solar and battery storage There has been a common theme of community and battery storage projects leading the charge in the solar sector in recent years. Kyle McAdam, Senior Development Manager at Lightstar, stated the following: “We believe that clean energy development must work hand-in-hand with the local community. By protecting the land, engaging with incredible students right here in Fulton County, and now investing directly in the VIT athletic field, we ensure this project leaves a positive, lasting mark on the region for decades to come.” Lightstar is well respected as a trailblazing community solar developer that was founded on the principles of advanced design and strategic project development. As a proud American company, Lightstar is a trusted partner for landowners, focusing on community solar and agrivoltaics projects that preserve agricultural land while generating energy. artigo.texto: The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said the measures establish rules covering the development, registration and monitoring of voluntary forest carbon projects and lay the groundwork for a credible domestic carbon market. Environment Assistant Secretary for Integrated Management System and Information Systems Daniel Darius Nicer presented the policies at a high-level roundtable on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. Market roadmap The first policy adopts the Philippines’ Readiness in the Voluntary Forest Carbon Market Roadmap for 2026 to 2030. The roadmap sets the national direction for policy development, measurement, reporting and verification systems, data management and registry readiness—all considered important in determining whether carbon credits can be reliably measured and tracked. “To date, the Philippines, through its Department of Environment and Natural Resources, issued two major policy instruments that establish the foundations of a credible forest carbon market directly addressing private sector expectations for clear rules, credible safeguards, and transparent project pathways,” Nicer said. He spoke during the “Shaping High-Integrity Carbon Markets” session convened by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development during Climate Week NYC. Project safeguards The second policy establishes national guidelines for the creation, registration and monitoring of voluntary forest carbon credit projects. The rules require environmental safeguards, compliance with Free, Prior and Informed Consent and benefit-sharing with communities. They also mandate transparent project registration, which the DENR said would help reduce reputational and delivery risks for carbon credit buyers. “For the Philippines, carbon markets—both voluntary and compliance pathways—are central to our strategy for accelerating mitigation and unlocking climate finance,” Nicer said. “But for markets to function, the private sector needs clarity, predictability, and confidence that the credits they purchase are real, additional, and backed by strong governance.” Carbon framework The forest policies form part of wider government efforts to develop the country's carbon market infrastructure. Nicer cited Department of Energy guidelines for renewable energy projects, the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework and the rollout of the Philippine National Carbon Registry. The registry is intended to provide accounting and traceability of carbon credits and prevent double counting. Nicer said Philippine policies are also being aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement through bilateral arrangements, including an implementation agreement with Singapore and the Joint Crediting Mechanism with Japan. Looking ahead to the COP31 climate summit, he called for stronger international guidance on market infrastructure and supply-side integrity for forest and blue carbon ecosystems. “High-integrity markets should not only accelerate global ambition, but also deliver real, measurable mitigation outcomes that directly benefit and reach the communities, ecosystems, and sectors that need them most,” Nicer said. — Ed: Corrie S. Narisma

artigo.texto: Origin plans a 500 MW, 4,942 MWh battery at Eraring Origin proposes adding a 500 MW storage system at the Eraring power station site. The project, which still has to clear the approval stages, would target commercial operations between early and mid-2031. Origin is proposing Eraring BESS North, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with a discharge capacity of 500 megawatts (MW) and an accessible energy storage capacity of approximately 4,942 megawatt hours (MWh). The project would require up to 22 hectares on Origin-owned land at the Eraring power station site in New South Wales. It is located in the suburb of Eraring, within the Lake Macquarie local government area. A combined facility of about 1,200 MW The project would operate alongside the existing Eraring BESS, part of Origin's generation portfolio. The existing project received State Significant Development consent SSD-15950052 on 10 May 2022. According to the project document, the two facilities together would provide a combined maximum registered active power capacity of around 1,200 MW and an accessible storage capacity of approximately 8,600 MWh, subject to detailed design. The storage sector is drawing other projects from Europe to Asia. ML System secured two energy storage contracts in Poland worth â¬4.1 million, while Vena Energy won a 46.8 MW battery storage contract in Japan. In power transmission, Iberdrola expanded its alliance with GIC in Brazil. Company Origin Energy: company profile ORG A regulatory pathway ahead Origin expects the project to qualify as a State Significant Development (SSD) under Section 2.6(1) of the 2021 Planning Systems state environmental planning policy. It would be subject to Part 4, Division 4.7, Section 4.36 of the 1979 Environmental Planning and Assessment Act, as an electricity generating works development whose estimated cost exceeds the set thresholds. An environmental impact statement will have to be prepared in line with the Secretary's Environmental Assessment Requirements. The existing BESS received a "not controlled action if undertaken in a particular manner" decision on 19 July 2021 under the federal Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 [2021/8956]. The new project includes approximately 11 hectares of vegetation clearance outside the previously assessed disturbance area. Origin says it reviewed alternative locations and consulted key stakeholders and the community to limit impacts. Components and timeline The project covers construction, operation, decommissioning and rehabilitation as far as reasonably practicable. It would include transmission works to connect the BESS to TransGrid's switching station, along with an extension of the existing substation. It also provides for extended water supply infrastructure, new electricity buildings, internal access roads and new operation and maintenance compounds. Construction is expected to start in 2028 and last about 2.5 years, with commercial operations anticipated in early to mid-2031, subject to approvals. Operations would run for up to 25 years, with a possible extension. Works would be staged, including site establishment, then earthworks for the battery compound and transformer yard, and finally civil and foundation works. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 % Origin presents the project as a response to the National Electricity Market's shift from coal toward variable renewables, supported by dispatchable storage capacity. artigo.texto: O setor elétrico brasileiro vive um momento de transformação acelerada com a crescente demanda por infraestrutura digital de alto desempenho. A aprovação do regime de incentivos fiscais (Redata) aqueceu o mercado, mas acendeu um alerta sobre a capacidade da rede em suportar a carga exigida pelos novos centros de processamento de dados. Segundo a redação do Imprensa 24h, o desafio atual não é a falta de geração, mas sim a eficiência no escoamento dessa energia para os polos de consumo. Resumo da Notícia - Investimento previsto de R$ 120 bilhões em linhas de transmissão até 2035. - Projetos de data centers somam 10 GW em contratos e pedidos firmes de conexão. - Brasil desperdiçou 33 milhões de MWh em 2025 por falta de malha para escoar energia. - Descompasso temporal: obras de transmissão levam 7 anos, enquanto data centers ficam prontos em 18 meses. Para quem acompanha as notícias de Sergipe, o estado se posiciona estrategicamente nesse cenário, dada sua relevância na matriz energética nacional. A integração de fontes renováveis, especialmente as vindas do Nordeste, depende diretamente da robustez do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). As informações de Aracaju reforçam que a estabilidade elétrica é o principal atrativo para indústrias que buscam se instalar na região, transformando a infraestrutura em um motor de desenvolvimento local. O papel estratégico da transmissão no cenário nacional A malha de transmissão é o elemento que conecta a abundância de energia renovável produzida no Nordeste aos grandes centros industriais e tecnológicos do Sudeste e Sul. Sem essa conexão, o potencial de geração solar e eólica acaba subutilizado. Em 2025, o fenômeno conhecido como curtailment — a limitação da geração por falta de espaço na rede — resultou no corte de 33 milhões de MWh, volume comparável ao consumo anual de todo o estado do Rio Grande do Sul. A expansão da rede é, portanto, a solução para evitar esse desperdício e garantir que a energia limpa chegue aos novos polos de tecnologia. O mercado de data centers, que exige alta confiabilidade e grandes volumes de carga, monitora de perto os leilões de transmissão. Para mais detalhes sobre como esses movimentos impactam a economia regional, acompanhe no portal Imprensa 24h. Descompasso entre demanda tecnológica e obras de infraestrutura Um dos pontos críticos identificados pelo setor é a diferença de ritmo entre a construção de um data center e a entrega de uma linha de transmissão. Enquanto uma unidade de processamento de dados pode ser erguida em cerca de um ano e meio, o ciclo completo de uma obra de transmissão — que envolve planejamento, licenciamento ambiental pelo Ibama e construção — leva, em média, sete anos. Esse intervalo exige uma coordenação fina entre órgãos como a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) e investidores privados. A sinalização antecipada da demanda é fundamental para que os traçados das linhas sejam definidos antes que a necessidade se torne uma urgência crítica, garantindo que o crescimento tecnológico não seja freado por gargalos logísticos de energia. Planejamento decenal e aportes bilionários na rede O governo federal, por meio do Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2035), já traçou a rota para mitigar esses riscos. A previsão é de que sejam investidos aproximadamente R$ 120 bilhões na próxima década. Esse montante será destinado à construção de 30 mil quilômetros de novas linhas e ao acréscimo de 82 mil MVA em capacidade de subestações em todo o território nacional. Onde há linha de transmissão, há crescimento econômico e geração de empregos. A consolidação dessa infraestrutura permitirá que o Brasil não apenas atenda sua demanda interna, mas se torne um hub global para serviços de inteligência artificial e armazenamento de dados em nuvem. Fique por dentro das últimas notícias em Sergipe e no Brasil acessando nossa página inicial. Mantenha-se atualizado com as principais movimentações do setor de energia e tecnologia. Continue bem informado navegando pelas editorias do Imprensa 24h, o seu portal de referência para notícias de Sergipe e do mundo.

artigo.texto: Os candidatos à Presidência incluem em seus planos de governo incentivos para a instalação de data centers no país, segundo o g1. A aposta no setor ocorre em meio ao avanço da inteligência artificial e ao crescimento da resistência a esses empreendimentos nos Estados Unidos. Os americanos reúnem mais de 4.700 unidades do tipo, conforme dados de setembro do Data Center Map, contra 218 no Brasil, que aparece em 12º lugar no ranking. A Brasscom, associação de empresas de tecnologia, informa que o Brasil fechou 2025 com déficit de US$ 8 bilhões na conta de Serviços de Computação e Informação — parte relevante do processamento de dados fica, portanto, no exterior. Resistência nos EUA A matriz elétrica americana é sustentada sobretudo por combustíveis fósseis, como petróleo e gás, enquanto a brasileira depende em larga escala de hidrelétricas e outras renováveis. Nos dois casos, porém, o alto consumo de energia e água dessas estruturas é alvo de críticas: cidades americanas registraram protestos e autoridades brasileiras já questionaram os impactos dos projetos. Levantamento Reuters/Ipsos apontou que 64% dos americanos discordam da avaliação de que a construção acelerada de data centers será benéfica ao país, e 57% não querem os complexos perto de casa. Mesmo assim, o presidente Donald Trump defendeu os empreendimentos ao receber executivos do setor na terça-feira (29). Estavam presentes Elon Musk (xAI), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Sundar Pichai (Google) e Jensen Huang (Nvidia); as companhias assumiram o compromisso de ampliar a segurança de seus sistemas de inteligência artificial. Disputa no Brasil O Redata, regime sancionado por Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva em setembro, elimina tributos de importação de equipamentos usados pelos data centers. Para obter o benefício, as empresas teriam de usar fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, consumir no máximo 50 mililitros de água por quilowatt-hora, destinar 10% da capacidade ao mercado interno e aplicar 2% do valor dos equipamentos em pesquisa no país. Lula (PT) defende apoio a companhias nacionais de IA e o desenvolvimento de modelos de linguagem brasileiros. Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) propõe reduzir tributos sobre a energia e vincular a demanda do setor à extração de minerais críticos. Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) insere os data centers em uma cadeia de inovação ligada a semicondutores; Renan Santos (Missão) quer fazer do Brasil o maior exportador de processamento de dados para IA; e Romeu Zema (Novo) fala em ambiente regulatório estável. Os demais candidatos não tratam do assunto nos planos. Para Daniel Cordeiro, professor da USP, o país precisa ampliar sua capacidade computacional, mas deve se precaver contra problemas já observados no exterior. Thais Ortega, da consultoria Reglab, afirma que a atração dessas instalações é ponto de convergência entre os candidatos, embora os modelos propostos variem, e lembra que partes do Redata seguem pendentes de regulamentação — entre elas, a definição do que seria considerado baixo carbono, ponto que poderia liberar o uso de gás natural. Marina Garrote, diretora de operações da Reglab, vê no Redata um instrumento para o Brasil evitar parte dos desafios americanos, já que uma expansão baseada em fontes eólicas e solares teria custo social diferente. Segundo ela, a disputa eleitoral deixou de ser sobre a instalação dos data centers e passou a girar em torno das regras que vão regê-los.

artigo.texto: Kota Kinabalu: Sabah currently has two ongoing carbon projects, namely Innoprise-Face Foundation Rainforest Rehabilitation Project (Infapro), which dates back to 1992, and the Kuamut Rainforest Conservation Project with Permian, which uses NBS. The State was not merely looking at a second project, but potentially a third and subsequent projects, said Sabah Forestry Department (SFD) Forest Sector Planning Division Head Rosila Anthony. The Forest Enactment 1968 was amended by the State Assembly in 2025 to introduce a regulatory framework for forest cover activities in Sabah. She said Section 28D of the Forest Enactment 1968, which came into effect on May 15, 2025, regulated forest cover activities in Sabah through a licensing and enforcement framework. It applied to forest cover activities carried out within forest reserves and other forest areas prescribed under the Forest Enactment, with such activities only permitted under a licence issued pursuant to Section 28D and subject to prescribed conditions. Meanwhile, the Sabah Climate Change and Carbon Governance Enactment 2025 established the broader statewide framework for climate governance, carbon rights administration, carbon project registration and carbon market oversight. It applies to carbon rights, carbon projects, carbon credits and carbon-related activities throughout Sabah, with carbon projects required to comply with registration, permitting and governance requirements under the Enactment. Rosila said the Forest Enactment regulated the conduct of forest cover activities within forest areas through a licensing regime administered by the Forestry Authority, while the Sabah Climate Change and Carbon Governance Enactment 2025 provided the broader governance framework for carbon rights, carbon projects, registry administration and climate governance. “Compliance with both frameworks may be required depending on the nature, location and scope of the proposed carbon project,” she said. She said the integrated approach ensured that forest carbon projects were aligned with Sabah’s broader climate governance and carbon market infrastructure. Rosila said NBS provided significant co-benefits extending beyond climate change mitigation. From a climate perspective, SFM, mangrove conservation, peatland ecosystem restoration and forest carbon initiatives enhanced carbon sequestration, reduced greenhouse gas emissions and strengthened ecosystem resilience. The interventions also improved the capacity of communities and ecosystems to adapt to climate-related risks such as flooding, drought, coastal erosion and extreme weather events. From a socio-economic perspective, she said NBS created opportunities for green economic growth by generating employment, supporting sustainable livelihoods, enhancing ecotourism potential, strengthening community participation and attracting climate and conservation financing. Sabah’s NBS agenda also aligned closely with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and reflected the principles outlined in the IUCN Global Standards for Nature-Based Solutions, which emphasise effective governance, biodiversity, adaptive management, stakeholder engagement and long-term sustainability.
