artigo.texto: As the AI boom becomes a major part of political debate, the public backlash against data centers in the U.S. is spreading to Europe and Asia — raising risks for investors. Across the Atlantic, negative sentiment is growing in Europe, which has more at stake due to its densely populated countries and higher electricity prices, experts told CNBC. Similar tensions are emerging in South Korea, with growing opposition to data centers near residential areas and proposals for tighter local restrictions, even as the national government pushes to accelerate development. Public opposition has already impacted around $42 billion of data center investments in Europe, in account delays and cancellations, according to research from STL Partners. That compares to around $77 billion in the U.S. The pushback could be the "straw that breaks the camel's back," Olivier Darmouni, associate professor at HEC Paris who specializes in the energy transition, told CNBC. Data center opposition is growing in Europe More than 70 data center projects in Europe were rejected or restricted between January and April — more than in all of 2025, according to the European Data Center Monitor. It found that pushback had snowballed from local town halls to courts, regulators and parliaments. Scotland has paused planning approvals for new hyperscale data centers after campaigners called on the government to avoid the "cautionary tale" of Ireland, where overwhelming power demand led to a moratorium. Constraints have been rising in the Nordics, where investors were drawn to large tracts of land and renewable energy. After a surge in power applications, Denmark passed an emergency law that could see data centers at the back of the queue for grid power applications. Spain also proposed new data center rules this summer, requiring data centers to source 80% of their electricity from renewables. Projects in the U.K. have stalled after pushback from locals. Much of the concern centers around water usage, power consumption, electricity prices, and the sheer amount of space that some centers require. There is also little agreement on how many permanent jobs the sector creates, and no precedent for projecting a center's economic value per megawatt. "The gains of AI are very diffused," Darmouni told CNBC. "There's definitely been more understanding of the scale of the potential AI build-out and its geographical spread, and perhaps ... more information about how much bigger these are, and that they're a little bit more like giant ghost warehouses that consume a lot of resources and can hurt local communities in some ways." Europe's denser population, and the fact that many data center operators are U.S. companies, might mean that the backlash hits harder, the professor added. What's happening in Asia South Korea, home to tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, sits at the heart of the AI supply chain. In June, its government named AI data centers as one of three major investment projects, alongside semiconductors and physical AI. But its push to build the infrastructure needed is running into resistance at the local level. In the Geumcheon district of southwestern Seoul, residents have called for authorities to revoke the building permit and halt construction of a data center near their homes, according to the local government. In July, officials announced plans to require consent from a majority of residents living within 200 meters of proposed data center sites and to introduce a three-stage system for reviewing projects and mediating disputes. Residents have also gathered outside the local government office on weekday mornings for months to protest against the project. The demonstrations had continued for 172 days as of mid-August, according to local media. In Gwacheon, a city just south of Seoul, a local council member proposed an ordinance aimed at protecting nearby residents from risks associated with data centers operating around the clock, including potential fires involving backup batteries. Should investors be worried about the backlash? Despite the pusback, the AI boom shows little sign of slowing down. But a community's ability "to derail a $10 billion [data center] plan is quite powerful," said Asya Walters, managing director at Alvarez & Marsal. She told CNBC the business-friendly environment in the U.S. has historically made it easier to overcome pushback. But in Europe and Asia, there's some "hot and coldness" at the country level about where demand is going, Walters said. The "push and pull" between favorable conditions for data centers and more restrictive regulation can be challenging for investment. Public backlash can also end up raising costs for operators, because even if they pull out of a project before construction starts, money will likely have already been spent. Though most capex expenditure happens after the permits are in place, operators spend a lot to reach that point, "so there is some loss that could happen there if they never get the permits," Walters said. We used to be a completely unknown part of the economy. We were just a black box. Now we are one of the fundamental layers driving the economy.Dominic WardVerne CEO "Digital infrastructure is becoming more visible and it's understandable that communities want to understand what's being built near them, why it's needed and how local impacts are being managed," said Eulalia Flo, vice president of growth and emerging markets, EMEA at Equinix, one of the biggest data center operators in Europe. "We don't see this as a structural constraint on growth, but the policy environment is genuinely tightening in some markets," said Flo. But the AI buildout has meant "a misunderstanding of the industry in a very broad sense," according to Dominic Ward, CEO of data center operator Verne. artigo.texto: Carmakers, including Hyundai Motor, are pouring their efforts into developing Solid-state Battery. A Solid-state Battery replaces the liquid electrolyte (a substance that conducts electricity) in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a nonflammable solid, reducing fire risk, and can extend driving range with higher energy density, earning it the nickname "dream battery." According to the auto industry on the 4th, Manfred Harrer, head of R&D (president) at Hyundai Motor Group, told reporters at the HMG Tech Talent Forum 2026, held in San Jose, California, for two days starting on the 17th of last month (local time), that he would continue investing in the development of Solid-state Battery. Harrer said, "We must take part in the race to develop Solid-state Battery," and "We will continue investing to secure leadership in this technology, which represents the biggest game-changer in the car industry." Hyundai Motor has recently been pursuing a "battery internalization strategy," under which it develops battery cell specifications and architecture in-house while outsourcing mass production to external manufacturers. In particular, if it succeeds in developing Solid-state Battery, considered a next-generation cell, ahead of battery makers, it could gain the upper hand in price negotiations and is expected to significantly increase electric vehicle sales. A single charge of a lithium-ion battery provides a driving range of about 500–600 km. Because this battery fills the space between the cathode and anode with a liquid electrolyte, it is vulnerable to fire risk and has limits to increasing energy density. By contrast, Solid-state Battery uses a solid electrolyte to improve heat resistance and durability, and increases density to extend driving range to more than 1,000 km on a single charge. For this reason, Solid-state Battery is seen as a "game changer" that could shake up the electric vehicle market. China's battery manufacturers, which mass-produce low-cost LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries, are currently encroaching on the global EV market. However, if Solid-state Battery, which eliminates fire risk and dramatically improves energy efficiency, is commercialized, analysts say the strengths of China-made batteries that emphasize "value for money" could also fade. Hyundai Motor is not the only carmaker betting its future on Solid-state Battery. Toyota, which had been cautious about EV development, is working with energy company Idemitsu Kosan and others with a goal of starting mass production as early as next year. Honda has also teamed up with U.S. battery startup QuantumScape and recently embarked on Solid-state Battery development. Chinese carmakers are also joining the race to develop Solid-state Battery. BYD, China's largest EV manufacturer, said it plans to begin pilot production of vehicles equipped with Solid-state Battery in the first quarter of next year. It also unveiled a roadmap to start mass production in 2028 and move into full-scale popularization after 2030. Stella Li, senior vice president at BYD, said in an interview with a local outlet in Valencia, Spain, last month, "We will unveil the first model equipped with Solid-state Battery technology next year." However, Li did not mention a specific mass-production schedule or launch timing for general consumers. Because of this, the auto industry interprets the Solid-state Battery-equipped vehicle Li mentioned as a test vehicle to validate the technology, rather than a mass-production model. Geely Automobile Holdings, a major Chinese car group, said in a five-year strategy released early this year that it would complete in-house development of Solid-state Battery within the year and begin verification. Other EV manufacturers are also working on Solid-state development, and some corporations, including Li Auto, are said to have produced samples. Still, a "cautious view" is emerging in the battery industry that it is difficult to predict when Solid-state Battery will actually be commercialized. The technology is hard to develop and the manufacturing process is demanding, and initial mass production is likely to be priced at a high level, making it unlikely that the battery market landscape will change in a short period. Zeng Yuqun, chairman of CATL, the world's largest battery maker, said at the World Economic Forum annual meeting in Dalian, China, in June, "If we divide the maturity of battery technology into stages 1 through 9, Solid-state Battery is only now at stage 4." At the time, China's battery industry also projected that the manufacturing expense for Solid-state Battery would exceed three times the cost required to make a battery with a 500 km range. President Manfred Harrer also drew a line under mass-production prospects, saying, "I expect high-performance vehicles equipped with Solid-state Battery to hit the market within five years, but I do not think the issue of materials and supplies expense can be resolved within that period."

artigo.texto: Incentivos fiscais, fabricação local de componentes e IA brasileira: os candidatos à Presidência mais bem colocados nas pesquisas apresentam essas como algumas das propostas em seus planos de governo para atrair a construção de data centers no Brasil. ❓ Um data center ("centro de dados", em inglês) é um local que armazena e processa informações. Entre os modelos mais comuns, estão os de nuvem — cloud, para armazenar arquivos e operar serviços na internet — e de inteligência artificial, para treinar modelos de linguagem complexos. Facilitar a construção de data centers é uma ação que alguns dos candidatos consideram importante para aproveitar o avanço da IA. Mas, enquanto o Brasil tenta atrair essas instalações, países como os Estados Unidos têm enfrentado protestos contra o avanço do setor. Com rejeição em outros lugares, por que candidatos no Brasil querem atrair mais data centers? Entre os motivos, estão as diferenças no tamanho dos mercados e nas matrizes energéticas dos países. Manifestantes protestam contra expansão de centros de dados de IA nos EUA Os EUA têm mais de 4.700 data centers e lideram o segmento, segundo dados de setembro do site Data Center Map. O Brasil, por sua vez, tem 218 complexos desse tipo e ocupa o 12º lugar no ranking. Com menos instalações, é preciso armazenar e processar muitos dados no exterior: o Brasil terminou 2025 com déficit de US$ 8 bilhões na balança comercial de Serviços de Computação e Informação, segundo a Brasscom, associação de empresas brasileiras de tecnologia. E, enquanto os EUA dependem principalmente de energia gerada por combustíveis fósseis, incluindo petróleo e gás natural, a eletricidade no Brasil é gerada em larga escala por fontes renováveis, como usinas hidrelétricas. O que há de comum no Brasil, nos EUA e em outros países é a discussão sobre o consumo elevado de energia e água por data centers: moradores de várias cidades americanas protestaram contra o avanço dessas instalações, e autoridades brasileiras questionaram os impactos desses projetos. Para Daniel Cordeiro, professor na Universidade de São Paulo (USP) e especialista em computação sustentável e de alto desempenho, o Brasil precisa aumentar sua capacidade computacional, mas deve tentar evitar problemas que estão sendo enfrentados em outros países. "Ainda não chegamos na quantidade de data centers e de problemas que esses outros países já têm. Temos que olhar para os problemas que estão acontecendo nos outros países e nos precaver para que o mesmo não aconteça aqui", diz. Segundo Thais Ortega, coordenadora de pesquisa da consultoria Reglab, a atração de data centers é um consenso entre os principais candidatos, mas há diferenças nos modelos previstos para alcançar esse objetivo. "Todos convergem para atrair, mas como será a atração? O Brasil tem uma posição estratégica, com vários pontos positivos. Não temos como prever se teremos ou não os problemas dos EUA, mas temos como tentar mitigar com regulações", destaca. Marina Garrote, diretora de operações do Reglab, diz que o Redata, regime brasileiro que reduz impostos para data centers, mas exige contrapartidas socioambientais, pode fazer o país superar alguns dos desafios enfrentados nos EUA. "Com a matriz energética dos EUA, mais data centers significam mais emissões de carbono e conta de luz mais alta para o vizinho. No Brasil, se a expansão for, de fato, baseada em energia eólica e solar, o custo social será um pouco diferente", afirma. Rejeição americana Nos EUA, 64% da população discorda da ideia de que construir data centers rapidamente será positivo para o país, revelou uma pesquisa Reuters/Ipsos. O levantamento indicou que 57% são contrários à criação desses complexos em seus bairros. Mesmo com a forte rejeição, o presidente Donald Trump tem defendido o avanço das instalações. Em encontro com executivos de gigantes de tecnologia na última terça-feira (29), ele afirmou que esses empreendimentos serão muito populares no país. Entre os convidados, estavam Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg e Sundar Pichai, líderes da xAI, da Meta e do Google, empresas que desenvolvem modelos de inteligência artificial, além de Jensen Huang, da Nvidia, principal fabricante de chips para treinamento de IA. O encontro terminou com um compromisso das empresas para reforçar controles de segurança de seus modelos de IA após episódios em que eles saíram do controle e fizeram ataques cibernéticos. Trump disse que as companhias "querem fazer o que é certo" e vão se "autorregular". "Essas empresas grandes, poderosas, muito ricas e inteligentes farão contribuições enormes para as comunidades", disse Trump sobre os data centers. "Farão coisas realmente benéficas, tanto financeiramente quanto de outras formas". Trump reúne CEOs de IA e anuncia compromisso para reforçar controles de segurança Renúncia fiscal no Brasil O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) sancionou em setembro o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata), que zera impostos de importação de equipamentos usados nos data centers. Para aproveitar o benefício, as empresas deverão usar apenas energia renovável ou de baixo carbono e gastar, no máximo, 50ml de água por quilowatt-hora (kWh). Elas também deverão destinar 10% da capacidade para o mercado brasileiro e 2% do valor dos equipamentos em pesquisa no país. - Em suas propostas, Lula (PT) defende fomentar empresas brasileiras de inteligência artificial e criar versões nacionais de modelos de linguagem, como os usados por serviços como ChatGPT e Gemini. - O candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) defende reduzir impostos sobre energia para data centers e ligar a demanda dessas instalações à exploração nacional de minerais críticos, usados na fabricação de chips de IA. - O plano de governo de Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) estabelece data centers como parte de uma cadeia de inovação, conectando-os ao desenvolvimento de semicondutores e modelos de linguagem no país. - Renan Santos (Missão) propõe transformar o Brasil no maior exportador

artigo.texto: Akzo Nobel N.V. Leading supplier of electrostatic dissipative coatings for electronics and cleanrooms. According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Electrostatic Dissipative Coatings market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The World Electrostatic Dissipative Coatings market is entering a phase of sustained expansion, with demand projected to grow at a compound annual rate in the high single digits (7–9%) between 2026 and 2035. This growth is anchored in the accelerating miniaturization of electronic components and the rapid build-out of automated manufacturing environments, where uncontrolled static discharge poses a direct threat to product yield and operational safety. Asia-Pacific remains the dominant production and consumption hub, representing an estimated 45–50% of worldwide demand, supported by semiconductor fabrication clusters in Taiwan, South Korea, and mainland China, as well as a rapidly scaling electric-vehicle battery manufacturing base. A pronounced shift toward premium, high-purity, and low-VOC formulations is reshaping the competitive landscape, with waterborne and solvent-free systems projected to account for more than 60% of new-installation volume by 2030 as global cleanroom and food-processing standards tighten. At the same time, feedstock cost volatility—particularly for epoxy resins, isocyanates, and specialty conductive fillers—remains the primary margin risk, with raw materials constituting an estimated 60–70% of total manufactured cost for standard-grade coatings. Qualification cycles for new ESD coating formulations in regulated end-markets frequently extend beyond 12 months, creating long sales cycles and high customer-acquisition costs for new entrants. Supply-chain concentration risk is elevated for advanced conductive fillers such as indium tin oxide and single-wall carbon nanotubes, where production capacity is geographically and technologically concentrated, exposing downstream formulators to disruption and price spikes. This report provides a data-driven view of market size, structure, key trends, and the competitive dynamics shaping the global ESD coatings industry through 2035. The baseline scenario for the World Electrostatic Dissipative Coatings market assumes continued expansion at a compound annual growth rate of 7–9% from 2026 to 2035, with the market index reaching approximately 210 by 2035 (2025 = 100). This outlook is supported by the structural demand pull from electronics manufacturing, where device miniaturization and higher circuit densities increase sensitivity to electrostatic discharge, and from the rapid scaling of electric-vehicle battery production, which requires ESD-safe environments for cell assembly and module handling. In volume terms, functional-grade ESD coatings are expected to retain the largest share, but high-purity and specialty formulations will drive value growth as end-users in semiconductor, pharmaceutical, and medical-device segments demand lower particulate emission and tighter surface resistivity tolerances. The competitive landscape is consolidating around specialty chemical firms that can offer integrated supply, application services, and long-term performance warranties. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will remain the largest and fastest-growing market, while North America and Europe see steady replacement demand and regulatory-driven upgrades toward waterborne and solvent-free systems. Latin America and the Middle East & Africa will grow from a smaller base, with infrastructure and industrial diversification projects supporting incremental adoption. Key risks to the baseline include raw material price volatility, extended qualification cycles in regulated end-markets, and supply-chain concentration for advanced conductive fillers. Overall, the market is forecast to expand steadily, with the strongest momentum in high-purity and specialty segments that align with contamination-control and safety-critical applications. The contamination control segment encompasses cleanrooms, electronics assembly, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and biotechnology facilities where static discharge can damage sensitive components or compromise sterile environments. Currently, this segment is the largest consumer of ESD coatings, driven by the expansion of semiconductor fabrication and the tightening of cleanroom standards. Through 2035, demand will shift toward high-purity formulations with low outgassing and minimal particulate emission, as device geometries shrink and contamination tolerances tighten. Demand-side indicators to watch include semiconductor capital expenditure, cleanroom construction activity, and regulatory updates on particulate and VOC limits. The mechanism is straightforward: as cleanroom classifications become more stringent, traditional carbon-black ESD coatings may not meet particulate requirements, pushing end-users toward carbon-nanotube and conductive-polymer systems that offer superior clarity and lower loading levels. This segment will also benefit from the growth of biologics and advanced therapies, which require highly controlled environments. Major companies supplying this segment include PPG Industries, AkzoNobel, and Henkel, among others. artigo.texto: CATL in Debrecen is expanding its workforce CATL’s Chinese battery factory in Debrecen is increasing its workforce: now that trial production of battery cells has begun following the ongoing production of modules, the workforce will be expanded from the current 2800 to 3300 by the end of the year. Qin Liang, the chief operating officer of the Debrecen battery factory, said at a press event showcasing the plant that the third production line has already been launched in the module manufacturing operation that began in 2024; since then, more than 500.000 modules have been produced, powering approximately 10,000 vehicles across Europe. Module production has generated 100 billion forints in revenue for the company to date, on which taxes were paid in Hungary, the director noted. The Debrecen plant is designed to meet the needs of European automakers, producing nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, the director said, adding that the Debrecen plant ensures long-term stability, jobs, and new business opportunities for the region. Qin Liang noted that the cell factory received its operating permit in August, fulfilled all the conditions specified in the permits, and began trial production of battery cells on the first two production lines on September 22. Production will expand soon Following a few technical adjustments, the company will begin cell production on the other two lines as well. During the trial run, CATL experts are continuously monitoring the equipment, the quality and safety of the products, and full compliance with regulatory requirements. The new cell factory has a maximum annual capacity of 40 gigawatt-hours, all of which has already been fully reserved by customers. It was also announced at the press conference that the first phase of the project has now been completed at a cost of approximately 900 billion forints, and that once full capacity is reached, 4000 people will be employed at the plant. In response to a query from MTI, however, they confirmed that the entire project is planned in three phases; the total investment of 3000 billion forints will provide jobs for 9000 people and have an annual capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours. They added that they are open to negotiations with the government regarding the project, noting that they had an agreement for 129 billion forints in state subsidies to implement the first phase. They plan to rely on local labor Shen Feng, CATL’s managing director responsible for European operations, said at the press conference that cell production began in Germany in 2022; initially, the ratio of Chinese to German workers was 40 to 60 percent, but today 90 percent of the workforce is German. In Debrecen, the ratio of Chinese to local workers is currently 50–50 percent; according to their plans, the proportion of Hungarian workers will reach 90 percent by 2030. Qin Liang added that they will launch a supplier campaign in October to increase the involvement of local businesses in production. He noted that they currently have more than 300 local suppliers, 80 percent of whom are from Debrecen and the surrounding region. The plant manager also addressed the Debrecen plant’s water consumption, which is a particularly sensitive issue in Debrecen. He noted that they have developed water-saving technology—specifically, a cooling tower—that drastically reduces the plant’s water requirements. It was announced at the press event that the company will continuously provide the authorities with information on the plant’s water and energy consumption as well as its emissions, and that monitoring data will be published every two months so that the public can also access it. artigo.texto: An experimental solid-state battery continues to work perfectly at −40 °C, a temperature at which cold normally severely reduces the performance of this type of battery. In a battery, tiny charged particles called lithium ions must move between two electrodes. This movement makes it possible to store and then release energy. In conventional batteries, the ions pass through a liquid. Solid-state batteries seek to replace this liquid with a solid material. The problem appears particularly when it is very cold. The ions then move much more difficultly through certain solid materials. The battery loses efficiency and may eventually stop working properly. Researchers at Tsinghua University in China therefore sought to facilitate this movement. To do so, they added a conductive substance called polyaniline to their material. Its role is to modify the distribution of electrical charges inside the battery. This helps more lithium ions move, even when the temperature drops sharply. The researchers also observed another effect. When in contact with lithium, the new material promotes the formation of a thin protective layer. This reduces certain undesirable reactions that progressively degrade the battery during charging and discharging. In practice, the small batteries made in the laboratory worked between −40 °C and 45 °C. This resistance to cold could be useful for devices used in winter, in polar regions or at high altitudes. However, these performances still need to be verified with much larger batteries. In another test, the cells exceeded 13,000 charge and discharge cycles. However, these impressive figures should be put into perspective, as laboratory conditions are specific and actual service life depends in particular on the battery's size and how it is used. The next step is therefore to manufacture cells more similar to those used in real devices. The researchers will need to verify whether their material retains its properties with larger batteries and more energy-storing material.

artigo.texto: In Festus, Missouri, a town that gave Donald Trump 67 percent of its vote, residents have filed to recall the mayor and three council members over a $6 billion data center. In New York, a Democratic governor has signed the first statewide moratorium on new ones. Across seven states, at least 33 recall campaigns are targeting as many as 58 local officials for the same reason, and the reason is not a party. It is a building. That makes data centers the rarest thing in American politics right now: an issue where the folding chairs in a red county and a blue one are filled with people saying the same words. They are not saying "no technology." They are saying the box across the road raises their power bill, drains their water, takes the farm, and was negotiated behind a nondisclosure agreement before anyone in town knew its name. In Luther, Oklahoma, the moratorium passed only after word leaked that the mayor had been in closed talks with a developer for months. The anger is not about servers. It is about being handed a decision that was already made. Here is what almost nobody in those rooms has been told, and what both sides would want if they knew it. Every data center is a furnace. Nearly all the electricity that goes in comes out as heat, and in every facility in America that heat is thrown into the sky through cooling towers, at the owner's expense. The newest liquid-cooled halls release it as warm water, exactly what a greenhouse wants in January. A two-and-a-half-acre greenhouse on that water grows on the order of 695,000 pounds of fresh produce a year with no boiler and nothing burned. Write into the rezoning that at least 15 percent of it is covenanted to the host community, to the schools, the food bank, the farm store on the road, and one building's waste feeds about 400 of its neighbors, year-round, in towns where the nearest winter tomato has traveled 1,500 miles. Put the fish house on the same loop and homes on radiant floors at the end of it, and the campus that was going to bury the farmland has built a farm. Notice what that covenant is. It is the opposite of an NDA. It is a promise, written into a public document, that a resident can read at the county clerk's office and hold the developer to at every hearing for the life of the project. The reason people in Festus and Luther and Prince William County feel the technology is being forced on them is that the terms were hidden. A heat covenant puts the terms on the wall. And it is the one proposal that does not ask either side to give up what it wants. Conservatives want the tax base, the jobs, and the AI race won; Loudoun County, Virginia, collected $1.2 billion in data-center property taxes this year and cut its residential rate for the tenth straight year, so the money is real. Progressives want communities protected, ratepayers held harmless, and food grown close to home; a farm on the fence line does all three. Michelle Obama and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. agree on almost nothing, but they agree that Americans should eat real food grown nearby. A data center that powers the cloud and feeds the town is not a compromise between the two camps. It is both of them, in one site plan. Virginia noticed first. This spring its General Assembly passed the first law in the country directing the state to put data-center waste heat to use, and the Senate vote was 39 to 0. In a legislature that spent the same session at war with itself over data-center tax breaks, that is what an issue looks like when it belongs to no one. Wall Street has noticed too. Lenders now weigh local opposition and permitting status before financing a campus, and local resistance blocked or delayed some $130 billion in projects in the first quarter of this year alone. The developer who arrives with a public covenant and a farm in the first phase of the site plan is not being generous. He is de-risking his loan. So, to the organizers running recall petitions and the officials facing them, to the governors weighing a pause and the developers hoping they don't: there is a yes here that both of you can sign. Put one question in every rezoning, in public, in writing: where does the heat go, and what share of what it grows stays here? A moratorium buys a town a year. A covenant buys it a farm. The fight in Festus and the fight in Albany are the same fight, and this is the same answer. Andrew Potter is the founder and CEO of Intelligent Harvest, a Lynchburg, Virginia company that develops greenhouses and community farms powered by data-center waste heat.

artigo.texto: Chinese battery giant CATL has reached a key milestone in proving the durability of its technology, demonstrating impressive laboratory analysis results. The prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells tested, which have been operating without interruption for almost fourteen years, have retained about 85 percent of their original energy capacity. The cells analyzed are part of the world's first large-scale energy storage facility, the 63 MWh Zhangbei, which began operation in 2011 and even provided clean energy for the 2022 Winter Olympics. The complete decommissioning of the facility in the summer of 2025 has allowed engineers to subject the components to detailed chemical and physical destructive testing. Over 50 samples taken from the original cells reveal remarkable material durability: the anode and cathode layers have retained perfect geometry, and the graphite shows no structural defects or critical signs of aging. An interesting detail is the fact that not a single cell from this manufacturer had to be replaced over the entire 14-year cycle. The test results open up new perspectives for the so-called “second life“ of industrial batteries. According to the company's experts, the retired cells have a resource for about 1,000 more complete charge and discharge cycles. This makes the components fully suitable for reintegration into smaller secondary storage systems for at least another decade. The current findings reconfirm the expectations from the control tests carried out on the ninth year of the facility's launch. LFP technology is also gaining in importance in the automotive sector. While these chemistries are inferior in specific energy density to nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) alternatives, they offer significantly lower manufacturing costs and unrivaled durability under extreme temperature and operating conditions. The achieved lifespan solidifies the technology's position as a key pillar for the future of sustainable mobility and green energy.

Amazon Web Services made the announcement on Friday. The plan covers education, job training, and energy affordability. It also covers water and energy preservation. AWS also promised to tackle the impact of its data centers on electricity and water use. The move makes sense. Data centers power and run AI models. But communities across the US have pushed back. They worry about electricity demand and utility costs. AWS noted that more than 100 data center moratoriums are being considered nationwide. The backlash is also a political issue ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. Amazon said it invested $276 billion in data centers between 2011 and 2025. It has large projects or expansions planned in Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Virginia, and Mississippi. AWS CEO Matt Garman said the buildout is urgent. He said other countries also see the benefits of AI. He added that the countries leading in AI will shape it. AWS also said it will be water positive by 2030. That means it will return more water to communities than it uses. It says it is 75% of the way there. See analysts’ growth forecasts and price targets for Amazon stock (It’s free) >>> What the Market Is Telling Us About Amazon Stock $1 billion is small compared with what Amazon spends. On the Q2 call, management said it expects about $220 billion in cash capex this year. Most of that supports AI and AWS. So this pledge is more about public trust than cost. That trust matters for Amazon stock. AWS is the growth engine. Revenue rose 36.7% last quarter, its fastest pace in 18 quarters. Backlog reached $496 billion. AWS also posted $16.6 billion in operating income. Management says demand is higher than capacity. It expects that to stay true in 2027. New data centers are how Amazon meets that demand. If local opposition slows approvals, that could hold back growth. That is the real risk for Amazon stock. Amazon also said it plans to double its power capacity by the end of 2027 from 2025 levels. Community support will help make that possible. For now, the market will likely stay focused on AWS growth and capex returns. Still, rising local pushback is worth watching. Any new moratoriums could affect how investors view Amazon stock. A clear community plan may ease some of that worry for Amazon stockholders. artigo.texto: Adani Green Energy Ltd. (AGEL), one of India’s largest renewable energy company, increased its operational battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity to 6.63 GWh at Khavda, Gujarat. The company expanded the capacity from 3.55 GWh in June 2026 and now accounts for more than half of India’s approximately 12.6 GWh of operational BESS capacity. According to AGEL, the milestone establishes Khavda as the world’s largest operational battery energy storage installation at a single location, with 6.63 GWh of operational capacity. BESS Expansion Supports Khavda Renewable Energy Project AGEL achieved the 6.63 GWh milestone within 14 months of starting BESS construction at Khavda. The latest capacity addition took just 10 months to commission from the beginning of construction. The battery storage system forms an integral part of AGEL’s renewable energy development at Khavda, where the company is developing a 30 GW renewable energy plant across 538 sq km of barren land. The company said its 6.63 GWh BESS can store enough clean energy to power around two million homes for a day. It can also support peak electricity demand in cities such as Nagpur, Patna and Vizag for several hours. Moreover, the storage capacity is equivalent to the battery capacity of more than 150,000 mid-sized electric vehicles and can store enough energy each day to meet almost twice the estimated daily electricity requirement of the Delhi Metro. Battery Storage Strengthens Renewable Power Reliability “Reaching 6.63 GWh of operational battery storage in just 14 months is a significant milestone for AGEL and India’s clean energy transition,” said Sagar Adani, Executive Director, Adani Green Energy Ltd. He added that storage at this scale can make renewable power firmer, more reliable and dispatchable when the electricity grid requires it. The BESS uses lithium-ion battery technology, supported by energy management systems (EMS) and automated telemetry. These systems manage charging and discharging, optimise battery performance and enable the facility to provide grid services. AGEL Targets More Than 10 GWh of BESS Additions Looking ahead, AGEL plans to add more than 10 GWh of BESS capacity during FY 2026–27. The company is also targeting 50 GWh of energy storage capacity over the next five years. In addition, AGEL is pursuing pumped storage projects (PSPs) as part of its broader strategy to develop large-scale renewable power that can deliver firm and dispatchable electricity. AGEL Expands Renewable Energy Portfolio AGEL develops, owns and operates utility-scale grid-connected solar, wind, hybrid and energy storage projects. The company currently has an operating renewable energy portfolio of 20.76 GW, along with 6.63 GWh of operational BESS capacity across 12 states. As reported by pv-magazine-india.com, AGEL aims to reach 50 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030, supporting India’s broader decarbonisation and clean-energy transition goals.

artigo.texto: Technology group Wärtsilä has secured an order to supply a 282 MW onsite power solution for a data center project being developed by a major US independent power producer in the United States. The power plant will operate with 15 Wärtsilä 50SG engines. The order demonstrates the growing need for fast-deployable onsite power solutions as grid constraints, lengthy connection timelines, and accelerating AI-driven electricity demand create power availability challenges for new data center developments. The order was booked by Wärtsilä in Q3 2026. The project further strengthens Wärtsilä's proven position in the rapidly growing U.S. data center power market. It marks the company's seventh data center-related order in the United States, bringing the total power capacity sold by Wärtsilä for U.S. data center applications to more than 3 GW. The customer selected Wärtsilä engine-based solution for its ability to provide large-scale power capacity on efficient timelines while enabling phased expansion as computing demand grows. The Wärtsilä 50SG engines provide high efficiency in demanding operating conditions, feature a closed-loop cooling system that minimises water consumption compared with conventional thermal power alternatives and offer flexibility to convert the engines to run on future fuels. For data center developers, these features translate into dependable power availability, scalable growth, and greater long-term optionality. “The U.S. data center market is moving faster than traditional power infrastructure can support,” says Risto Paldanius, Vice President, Americas at Wärtsilä Energy. “This order shows how flexible onsite power can help developers secure reliable power, reduce deployment risk, and scale their operations with confidence. Our growing portfolio of data center projects to date demonstrates the critical role flexible engine technology can play in solving one of the sector’s most urgent growth challenges.” The Wärtsilä equipment is scheduled for delivery in 2028, and the project is expected to become fully operational in 2029. Our solutions include flexible engine power plants and services for the whole lifecycle of our installations. Our engines are future-proof and can run on sustainable fuels. Our track record comprises 81 GW of power plant capacity in 180 countries around the world. artigo.texto: Home › Energy Storage ›SECI Invites Bids for 800 MW/3,200 MWh BESS SECI Invites Bids for 800 MW/3,200 MWh BESS Solar Energy Corporation of India has issued a tender for supplying energy from 800 MW/3,200 MWh standalone battery energy storage system in India. Bid submission ends on October 30, 2026. October 05, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) has floated a tender for the supply of energy from 800 MW/3,200 MWh ISTS-connected standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in India. The projects must be set up under the build, own, operate (BOO) model. Bidders must pay INR 59,000 as a tender document fee. They also need to deposit INR 20,000/MW (plus GST) as a bid processing fee, subject to a maximum amount of INR 20 lakh (plus GST). Further, they need to furnish INR 7.184 lakh/MW as an earnest money deposit (EMD). Selected bidders must deposit INR 17.96 lakh/MW as a performance bank guarantee (PBG). The last date for submission of bids is October 30, 2026. The techno-commercial bids will be opened on November 4, 2026. The minimum capacity for bidding will be 50 MW/200 MWh. The BESSD must set up, operate, and maintain a BESS, with the primary objective of providing stored energy from the BESS to the buying entities on an “on-demand” basis. Identification of land, installation and ownership of the project, along with obtaining connectivity and necessary approvals and interconnection with the ISTS network/ STU or InSTS network (as applicable) will be under the scope of the BESSD. The charging power for the BESS project must be arranged by the BESSD such that at least 51 percent of the energy used for charging the BESS is procured from renewable energy sources. The BESSD must guarantee a minimum system availability of 85 percent on a monthly basis. The net worth of the bidder must be at least INR 71.84 lakh/ MW, as on the last date of FY26, or as on the day at least 7 days prior to the bid submission deadline. To demonstrate adequate financial capacity for the project, the Bidder must meet at least one of the following criteria: an annual turnover of at least INR 87.514 lakh/MW in FY26 or as of at least seven days before the bid submission deadline; PBDIT, excluding other and exceptional income, of at least INR 17,50,280/MW as of the end of FY26 or at least seven days before the bid deadline; or an in-principle bank/lender sanction for a working capital line of credit of at least INR 21,87,850/MW. artigo.texto: Data Center Design in the AI Era The unprecedented performance demands of AI workloads require a reimagined approach to data center design toward fully autonomous operations. October 5, 2026 Sponsored by HPE It wasn’t long ago that organizations thought their data centers would play a less central role in IT service delivery. Virtualized infrastructure, cloud computing, colocation, SaaS applications, and other factors pointed to more computing being done off-premises. But the rapid acceleration of compute-intensive workloads, generative AI, and ever-increasing network complexity is driving organizations to reimagine and, in some cases, completely re-engineer their data centers. The same is true for third-party data centers leveraged by so many organizations, often in tandem with their on-prem facilities. AI training and inference, combined with a rapid swing toward agentic AI, is intensifying pressure on data centers. Even with the impressive advances in compute and storage density, enterprises are realizing that incremental component refreshes cannot solve operational complexity; they require a modern fabric design and shift toward self-driving networks to improve IT agility, increase reliability, and optimize the end user experience. The trends have been exacerbated by huge demands for power and cooling, which data centers have struggled to meet. Research from Uptime Institute notes that 82% of data center operators report their highest-density racks are still below 30 kilowatts, a level unlikely to meet the growing demands of AI-level performance as rack densities increase. New Challenges Force Changes to Data Center Design The harsh reality is that traditional data centers were never designed for the performance, scalability, security, and resilience demands of the AI era. The massive growth in data volumes has created important opportunities for new insights, but also requires a fundamentally different approach to network design. Servers, networks, storage, end-user devices, cloud gateways, applications, security tools, and other sources generate unprecedented amounts of data, making it more difficult for networks to discern whether an alert indicates a potentially serious failure or a minor problem elsewhere. But it’s not just the proliferation of data sources that renders legacy data centers inadequate for the AI era. Traditional data center traffic usually had a fair amount of entropy, making it easier to design for capacity and accommodate occasional demand spikes that could impact network performance. AI has changed that in a big way. Modern AI workloads running on GPUs require deterministic, low-latency, higher-bandwidth networks, and massively scalable storage infrastructure, meaning that both existing and greenfield data centers need to support significantly higher performance. In addition, the traditional siloed approach to IT infrastructure that reflects organizational boundaries rather than end user needs—compute, storage, and networking—has given way to new design principles that promote tighter cross-domain integration for better overall data center and application performance. Shifting the Data Center to Autonomous Operations Although data centers have increasingly embraced automation, the next step is for data center design to progress toward autonomy. Data center personnel are simply too hard-pressed to address the increasing telemetry volume and complexity in real time without tools that provide full-stack, cross-domain visibility across the entire enterprise. AI agents should be an important element in the move toward autonomous operations because they enable lightning-fast assessments, analysis, and decision-making across the full spectrum of infrastructure and data sources. Management should focus not just on automating operations to reduce headcount, but on autonomous operations that improve the quality of application and user experience. The Importance of a Self-Driving Framework AI-era data centers now have the potential for unsurpassed levels of intelligence, autonomous operations, observability, and contextually aware decision-making. This is where self-driving frameworks coordinate data center operations with AI-era requirements. The emphasis has swung decisively away from historically fragmented management frameworks in favor of approaches that collect information from all available sources and put them into an actionable context across infrastructure. A key first step is intent-based networking, which defines the desired state of the network based on operator-intent and continuously validates its conformance to that standard. Problems are identified faster and with greater precision, relieving the data center team of tedious, time-consuming, and often inaccurate triage to avoid failures and downtime. A well-planned and meticulously executed approach to building the right data center architecture helps organizations establish validated topologies, automate deployment, improve visibility, automate remediation, and balance the strengths of AI tools with human experience. How HPE Networking Facilitates Data Center Transformation Working with an experienced technology partner that understands infrastructure, data center architecture, and AI workloads is a must. HPE’s history as a networking leader and enterprise IT pioneer gives it a significant leg up in helping data center decision-makers prepare their facilities for success in the AI era. artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil: candidatos querem mais, EUA rejeitam Com propostas de redução de impostos e criação de polo nacional, candidatos a presidente mais bem colocados têm planos parecidos para data centers. Nos EUA, maioria é contrária à construção desses complexos em seus bairros. A divergência entre os dois países reflete diferenças estruturais e estratégicas no setor de tecnologia. Incentivos fiscais, fabricação local de componentes e IA brasileira: os candidatos à Presidência mais bem colocados nas pesquisas apresentam essas como algumas das propostas em seus planos de governo para atrair a construção de data centers no Brasil. A fonte não detalhou os valores ou prazos desses incentivos. Facilitar a construção de data centers é uma ação que alguns dos candidatos consideram importante para aproveitar o avanço da IA. Mas, enquanto o Brasil tenta atrair essas instalações, países como os Estados Unidos têm enfrentado protestos contra o avanço do setor. Manifestantes protestam contra expansão de centros de dados de IA nos EUA. O que é um data center? ❓ Um data center (“centro de dados”, em inglês) é um local que armazena e processa informações. Entre os modelos mais comuns, estão os de nuvem — cloud, para armazenar arquivos e operar serviços na internet — e de inteligência artificial, para treinar modelos de linguagem complexos. Essas infraestruturas são essenciais para a economia digital. Por que candidatos querem atrair? Com rejeição em outros lugares, por que candidatos no Brasil querem atrair mais data centers? Entre os motivos, estão as diferenças no tamanho dos mercados e nas matrizes energéticas dos países. O Brasil busca reduzir sua dependência de processamento no exterior. Com menos instalações, é preciso armazenar e processar muitos dados no exterior: o Brasil terminou 2025 com déficit de US$ 8 bilhões na balança comercial de Serviços de Computação e Informação, segundo a Brasscom, associação de empresas brasileiras de tecnologia. Esse déficit pressiona a economia e limita a competitividade das empresas locais. Energia renovável como diferencial E, enquanto os EUA dependem principalmente de energia gerada por combustíveis fósseis, incluindo petróleo e gás natural, a eletricidade no Brasil é gerada em larga escala por fontes renováveis, como usinas hidrelétricas. Essa matriz mais limpa pode atrair empresas globais preocupadas com sustentabilidade. O que há de comum no Brasil, nos EUA e em outros países é a discussão sobre o consumo elevado de energia e água por data centers: moradores de várias cidades americanas protestaram contra o avanço dessas instalações, e autoridades brasileiras questionaram os impactos desses projetos. A fonte não detalhou quais autoridades brasileiras se manifestaram. Especialistas pedem cautela Para Daniel Cordeiro, professor na Universidade de São Paulo (USP) e especialista em computação sustentável e de alto desempenho, o Brasil precisa aumentar sua capacidade computacional, mas deve tentar evitar problemas que estão sendo enfrentados em outros países. Ele não especificou quais medidas regulatórias seriam necessárias. Segundo Thais Ortega, coordenadora de pesquisa da consultoria Reglab, a atração de data centers é um consenso entre os principais candidatos, mas há diferenças nos modelos previstos para alcançar esse objetivo. “Todos convergem para atrair, mas como será a atração? O Brasil tem uma posição estratégica, com vários pontos positivos. Não temos como prever se teremos ou não os problemas dos EUA, mas temos como tentar mitigar com regulações”, destaca. Para empresários e comerciantes do noroeste paulista, a eventual instalação de data centers pode gerar empregos diretos e indiretos, além de demandar serviços locais. No entanto, os impactos sobre o consumo de energia e água devem ser monitorados de perto pelas entidades empresariais. Perguntas Frequentes Por que os candidatos à presidência do Brasil querem atrair mais data centers? Os candidatos querem atrair data centers para aproveitar o avanço da IA e reduzir o déficit de US$ 8 bilhões na balança comercial de Serviços de Computação e Informação, segundo a Brasscom. Quais são as principais propostas dos candidatos para atrair data centers no Brasil? As propostas incluem incentivos fiscais, fabricação local de componentes e desenvolvimento de IA brasileira, conforme os planos de governo dos candidatos mais bem colocados. Por que há rejeição a data centers nos EUA enquanto o Brasil tenta atraí-los? Nos EUA, a rejeição se deve ao alto consumo de energia e água e à dependência de combustíveis fósseis, enquanto no Brasil a matriz energética é majoritariamente renovável, o que torna a atração mais viável.

artigo.texto: EP Cube displayed its EP CUBE Single-Phase 2.0 for new or existing residential and Three-Phase Light C&I Solution for small commercial PV-plus-storage systems The residential system supports a maximum PV capacity of 15 kW and lists its storage capacity range of 5 to 40 kWh with a rated 10 kVA full-load power It also integrates with the company’s upcoming 7.4 kW AC EV charger, updated EP Cube App, and a new HMI for a connected and smarter home energy ecosystem EP Cube, an independent subsidiary and residential energy storage brand of Canadian Solar Inc., introduced its residential EP CUBE Single-Phase 2.0 and Three-Phase Light C&I Solution at Solar & Storage Live UK 2026 in Birmingham. The company's booth also displayed an EV charger, a Human Machine Interface (HMI) display, and a new dynamic tariff pricing AI mode as part of a smart home energy ecosystem. Both energy storage systems (ESS) feature an 'All-in-One' configuration, which combines a hybrid inverter and modular battery packs, stacked on one another. They use lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) battery units, each measuring 600 × 266 × 200 mm and providing 5 kWh of storage capacity at a 51.2 V rated voltage. While the configuration and battery pack are identical, their inverter and total storage capacities vary. The EP CUBE Single-Phase 2.0 features a 10 kVA hybrid inverter and a storage capacity range of 5 to 40 kWh by connecting to eight battery packs. With 4 built-in MPPTs, the inverter supports up to 15 kW of PV capacity with a 600 V maximum PV input voltage. In comparison, the Three-Phase Light C&I Solution combines a higher-capacity hybrid inverter (12 kVA) and storage capacities of 10 to 40 kWh using the same 5 kWh battery packs mentioned above. Its inverter lists a higher PV capacity of 24 kW and a maximum input voltage of 1,000 V, though the MPPT numbers remain the same. The product datasheets specify compatibility with new and existing PV arrays to make an AC-coupled PV-plus-storage system. The residential ESS supports up to 10 kVA (single-phase) emergency backup within 10 ms of a grid outage, while this function is optional for the C&I product. It switches to off-grid mode in less than 20 ms of a grid blackout and delivers up to 12 kVA (3-phase) backup power. Backup duration varies based on total connected storage capacity, rated discharge limit, and operational conditions, among others. EP Cube also introduced its new AC EV chargers in two variants – 7.4 kW single-phase and 11 kW 3-phase. According to the company, it planned to launch the 3-phase charger by the end of September 2026, while the launch of its single-phase counterpart is slated for Q4 2026. The single-phase charger supports direct connection with the EP Cube Single-Phase 2.0 through a dedicated built-in port, enabling a connected home energy ecosystem. These ESSs (mentioned above) integrate with the EP Cube App (installed on the user's device) and help monitor and support multiple applications, including PV self-consumption maximization and time-of-use (TOU) tariffs, among others. It also enables smart EV charging from excess PV generation during peak hours and use of low-priced electricity at night or during low solar generation periods. This increases PV self-consumption and optimizes charging costs. The company says it has updated the app with features that support the UK's dynamic electricity tariff management services. It added that these features will soon be embedded in a new Dynamic Pricing AI mode for more accurate low-price capturing and battery charging/discharging decisions. EP Cube is also expecting to include new Open APIs with the app. This will enable the home ESS platform to integrate with an existing third-party home energy management system (HEMS), like Home Assistant, to make the connected energy ecosystem smarter. In addition to remote monitoring and data visualization, the booth displayed the new 7-inch HMI for local data accumulation and visualization with local data storage, supporting data independence for end users.

artigo.texto: Amazon investirá US$ 1 bilhão em comunidades de data centers em meio à pressão por consumo de energia e água A Amazon Web Services (AWS), divisão de computação em nuvem da gigante de tecnologia, anunciou que investirá mais de US$ 1 bilhão ao longo dos próximos cinco anos em comunidades locais nos Estados Unidos que abrigam seus data centers. O plano surge como resposta direta às crescentes preocupações públicas e críticas sobre a pressão que as estruturas exercem sobre o abastecimento de água e a rede elétrica local. Os centros de dados desempenham um papel indispensável no fornecimento do poder computacional maciço exigido para o treinamento e a execução de modelos avançados de Inteligência Artificial (IA). No entanto, o ritmo acelerado de construção dessas instalações tem provocado fortes resistências em diversos condados e municípios norte-americanos, gerando debates sobre o impacto nas tarifas públicas de energia e o equilíbrio ambiental das regiões vizinhas. Foco em capacitação, sustentabilidade e infraestrutura local O montante de US$ 1 bilhão será canalizado para iniciativas voltadas ao desenvolvimento socioeconômico e ambiental das regiões onde a AWS opera. O programa contempla: - Preservação e eficiência de água: Projetos comunitários para conservação de recursos hídricos e devolução de água tratada aos mananciais locais. - Acessibilidade e transição energética: Apoio a programas que ajudam a mitigar impactos nas contas de luz das populações vizinhas e investimentos em fontes renováveis. - Educação e qualificação profissional: Treinamento técnico e capacitação em tecnologia da informação e computação em nuvem para residentes locais. - Financiamento de prioridades comunitárias: Apoio a serviços essenciais, segurança hídrica e infraestrutura pública regional. Segundo a empresa, a AWS mantém o compromisso de alcançar o status de “positiva em água” (water positive) até 2030, o que significa devolver mais água às comunidades do que o volume total consumido pelas operações de resfriamento. A companhia afirma já ter atingido cerca de 75% dessa meta global. Corrida pela IA e os desafios regulatórios nos EUA Entre 2011 e 2025, a Amazon investiu aproximadamente US$ 276 bilhões em data centers nos Estados Unidos, com megaprojetos e expansões em andamento em estados estratégicos como Virgínia, Indiana, Carolina do Norte, Louisiana e Mississippi. A rápida proliferação dessas estruturas, impulsionada pelo boom da inteligência artificial generativa, levou mais de uma centena de municípios e governos locais a avaliarem moratórias e restrições para novas construções, tornando o consumo energético dos data centers um dos principais pontos de debate político e de infraestrutura no país. Em pronunciamento oficial, Matt Garman, CEO da AWS, ressaltou a relevância estratégica da infraestrutura para a soberania tecnológica: “Há urgência na construção desses data centers porque não somos o único país que vê os benefícios da IA para a economia e a segurança nacional. Os países que liderarem em inteligência artificial irão moldá-la e extrair o máximo proveito dessa revolução tecnológica.” Com o novo aporte bilionário, a Amazon busca equilibrar a expansão acelerada de sua capacidade de processamento em nuvem com o fortalecimento das relações institucionais e a sustentabilidade das comunidades que sustentam o ecossistema de IA.

artigo.texto: expansão dos data centers da Amazon está revelando uma conta que não termina em chips, servidores e galpões. A AWS anunciou nesta sexta-feira (2) mais de US$ 1 bilhão nos próximos cinco anos para comunidades dos Estados Unidosonde mantém essas estruturas. Enquanto isso, o Brasil começa a enfrentar outra parte do mesmo desafio: preparar energia, transmissão e regras para receber a infraestrutura exigida pelo avanço da inteligência artificial. A Amazon afirma ter investido US$ 276 bilhões entre 2011 e 2025 em data centers e mantém grandes projetos ou expansões em estados americanos como Indiana, Louisiana, Carolina do Norte, Virgínia e Mississippi. Esse crescimento ajuda a explicar por que uma infraestrutura antes restrita ao debate tecnológico passou a aparecer também nas discussões sobre energia, água, emprego e investimento público. Por que se fala tanto em data centers agora A resposta está, em grande parte, na inteligência artificial. Serviços digitais já dependiam de centros de processamento. No entanto, treinar e executar modelos de IA amplia a necessidade de capacidade computacional. Por trás de uma ferramenta acessada pelo celular ou computador existem instalações físicas que precisam de servidores, sistemas de refrigeração, conexão e fornecimento contínuo de eletricidade. Nos Estados Unidos, essa expansão também enfrenta resistência local. Segundo a AWS, mais de 100 propostas de moratórias para data centers estavam em discussão no país. O novo programa Built Together prevê recursos para educação, treinamento profissional, acesso à energia, conservação de água e energia e outras prioridades das comunidades. Entre as ações previstas estão treinamentos para eletricistas, profissionais de climatização, fibra óptica e tecnologia da informação. A curiosidade econômica está justamente aí: o investimento necessário para ampliar a capacidade de IA começa a alcançar também o entorno dos data centers. Não envolve apenas os equipamentos instalados dentro deles. Matt Garman, presidente-executivo da AWS, defendeu a urgência da expansão e relacionou a liderança em inteligência artificial à economia e à segurança nacional. A companhia também afirma que pretende tornar suas operações de data centers positivas em água até 2030. Para isso, quer devolver às comunidades mais água do que utiliza, e diz estar 75% próxima dessa meta. Data centers da Amazon encontram novas exigências no Brasil O Brasil já faz parte dessa corrida. A AWS anunciou R$ 10,1 bilhões em investimentos até 2034 para expandir, construir, conectar, operar e manter sua infraestrutura de data centers no país, principalmente em São Paulo. Segundo a própria companhia, outros R$ 19,2 bilhões foram investidos no Brasil entre 2011 e 2023. Mas atrair os projetos é apenas uma parte da equação. O Redata, sancionado em 15 de setembro, concede benefícios tributários para equipamentos destinados a data centers e estabelece contrapartidas para as empresas participantes. Entre elas está a obrigação de disponibilizar ao mercado interno pelo menos 10% do fornecimento efetivo dos serviços de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados. Os empreendimentos também devem atender sua demanda elétrica por contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução provenientes de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão de carbono. A legislação estabelece ainda índice de eficiência hídrica igual ou inferior a 0,05 litro por kWh, aferido anualmente. Além disso, existe a obrigação de investir no país valor equivalente a 2% das aquisições beneficiadas em projetos de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. Energia transforma corrida digital em obra física É na rede elétrica que o tamanho potencial dessa corrida aparece de forma mais concreta. Segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), projetos de data centers com pedidos em processo no Ministério de Minas e Energia passaram de 19,8 GW em setembro para 26,2 GW em novembro de 2025. Isso não significa que 26,2 GW serão efetivamente instalados. A própria EPE ressalta que a concretização dos empreendimentos depende de diferentes condicionantes, incluindo disponibilidade de transmissão, telecomunicações, licenciamento e viabilidade econômico-financeira. São Paulo oferece uma dimensão financeira desse desafio. A EPE informou que estudos recomendaram cerca de R$ 1,6 bilhão em investimentos na transmissão, com potencial para liberar aproximadamente 4 GW adicionais de margem de conexão para grandes consumidores na região. A comparação com os Estados Unidos revela duas contas diferentes produzidas pela mesma corrida tecnológica. Lá, a Amazon decidiu reservar mais de US$ 1 bilhão para comunidades próximas aos seus centros de dados. No Brasil, além dos R$ 10,1 bilhões previstos pela AWS até 2034, a expansão encontra exigências regulatórias. Além disso, enfrenta uma rede elétrica que já demanda novos investimentos para abrir espaço a grandes cargas. Para os data centers da Amazon, AWS, data centers, inteligência artificial, data centers no Brasil, e de outros grupos que pretendam ampliar operações no Brasil, disponibilidade de energia, conexão à transmissão, eficiência hídrica e contrapartidas passam a fazer parte da viabilidade econômica dos projetos. O caso paulista dá dimensão prática ao desafio: há cerca de R$ 1,6 bilhão em transmissão recomendado para destravar aproximadamente 4 GW de capacidade de conexão. Isso ocorre antes mesmo de saber quantos dos projetos hoje em análise efetivamente sairão do papel.

artigo.texto: Opponents of a proposed Brighton data center development will push the City Council for a moratorium Tuesday night, as the populist backlash against the resource-hungry megacenters spreads across Colorado. Weld County data center opponents are also launching a signature drive to get a moratorium on a future countywide ballot. Questions about transparency from government officials, how much water and energy the data centers will use, and how much noise they will generate for nearby subdivisions are bringing unusual coalitions together to fight growth, said Jordan Forsyth, a Democratic Socialists of America activist in Adams County. “To see me, a very vocal member of DSA, and my neighbor who is very Republican and voted for Trump, being able to have a conversation on this issue and actually be united … it’s been really cool to see everybody be able to put politics aside and just engage for the good of the community,” Forsyth said. A nonpartisan Weld County group says it is circulating two data center petitions in coming weeks. One, requiring 10,000 signatures in 45 days, would petition the Weld County commissioners to refer their approval of Global AI’s proposed data center to all voters in a special election sometime after the November general elections. The second Weld County petition, also needing 10,000 signatures according to the coalition, would create a separate ballot measure that if approved would require a public referendum on any newly proposed data center or data center expansion. “This referendum puts power back in the hands of the people of Weld County,” said community advocate Patricia Garcia-Nelson, who also works as a fossil fuels transition advocate for GreenLatinos. “We have the right to decide what happens to our community, not just on this project, but on the ones that come next. Over the next 30 days, we’re going to make sure every voter in Weld County has that chance,” Garcia-Nelson said, in a statement announcing the petition drives. More chances for referendums on data centers arise as candidate positions on the controversial developments become a litmus test from city council races to U.S. Senate campaigns. Colorado Springs recently delayed approval of a proposed data center near Garden of the Gods after protesters were arrested at the public hearing. Aurora’s City Council rejected a moratorium on data centers but put in place new requirements on how much water projects might use. Seeking info in Brighton Activists in Brighton are organizing, and studying documentation filed with the city for a 2.5-million-square-foot, eight-building data center mapped out on farm land near 50th Avenue and Weld County Road 4, about 25 miles northeast of downtown Denver. The development would be in a portion of Brighton that is in Weld County, according to BizWest. Former Chicago TV anchor and current Brighton resident Stacey Baca has compiled the documents and explanations of the developer’s plans on her YouTube channel, and activists say they want answers from City Council on why the project has moved forward without public debate. Nondisclosure agreements or other proprietary negotiations might get in the way, Forsyth said, ““but I think they had the option for community involvement and input, and it doesn’t seem that they’re interested in it,” Forsyth said. Council members should have looked around Colorado and seen that data centers would be coming for the ample open space on co-op United Power’s grid, the activists say. A moratorium would give the community time to develop standards, from whether they want data centers at all, to whether they should be supported with tax breaks, to how water and power will be supplied, opponents say. Representatives of Dewberry engineers, the firm that has filed paperwork for the Brighton development, did not return calls seeking comment about the project. Activists say the developer is California-based Raeden, which did not return messages seeking comment. In addition to concerns about data centers’ cooling-water use amid historic drought conditions, activists also question how the centers’ massive power needs will be supplied. Data centers come with large fossil-fueled backup generators that emit pollution when fired up; their everyday needs require hundreds of megawatts of power. If the data centers are powered by new fossil-fuel generation such as natural gas, Colorado’s progress in switching to clean, renewable energy could stall further, opponents say. A United Power spokesperson said the co-op power supplier cannot talk about individual customer projects or proposals. United Power said it works with large-load prospective customers to ensure adequate supply will be available. Some Brighton City Council members have supported consideration of a 90-day moratorium on data center approvals. Forsyth said another council member will support a 180-day freeze at the Oct. 6 meeting. Weld County activists will be at the Brighton meeting, in neighboring Adams County, to gather signatures for their data center petitions, a campaign spokesperson said. Political leaders haven’t listened so far, said Matt Cheroutes, who is the campaign manager for the Weld County activists calling themselves Protect Our Water and Energy Resources, or POWER. “So now we’re taking this to the voters. The commissioners had their vote. Now it’s the people’s turn,” Cheroutes said.

artigo.texto: Nevada data centers promise big power demand. Who will pay the bill? As Nevada faces unprecedented demand for electricity from the data center industry, developers are pushing back against some of NV Energy’s proposed safeguards designed to prevent the cost of serving their projects from shifting to other customers. But as the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada weighs agreements with future data center customers, confidentiality claims and redactions are preventing the public from seeing project-specific information needed to determine whether those safeguards are sufficient. Many data center developers currently seeking electric service from NV Energy are requesting 300 to 500 megawatts of electricity, six to 10 times the roughly 50 megawatts a major casino or mine might use, said Shawn Elicegui, NV Energy’s senior vice president of regulatory and resource planning. “What we see from data centers is unprecedented,” Elicegui said in a recent interview. “There’s really nothing comparable to data center load.” Unlike most customers — such as households or small businesses, which typically receive a monthly bill based largely on how much electricity they use — data centers typically commit in advance to how much power they expect to need. If they take service under terms approved by the PUC, they can be required to make minimum payments based on those commitments, even if they ultimately use less electricity. The stakes are significant. NV Energy’s plans for future electricity needs account for the enormous demand expected from data centers and other large customers, as well as the infrastructure needed to serve them. If a data center ultimately uses less power than expected, the utility could be left with costs it expected the large customer to help cover, potentially shifting some of those costs to other ratepayers. NV Energy wants some of its largest new customers to pay minimum charges tied to at least 90 percent of the power demand and energy use they sign up for. At least one data center developer, however, wants that minimum set at 70 percent, according to PUC regulatory filings. The disagreement is a test of NV Energy’s promise that Nevada’s growing data-center industry will pay the costs it creates rather than shift them to other customers. Guardrails — but not enough information to test them A Las Vegas Review-Journal investigation found several guardrails in regulatory filings designed to support NV Energy’s repeated promise that data centers will pay their own way. They generally include proposed minimum payments, charges for new generation, financial guarantees and penalties if a customer leaves early. But simply having those protections does not show whether they are sufficient to prevent the costs of serving data centers from shifting onto other ratepayers, energy and utility-regulation experts told the Review-Journal. Sarah Wang, a researcher who studies massive customers called large loads, said regulators can calculate the minimum revenue a customer must provide and compare it with the costs the utility would not otherwise incur. “Without modeling, or some set of calculations, it’s really hard to figure out what 70 percent or 90 percent really mean,” said Wang, a senior associate at energy policy research organization RMI. Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, said the key question is whether the service agreements between utilities and data center developers cover all the infrastructure costs created by the new demand, rather than only some of them. “I believe that large loads should be required to pay for 100 percent of the incremental costs,” Peskoe said. Utilities around the country are confronting similar questions as they plan new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure to accommodate rapidly growing data center demand. New large-load customer rules increasingly use minimum payments, long-term contracts, financial guarantees and exit charges to reduce the risk that other customers are left paying for infrastructure built for projects that arrive late, use less power than expected or never fully develop. The Review-Journal examined proposed agreements between data center customers and NV Energy, utility testimony and power plans, and submitted multiple public records requests to the PUC. The public filings and records obtained for several data center projects the newspaper reviewed do not contain enough project-specific information to compare the minimum revenue those data centers would provide with the costs NV Energy would not otherwise incur — and determine whether any of those costs could shift to other ratepayers. What 90 percent vs. 70 percent really means The minimum-billing dispute is playing out in a pending commission case over proposed large-load electric service agreements between NV Energy and industrial real estate company Prologis for at least one data center project under development in North Las Vegas. The agreements would govern how NV Energy supplies data centers’ enormous power needs. Prologis argues that a 70 percent minimum better reflects how data centers actually operate, saying their electricity use does not consistently reach 90 percent of capacity in every billing period and can vary as tenants move in. Prologis did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Wang said a 70 percent minimum could recover all new costs incurred by a customer if the underlying rates, direct cost assignments, contract terms and exit provisions enable a utility to collect sufficient revenue. The reverse, she said, is also possible: Even requiring minimum billing at 100 percent of contracted demand would not guarantee full cost recovery if the rates or the way costs are assigned are inadequate. The goal, Wang said, should be 100 percent recovery of the total cost to serve — both the properly assigned new costs and the large customer’s share of existing infrastructure it uses.
