artigo.texto: Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) has committed €1.2 billion to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ (CIP) sixth flagship renewable energy fund, CI VI. NBIM said CI VI will primarily invest in renewable power generation and energy storage projects across OECD countries in North America, Western Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region. The investment builds on NBIM’s partnership with CIP, following a €900 million commitment to CIP’s fifth flagship fund in 2024 (see Norway Commits €900 Million To CIP’s Renewable Energy Fund). In March 2025, CIP said its CI V fund exceeded the target of €12 billion to support grid connection of 30 of new energy capacity (see Danish Fund Manager Exceeds €12B Target For New RE Fund). The renewable energy business of Australia’s Igneo Infrastructure Partners, Atmos Renewables, has reached financial close on two projects backed by Australia’s Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS). The projects comprise the 400 MW/1,600 MWh Teebar Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Queensland and the 470 MW Parron Maam Marang Wind Farm in Western Australia. Together with the 100 MW/400 MWh Merredin BESS, which reached financial close in June 2025, Atmos says it has now taken 970 MW of CIS-backed capacity through financial close. Teebar BESS will provide 4 hours of storage, storing electricity when supply is abundant and dispatching it during periods of higher demand. Atmos will retain ownership of both projects through construction and operate them once completed. Austrian independent power producer (IPP) Renalfa IPP and Danish renewable energy developer Eurowind Energy have inaugurated the Tenevo hybrid renewable energy complex in southeastern Bulgaria. The project combines a 242 MW solar PV plant with two co-located BESS totaling 311 MW/773 MWh. The Tenevo complex is expected to generate around 332 GWh of clean electricity annually. The solar plant and the first phase of the BESS have been operational since 2025, while the project has now reached its full announced storage capacity. The duo calls it one of Europe's largest hybrid renewable energy projects. Financed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Raiffeisen Bank International, with support from an InvestEU guarantee, the project is located next to a coal region undergoing transition. The Tenovo site is planned to expand with more than 250 MW of wind capacity, with total investment across all phases expected to exceed €500 million. US-based developer and manufacturer of iron-sodium battery systems Inlyte Energy and CutPeak Energy have announced plans for an 80 MWh long-duration BESS at Berkshire East Mountain Resort in western Massachusetts. CutPeak Energy develops battery storage projects at ski resorts. The project is targeted to come online in 2028. The project is one of two long-duration storage demonstrations selected under Massachusetts’ $40.3 million Advancing Massachusetts Power (AMP) Energy Storage Grant Program. The battery will help the resort manage electricity demand from snowmaking, which can reach about 4 MW during peak periods, while also providing backup power during grid outages. Inlyte says the project is designed to charge during periods of lower electricity demand and discharge during snowmaking peaks. European BESS projects operator GIGA Storage has achieved ready-to-build (RTB) status for its 350 MW/1.4 GWh Albatross battery energy storage project near Neuenkirchen in Lower Saxony, Germany. It is developing the project with Isenau Projects and will connect directly to Amprion’s 380 kV high-voltage grid. The project will comprise 264 battery units and is expected to supply electricity equivalent to the daily consumption of approximately 193,000 households. With the development phase completed, GIGA Storage plans to take the final investment decision (FID) in Q4 2026, start construction in H1 2027, and commission the project in 2028. Albatross is GIGA Storage’s first large-scale energy storage project in Germany. It is one of three projects being jointly developed by GIGA Storage and Isenau, with the three projects together representing more than 1 GW of power capacity and 4 GWh of storage capacity. Global energy infrastructure manager Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) has taken the FID on the Kilmarnock South BESS in southern Scotland. The company is investing more than €270 million in the 350 MW/1,400 MWh lithium-ion project. Construction is already underway, and it is expected to begin commercial operations in Q1 2028. The 4-hour BESS will store surplus wind power and discharge electricity to the grid when network capacity is available. CIP said this project is its fourth transmission-connected BESS investment in Scotland. It has an optimization agreement with Shell Energy Europe, ensuring long-term contracted revenue. Together, CIP shared that its four Scottish projects are expected to provide 1.85 GW of power capacity and 4.4 GWh of storage when fully operational. Excelsior Energy Capital-backed Lydian Energy has closed a $300 million holding company credit facility with Infranity, an infrastructure asset manager. Lydian will use the proceeds for the development, construction, acquisition, and operation of its utility-scale battery energy storage and solar projects across the US. Lydian said its portfolio includes about 6 GW of operating, construction-ready and development-stage projects. In April 2026, Lydian acquired 1.5 GW Atlas North solar-plus-storage portfolio from Hanwha Renewables (see Lydian Energy Acquires Hanwha’s 1.5 GW Atlas North Portfolio).

artigo.texto: SEATTLE — Amazon.com Inc. is pledging $1 billion or more over five years to communities where it builds and operates data centers. The company last week unveiled the “Built Together” investment framework for communities where the tech giant operates data centers across the United States. The increased investment will fund free community college for local residents, energy upgrades for homes and businesses, job training and protecting local water resources, the company said. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run,” Matt Garman, chief executive officer for Amazon Web Services, wrote in an October 2 post. “The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation’s focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so.” Amazon is a leading player in the tech industry’s massive AI buildout that relies, in part, on finding communities willing to host data centers. Garman noted that there are more than 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the United States. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race,” he said, “and the consequences would last generations.” Added Garman, “There are clearly areas in which the technology and energy industries can be doing better (along with their government partners) but just like in the past when the country has banded together to accomplish something that’s critical for our national security and economic prosperity — we should approach this as a long-term mission that the private and public sectors pursue together.” Amazon said it is responding to apprehension over the data center buildout by codifying a series of tenets in what the company is calling its “Amazon Data Center Commitment.” The company commits to “protect and enhance communities,” “provide jobs and economic opportunities,” “engage communities,” and “build and operate responsibly.” Submit Your Press Release Have news to share? artigo.texto: Good morning. Andrew Nusca here, back in action after a week in New York for our inaugural AIQ Summit about putting AI to work in large companies. (Many thanks to Alexei Oreskovic for steering the ship while I was away.) Miss the AIQ festivities? No sweat—you can watch the entire thing here or view a session of your choosing here. If you’re in the business of deploying AI in the enterprise, there are lots of good insights to be had. And today’s tech news? Well, let’s get right to it. —Andrew Nusca Thoughts? Suggestions? Hot tip? Drop me a line. THE BIG STORY Meta is building one of the world’s biggest undersea cable networks While data centers dominate headlines amid mounting local opposition over electricity bills, water use, and zoning fights, Meta has been expanding its infrastructure somewhere far less visible: the bottom of the ocean. On Sept. 21, the company announced Petal, a roughly 4,300-mile subsea cable connecting the U.S. and France. Meta says the cable, expected to enter service in 2029, will be the first to deliver petabit-scale capacity across an ocean—double what today’s most advanced transoceanic cables can handle, thanks to “two-core fiber” that fits two light paths inside each strand. Projects like this rarely make headlines in an industry fixated on AI models and apps, but they’re what make those products run. Products like Meta’s personal AI agent Muse depend on moving enormous volumes of data between its data centers and its users around the world. Subsea cables aren’t new territory for Meta, which is now valued at roughly $1.85 trillion. The company has spent the past decade building its presence on the seafloor and says it has invested in more than 20 subsea cable projects. Taken together, those projects touch every continent except Antarctica. The most ambitious is Project Waterworth, announced in February 2025. Meta says the system will stretch more than 31,000 miles, longer than the Earth’s circumference. It will connect the U.S., Brazil, South Africa, India, and other regions across five continents. Meta hasn’t built all of this alone. Petal is being developed with Japan’s NEC and Sumitomo Electric Industries, and French telecom Orange is handling the landing on France’s Atlantic coast. Meta has even partnered with rivals: The MAREA cable between Virginia and Spain, completed in 2017, is jointly owned with Microsoft and telecom company Telxius. These projects don’t come cheap. TechCrunch estimates that the Waterworth project could top $10 billion. —James LaForge THE BLIND BOX “Just because you are using AI, that is not a proxy for your productivity or you doing a good job at work.” THE RUNDOWN —Trump forms “Super Intelligence Force” led by National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton. —OpenAI CEO Sam Altman: “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” —Meta's Muse compiles “a page for every person in the user's life,” per Wired. —Firmus IPO: Investor demand far exceeds the offer size, one of Australia's largest. —Schneider Electric may buy PTC, the U.S. engineering software firm, for $20 billion. —Apple CEO John Ternus is in the design studio “several times per week,” per Bloomberg. —McKinsey: AI and automation will eliminate 36 million U.S. jobs by 2035 but add 41 million elsewhere. —U.K. neobank Monzo may sell a 15% stake to CVC and Advent after a Nubank deal fell apart. THE PARTING SLOP Sam told Mark not to say anything. Mark can't go in there, brazenly flaunt the rules and then think Sam’s gonna share his CUDA with him. Sorry! This is what comes from living under a Jensen regime.

artigo.texto: Cygni Energy and Indus Towers will explore BESS manufacturing capacity of up to 1.5 GWh for telecom applications The companies will evaluate higher-capacity and emerging battery technologies for telecom infrastructure Cygni currently operates a 4.8 GWh cell-to-container BESS facility in Hyderabad and plans to expand its overall capacity beyond 10 GWh Indian energy storage manufacturer Cygni Energy and telecom infrastructure company Indus Towers have joined hands to explore up to 1.5 GWh of battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing in India to serve telecom infrastructure. The duo has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) and plans to establish manufacturing capacity to meet the ‘evolving energy requirements’ of telecom infrastructure in India. The partnership will also evaluate advanced battery technologies for telecom applications. Formed by the merger of Bharti Infratel Limited and Indus Towers, Indus Towers Limited had over 267,611 towers and 432,250 co-locations as of June 30, 2026. It is present across 22 telecom circles. While Cygni's official statement does not reveal details about the MoU, telecom companies have been exploring energy storage as a backup power strategy to improve operational efficiency. According to Battery Council International (BCI), batteries can help provide stable power for data centers and telecom systems. Incubated at IIT Madras, Cygni Energy develops energy storage products for telecom, stationary energy storage, mobility, and other applications. Its battery portfolio currently includes 100 Ah solutions and could expand to higher-capacity systems, including 314 Ah. “We plan to develop capacity of up to 2 GWh, while building a portfolio that can evolve from today’s 100Ah solutions to higher-capacity 314Ah systems and emerging battery technologies,” said Cygni Energy Founder & CEO Venkat Rajaraman. In 2025, Cygni Energy opened a 4.8 GWh cell-to-container BESS Gigafactory in Hyderabad’s Maheshwaram, with plans to scale it up to exceed 10 GWh in the future. “Our ambition is to combine scale, reliability and Indian engineering to create future-ready energy storage solutions that can evolve alongside India’s rapidly expanding digital infrastructure,” added Rajaraman. According to Crisil, India could see up to 50 GWh of BESS installations by FY2028 as the technology helps improve power availability during peak demand. However, reducing reliance on overseas suppliers remains important to limit exposure to global supply disruptions and procurement uncertainties (see Crisil Projects India To Add 50 GWh BESS Capacity By FY2028).

artigo.texto: Amazon responde à reação contra seus centros de dados: fim das siglas e uma nova postura na era da transparência Recentemente, a Amazon Web Services (AWS) tentou acalmar as crescentes suspeitas e críticas relacionadas à operação de seus centros de dados, após uma forte repercussão negativa. Em uma resposta que surpreendeu muitos, a gigante do e-commerce declarou que não utiliza mais acordos de confidencialidade (NDAs) como ferramenta de blindagem, sinalizando uma tentativa de maior transparência. Este movimento é mais do que uma simples mudança administrativa: é um sinal de que gigantes de tecnologia estão sendo forçados a repensar suas estratégias de comunicação diante de uma sociedade cada vez mais consciente e questionadora. Rebatendo a desconfiança: a tentativa da Amazon de abrir os seus centros de dados O impacto da transparência na relação com o público Ao afirmar que não usa mais NDAs para esconder suas operações, a Amazon tenta reverter a narrativa de opacidade que assola a indústria de tecnologia. Essa postura pode ajudar a reconstruir a confiança dos consumidores e investidores, que hoje buscam mais do que apenas eficiência; querem responsabilidade e clareza. Em tempos de vigilância digital e debates sobre privacidade, a transparência deixou de ser um diferencial e virou uma necessidade. Por outro lado, essa mudança também pode ser vista como uma estratégia de marketing, uma tentativa de mostrar uma imagem mais aberta e ética diante de seus concorrentes. Afinal, a confiança não se conquista apenas com palavras, mas com ações concretas de transparência que comprovem a ausência de práticas questionáveis. A decisão da Amazon reforça a ideia de que, na era digital, informações são poder — e quem as controla, domina a narrativa. Por fim, essa postura pode influenciar toda uma indústria, levando outras empresas a adotarem uma postura mais aberta. Uma maior transparência pode criar um efeito dominó, promovendo uma cultura empresarial mais responsável e menos sigilosa, em benefício de toda a sociedade. O debate ético: confidencialidade versus transparência O uso de NDAs sempre foi uma ferramenta de proteção legal, mas também um método de esconder práticas que podem ser questionadas. A Amazon, ao anunciar que não utiliza mais essas siglas, coloca em xeque uma prática que há muito tempo é alvo de críticas na tecnologia. Afinal, quão transparente uma empresa precisa ser para atender às expectativas de uma sociedade cada vez mais informada? Por outro lado, há questões legítimas sobre segurança de dados, propriedade intelectual e estratégias comerciais que justificam certos níveis de sigilo. Equilibrar transparência e proteção não é uma tarefa simples, mas a postura da Amazon sugere que a balança deve pender mais para a abertura, especialmente em tempos de crise de confiança. Essa mudança de postura pode servir de exemplo para o setor, que frequentemente oscila entre sigilo e transparência. Por fim, essa discussão também revela uma mudança cultural: a sociedade está mais atenta e exige que as empresas sejam responsáveis e abertas. A ética corporativa, portanto, deixa de ser apenas uma questão de boas intenções e passa a ser uma estratégia de sobrevivência no mercado global. O futuro da comunicação corporativa na era digital A resposta da Amazon à reação contra seus centros de dados marca um ponto de virada na comunicação empresarial. Empresas que antes preferiam o sigilo agora precisam se adaptar a um cenário onde a transparência é cada vez mais esperada e exigida. Essa mudança pode impulsionar uma nova era de diálogo aberto, onde informações antes restritas se tornam acessíveis ao público. O impacto dessa postura pode se refletir em uma relação mais saudável entre corporações e sociedade, promovendo uma cultura de responsabilidade. Além disso, empresas que adotam uma postura mais transparente tendem a conquistar maior fidelidade e respeito, essenciais na construção de uma marca sólida e sustentável. Por outro lado, há o risco de que essa abertura excessiva gere vulnerabilidades e exposições desnecessárias. Assim, o desafio será encontrar um equilíbrio que permita transparência sem comprometer a segurança e a competitividade. O que a Amazon nos mostra é que, na era digital, a comunicação não pode mais ser uma via de mão única, mas um diálogo constante e sincero. Reflexões finais: a transparência como caminho para a credibilidade no mundo tecnológico A resposta da Amazon ao backlash, afirmando que não utiliza mais NDAs, é um passo importante na direção de uma maior transparência no setor de tecnologia. Essa mudança reflete uma sociedade que não aceita mais mistérios e busca entender melhor o funcionamento das grandes corporações que moldam seu cotidiano. A credibilidade, neste cenário, depende cada vez mais de ações que reforçam a confiança. Embora ainda existam desafios e limites para a abertura total, esse movimento sinaliza que o mercado está mudando. Empresas que adotarem uma postura honesta e transparente poderão se destacar em um ambiente cada vez mais competitivo e consciente. Para o consumidor, essa é uma oportunidade de exigir mais responsabilidade e ética de quem fornece produtos e serviços. Convido você, leitor, a refletir: até que ponto a transparência pode transformar a relação entre empresas e sociedade? Compartilhe sua opinião nos comentários ou compartilhe este artigo para ampliar o debate sobre o futuro da comunicação corporativa na era digital. Some cities and towns across the US are ultimately earning concessions as hyperscalers come under pressure: Teachers in Louisiana got bonuses thanks to Meta, for example, and NorthPoint Development proposed giving $10,000 to every household in a Pennsylvania township.

artigo.texto: A reação contrária à construção de data centers para inteligência artificial nos Estados Unidos está se espalhando para a Europa e a Ásia e aumenta os riscos para investidores, segundo reportagem da CNBC. Conforme a emissora americana, o sentimento negativo cresce do outro lado do Atlântico, onde países densamente povoados e preços de energia mais altos deixam a situação mais delicada. Tensões parecidas surgem na Coreia do Sul, com oposição a projetos perto de áreas residenciais e propostas de restrições locais mais rígidas, mesmo com o governo nacional tentando acelerar o desenvolvimento. Segundo levantamento da STL Partners citado pela CNBC, a oposição pública já afetou cerca de US$ 42 bilhões em investimentos em data centers na Europa, entre atrasos e cancelamentos. Nos Estados Unidos, o valor chega a aproximadamente US$ 77 bilhões. Pesquisa do European Data Center Monitor mostra que mais de 70 projetos europeus foram rejeitados ou restringidos entre janeiro e abril, número superior ao registrado em todo o ano de 2025. A resistência deixou de ficar restrita a prefeituras e chegou a tribunais, reguladores e parlamentos, informou a CNBC. Europa aperta as regras A Escócia suspendeu a aprovação de novos data centers de grande porte depois que grupos de campanha pediram ao governo que evitasse repetir o caso da Irlanda, onde a demanda por energia levou a uma moratória. Na região nórdica, a Dinamarca aprovou uma lei emergencial que pode colocar data centers no fim da fila de pedidos de conexão à rede elétrica. A Espanha propôs neste ano novas regras que exigem que 80% da eletricidade desses centros venha de fontes renováveis, e projetos no Reino Unido ficaram parados após a oposição de moradores, segundo a CNBC. As preocupações envolvem consumo de água, gasto de energia, preços da eletricidade e o espaço exigido por alguns centros. Olivier Darmouni, professor associado da HEC Paris especializado em transição energética, disse à CNBC que a resistência pública pode ter um peso decisivo sobre o setor e que os ganhos da inteligência artificial são muito difusos. Ele acrescentou que a população mais densa da Europa e o fato de muitos operadores serem empresas americanas podem fazer a reação ser mais forte no continente. Coreia do Sul no centro da disputa A Coreia do Sul, sede de Samsung Electronics e SK Hynix, classificou em junho os data centers de IA como um de seus três principais projetos de investimento, ao lado de semicondutores e IA física. No distrito de Geumcheon, no sudoeste de Seul, moradores pedem a revogação da licença e a paralisação das obras de um data center perto de suas casas. Em julho, autoridades anunciaram planos de exigir consentimento da maioria dos residentes num raio de 200 metros dos locais propostos e de criar um sistema de revisão em três etapas para mediar conflitos. Os protestos em frente à sede do governo local já duravam 172 dias em meados de agosto, segundo a imprensa local citada pela CNBC. Em Gwacheon, um vereador propôs uma norma para proteger moradores de riscos ligados ao funcionamento contínuo desses centros, incluindo incêndios em baterias de backup. Asya Walters, diretora-gerente da Alvarez & Marsal, disse à CNBC que a capacidade de uma comunidade de barrar um projeto de US$ 10 bilhões é bastante poderosa. Segundo ela, o ambiente favorável aos negócios nos EUA ajudou historicamente a superar resistências, enquanto na Europa e na Ásia a alternância entre condições favoráveis e regulação mais restritiva dificulta o investimento. Ela lembrou que os operadores gastam muito antes de obter as licenças. Eulalia Flo, vice-presidente da Equinix para mercados emergentes na Europa, Oriente Médio e África, afirmou à CNBC que a infraestrutura digital está mais visível e que o ambiente regulatório está de fato ficando mais rígido em alguns mercados, sem que isso represente um limite estrutural ao crescimento. Para Dominic Ward, CEO da Verne, o setor deixou de ser desconhecido e passou a ser uma das camadas fundamentais que movem a economia.

artigo.texto: DENR sets forest carbon market regulatory foundations Nicer called for stronger global guidance on market infrastructure and supply-side integrity for forest and blue carbon ecosystems. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) recently disclosed that the Philippines has already established the regulatory foundations of a credible forest carbon market by issuing two major policy instruments designed to directly address private sector expectations for clear rules, credible safeguards, and transparent project pathways. Atty. Daniel Darius M. Nicer, DENR assistant secretary for integrated management system and information systems, spoke at the High-Level Roundtable convened in the sidelines of 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York last week, and declared that these regulatory milestones position the country to attract high-integrity private investments in nature-based carbon projects. Addressing international ministers, climate envoys and business executives at the session titled “Shaping High-Integrity Carbon Markets,” Nicer emphasized that corporate buyers require predictability and environmental rigor before deploying capital at scale. “To date, the Philippines, through its Department of Environment and Natural Resources, issued two major policy instruments that establish the foundations of a credible forest carbon market directly addressing private sector expectations for clear rules, credible safeguards, and transparent project pathways,” he said during the meeting convened by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development at Climate Week NYC. The first policy instrument is the adoption of the Philippines’ Readiness in the Voluntary Forest Carbon Market Roadmap (2026 to 2030). The strategic framework sets out national direction for policy development, measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) systems, data management, and registry readiness — key elements corporate investors evaluate when assessing market reliability. The second instrument is the national guidelines for the establishment, registration and monitoring of voluntary forest carbon credit projects. These rules enforce environmental integrity, Free, Prior and Informed Consent compliance, and guaranteed community benefit-sharing, while mandating transparent project registration to significantly reduce reputational and delivery risks for corporate buyers. “For the Philippines, carbon markets — both voluntary and compliance pathways — are central to our strategy for accelerating mitigation and unlocking climate finance,” Nicer said. “But for markets to function, the private sector needs clarity, predictability, and confidence that the credits they purchase are real, additional, and backed by strong governance.” Beyond forestry, Nicer highlighted broader national carbon governance efforts, including the Department of Energy’s guidelines for renewable energy projects, the overarching Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework, and the rollout of the Philippine National Carbon Registry to ensure full accounting traceability and prevent double counting. He added that domestic policies are aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement through bilateral partnerships, such as the Implementation Agreement with Singapore and the Joint Crediting Mechanism with Japan. Looking ahead to the COP31 climate summit, he called for stronger global guidance on market infrastructure and supply-side integrity for forest and blue carbon ecosystems. “High-integrity markets should not only accelerate global ambition, but also deliver real, measurable mitigation outcomes that directly benefit and reach the communities, ecosystems, and sectors that need them most,” Nicer said. artigo.texto: What does the data say about data centers? People everywhere are talking about data centers, the high-tech facilities that house our nations growing digital infrastructure. Illinois is a Top 10 state for data centers, with a history dating all the way back to the 1970s, initially as a central repository to meet the technology needs of state agencies. More recently, however, data centers have become the foundation of a global technology race in the private sector, housing large computer servers, storage, and networking equipment necessary to support cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI). In Illinois, they comprise 7% of total electricity demand (and climbing). Many rely on water for cooling. And new data centers often come seemingly out-of-nowhere, as major technology companies use of nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) with elected officials instead of committing to public transparency. All of which has contributed to a public backlash against construction of these facilities that is playing out in statehouses and electoral campaigns around the country. Developments have been canceled or postponed, and Gov. JB Pritzker paused Illinois tax exemption for data centers. But data centers now are a fixture of the modern economy. Understanding their costs and benefits and identifying the guardrails needed to mitigate risk to our communities is of paramount importance. It is with these factors in mind that the Illinois Economic Policy Institute and the Project for Middle Class Renewal at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign recently undertook the most robust analysis of Illinois data centers to date. Specifically, we looked at 75 completed and ongoing projects and related reports culled from state, county, and industry data, and integrated industry-standard economic modeling to forecast potential impacts of $57 billion in planned data center projects across our state over the next decade. Here’s what we found. First, data centers mean jobs. More than 120,000 of them over the next 10 years, to be exact. About a third of these will be in skilled construction occupations or IT, engineering, and operations jobs that pay well into the six figures, and the other two-thirds in the supply chain or as a result of related increases in consumer spending across the economy. This investment will grow the Illinois economy by $5 billion a year during the construction phase, and about $2 billion per year thereafter. The facilities would also mean $300 million in new property tax revenue going to local communities each year nearly two-thirds of which will support public schools. When it comes to protecting communities from potential costs, the picture is more complex. By 2035, new data centers could use the same electricity as 4.5 million Illinois homes. Without any sort of requirements that data centers produce or otherwise offset their power demands, this would increase average Illinois household electric bills by $12 per month. Water resources can also be strained, unless new data centers use the air-cooling or closed-loop systems which recycle water instead of constantly drawing on new resources that are becoming commonplace. In both cases, there are tools available to policymakers to mitigate the risk and ensure responsible development of data centers. First, they can be required to pay for 100% of their energy, transmission, and interconnection costs and to use closed-loop or air-cooling systems to reduce water usage. The currently suspended sales tax exemption could be reformed to promote stronger energy and environmental standards, rewarding only those facilities that install Illinois-based clean energy. New data centers can be required to have battery storage. And policymakers can improve public disclosure around energy usage, water usage, and contact with elected officials. Even though the data on data centers shows they can be a net positive for our economy and our communities, there is a trust deficit. With commonsense guardrails, Illinois can modernize our energy system, protect workers and ratepayers, and improve transparency around an industry that too many people believe has been operating in the dark. Frank Manzo IV, MPP is an economist at the nonpartisan Illinois Economic Policy Institute.

artigo.texto: Cheyenne and Arapaho tribal citizens voted Saturday to impose a three-year moratorium on data center construction on tribal lands. During the tribal meeting, the floor was opened for anyone to speak about the topic. The primary concerns related to environmental, economic and transparency issues. Key Takeaways - Cheyenne and Arapaho tribal citizens voted Saturday for a three-year moratorium on data center construction on tribal lands. - Of 351 votes cast, 261 supported the moratorium, 83 opposed it and seven abstained. - Tribal citizens raised concerns about water use, environmental effects, potential economic benefits and transparency surrounding future data center proposals. - Cheyenne and Arapaho Gov. Reggie Wassana said no data center agreement has been signed and said any potential project would undergo further study and community discussion. Environmental Concerns “We have a spiritual responsibility because we are Cheyenne and Arapaho people and our traditional values respect this water of life,” said Kyle Spotted Horse, a member of the Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes. He brought up Mní Wičóni at Standing Rock, the location of a protest against an oil pipeline that crosses Sioux land in the Dakotas. In 2016, a vocal protest against the Dakota Access Pipe Line took place, creating the Mní Wičóni movement to protect water and tribal lands. Spotted Horse said a data center would require 300,000 gallons of water per day, adding up to 100 million gallons per year. RELATED: Oklahomans Gather In Downtown OKC In Support Of Standing Rock Sioux Tribe A group of Oklahomans gathered at downtown Oklahoma City’s Kerr Park to show support for the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe in their fight against the Dakota Access Pipeline. “Until we adjudicate our water rights, how do we move forward with such a massive amount of consumption of water?” Patrick Kincaid said. According to Oklahoma State University, water right adjudication is the process through which groups can establish who has ownership of which bodies of water. “You know what would be a dealbreaker for me is that through this whole process, there is 100% transparency. No NDAs and a full impact study, especially on our buffalo,” said another woman. “We’ve spent years building our herds. How will this affect our buffalo herd? And as good neighbors, what impact will this have on surrounding farms and farmland and animals? I want us to be informed all along the way.” Damon Dunbar raised the question of fracking and its comparable water usage to a potential data center. “They’re draining Canton Lake right now to feed Oklahoma City. That’s not funny, that’s very deadly. We’re not going to be having anything. We’re going to be looking like south Texas or the desert.” Another man was concerned about the effects of drought and further water usage on the community and environment. “I don’t get up and say much at these meetings, but this part is very important,” he finished, a sentiment echoed by another speaker. “Water is our way of life. If we don’t protect our lands, who’s going to? If we don’t stand up for our kids, who’s going to?” A woman said, supporting the moratorium. RELATED: How much water does AI really use? Governor’s Response Governor Wassanna responded to these concerns, saying a potential data center would use a closed loop system, challenging earlier estimates of 300,000 gallons of water per day being used. “The water usage has developed to where there’s little to none except filling it up because it’s a closed loop,” he said. Wassanna further clarified that data centers are now capable of using cooling coils which do not use as much water as previous facilities. “It won’t be 300,000 gallons a day. Actually, cities use more water on their golf courses than people would actually use probably for data centers.” Economic Concerns “I feel like it’s the old days of the old cattle barons, oil barons, people wanting to exploit our resources, snake oil salesmen,” Spotted Horse said of the economic impact of a potential data center. He questioned who would receive the profits from the facility. Governor’s Response “Data centers are huge profit making projects. They make over $1 billion a year. 20%, 30%, $200 million. Somebody told us the other day, ‘Reggie, we make $90 million a day.’ $90 million a day,” said Wassanna. “If you want to look at the tribe’s share, you look at elders, you look at per cap, you look at housing, renovations, all these things we talk about that we’re hurting. Food, gas, these things.” Wassanna further stressed that if a data center was built on tribal lands, those in the Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes wouldn’t have to worry about financial issues. “You’d be comfortable, the most comfortable tribe around in western Oklahoma.” Transparency Concerns “We have a responsibility not only to ourselves and this water and Mother Earth, but we also have a responsibility to our community. How many have heard about Yukon voting out their mayor because he did an NDA? Kudos to them for doing that,” Spotted Horse said in reference to the recent recall motion against Yukon mayor Brian Pillmore in Aug. “How would they feel if we just ripped right behind their back in their backyard and did our own thing, potentially causing water pollution, air pollution, not to mention electrical grid cost impacts.” RELATED: Yukon certifies recall petition against Mayor Brian Pillmore “If we make this decision today, in 3 years, we’ll have a better idea of how this is going to impact our future, our children,” said a woman named Vera. The moratorium would halt any data center construction for three years. Governor’s Response “I just want to say something. Before, there was going to be community meetings. This resolution came up, but there was going to be community meetings. Nothing’s been signed, there is a feasibility study that was going to be done. The legislators all acknowledged it. We ain’t done nothing yet. This is up to you guys to say yes or no.” RELATED:

artigo.texto: I’ll admit that I’m the Computer Village Idiot when it comes to using technology like personal computers and smartphones; I still struggle. And I’m in over my head trying to figure out this whole AI (artificial intelligence) thing that some Anthropic research experts believe could ultimately destroy mankind. Are you thinking about artificial intelligence? AI is in the news everywhere these days, and the subject of AI data centers popping up in one’s town or city is enough to freak out most people. There are many unknowns about artificial intelligence, and we need to learn as much as we can about this new technology. Here in the Granite State, there are multiple traditional data centers, but they aren’t the same as AI data centers. There’s often confusion about the two, and unfortunately, AI has become the catch-all term for modern tech infrastructure. For instance, data center space is available for lease in Nashua Technology Park off Exit 1 near the NH/MA border. The campus offers dedicated data center space equipped with heavy-duty corporate infrastructure, but it lacks the capacity and available land for a huge hyperscale or large-scale AI build. And the same could be said for my city’s Millyard Technology Park in the historic district. The tech park leases general office space to companies of all sizes under one roof, featuring “software firms, various service businesses, more than one corporate headquarters, and a few computer hardware companies,” its website says. I know of no AI data center proposals in Nashua, and that’s good news to me. However, a warehouse-sized data center using 40 acres of land on Old Turnpike Road was proposed for the town of Nottingham last May. Residents were up in arms, blasting Granite State developer Tom Moulton. He later withdrew his application because of heavy community opposition. Nottingham residents recently voted overwhelmingly on a 12-month moratorium on any data center development within town limits. That enormous proposal wouldn’t sit well with most people. Massive data centers consume tons of energy, thereby placing a significant strain on water infrastructure and the power grid. These facilities are also seen as a threat to residents’ income, quality of life and the environment. In Bow, residents have come out fighting hard against Granite Shore Power, which owns the shuttered Merrimack Station. The owners had filed a request with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to discuss connecting a 350-megawatt project to the regional power grid for a potential hyperscale AI data center. No data center development proposal has been submitted to the town yet, but that was enough to draw outraged locals to the Bow municipal building. Some of us also wonder about the harm AI could do to the journalism industry. Generative AI is considered a time-and-money-saving newsroom tool that can handle diverse data types like documents, videos and social media at speeds unmatched by traditional processing. But it could also eliminate jobs. However, AI has limitations and cannot replace human reporting, as Mike Reilley explained in an essay for the Red Line Project. Reilley is a University of Illinois Chicago digital journalism professor and an expert in artificial intelligence and data visualization within newsrooms. “Specifically, AI cannot: physically enter a courtroom or interview a defendant behind bars; cultivate trust with a whistleblower; brave the front lines of a war zone; provide the critical thinking, original reporting and smart editorial judgment that humans do.” Innovation should always be welcomed with responsibility. On that note, here’s to a free press!

artigo.texto: Trending VANDALIA, Ohio --- President Donald Trump defended data centers that power artificial intelligence projects but have become a contentious campaign issue nationwide, as he took his midterm tour to Ohio this weekend to insist his party will keep its majorities in Congress despite steep political headwinds. Trump took several minutes during his campaign rally in southwestern Ohio near Dayton late Saturday night to promote his administration's action on data centers, saying he was seeking to ensure they "benefit local communities" and praising Republican Sen. Jon Husted for an ill-fated attempt to push forward legislation on the issue. "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China," Trump said, repeating his defense of data centers that he had made before. The massive warehouse campuses generating energy for AI projects have become a toxic political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies. It's become especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centers to Ohio when he served as lieutenant governor. Trump is embarking on what he says will be a 32-day blitz ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, hitting the deep red states of Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama last week before pivoting to Ohio, a battleground state once again that's home to one of the top-tier Senate races this cycle. Husted -- who was appointed to fill the Senate vacancy left by now-Vice President JD Vance -- is running to win the seat outright. There is likely no path to a Senate majority for Democrats without flipping Ohio, where former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown is trying to return to the Senate after losing to Republican Bernie Moreno two years ago. Polls show that race is extremely tight. Since last year, Democrats have listed Ohio, along with states such as North Carolina and Maine, as key races to win control of the Senate. And this past week, the head of the Senate GOP's campaign arm said Ohio is among 10 battleground races that are "within striking distance." "The good news for us is that Jon Husted is a closer," Sen. Tim Scott, the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told reporters. "We're seeing the gap that was there between the two candidates, which was just a few points, now it is right at a dead-even race. So this is as tight as ticks, as we say in South Carolina." DATA CENTERS At his rallies, Trump has been trying to convince voters that the economy is better than they feel it is, even though polls show Americans are frustrated with the way he's handled it. The high cost of living, including gas prices elevated by Trump's war on Iran, is a top issue in the Dayton area, too. And just days before Trump's rally, nearly 1,400 people were laid off from a truck factory in nearby Springfield. "Your state is booming. Every -- I hate to say it -- every state is booming," Trump said Saturday. "They're all booming." Trump's rally comes as Republicans worry that Husted's campaign has failed to adequately catch fire with voters in the state. Brown and allied groups have hammered Husted for his data-centers role, and the NRSC has pinpointed it as a political vulnerability. The GOP-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats. "You got to remember, Sherrod Brown was for data centers, and Jon Husted is for data centers being responsible," Scott told reporters this week. "If a community doesn't want them, he doesn't want them either." But Trump has become one of data centers' most vocal proponents, shrugging aside voter concerns and arguing that the U.S. cannot cede advancements in AI to China. "Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio," Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump's visit. "Now, he's making Ohioans foot the bill." Brown's campaign also has hammered Husted for donations he's received from retail magnate Les Wexner, who once employed the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Husted has donated remaining Wexner contributions to an anti-human trafficking charity. There were several Epstein-themed signs outside the Vandalia school where the rally was being held, as more than a hundred protesters lined the road with a slew of anti-Trump and anti-Husted signs. But inside the school's gymnasium, the boisterous crowd -- decked out in red "Make America Great Again" hats and "Trump 47" jerseys -- greeted each Republican candidate enthusiastically as they awaited the president's arrival. From the stage, Husted said the state had been through "hard times," noting his dad had worked at a factory that closed down. But he said Republicans in the state had turned it around. "We now have the most jobs and the lowest unemployment rate we've ever had in the history of Ohio," he said. Meanwhile, in the governor's race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state's former COVID-era health director. A wealthy biotech entrepreneur and 2024 presidential candidate, Ramaswamy's star appeal among conservatives led to quick backing by Ohio Republicans and hopes of an easy victory in the Republican-dominated state. However, despite a massive fundraising lead and more than $12 million spent in campaign advertising, he is now locked in a close fight with Acton with weeks to go until Election Day. "I'm so grateful to this state and to this country for giving a kid like me opportunities that would not have been available to my family in any other country on planet earth," Ramaswamy said at the rally ahead of Trump's arrival, as he underscored the American dream for his Indian immigrant family.

artigo.texto: Dubai construiu a primeira usina hidrelétrica reversível da região das Arábias para transformar luz solar acumulada de dia em eletricidade disponível em segundos durante a noite. No meio do deserto montanhoso de Dubai, a escassez de rios volumosos exigiu uma solução ousada para estocar a energia sobressalente gerada por usinas solares do país. Como uma montanha no deserto consegue armazenar eletricidade sem usar baterias? Imagine usar o excesso de energia solar durante o dia para empurrar milhões de litros de água até o topo de um morro. Quando a noite chega e o sol se apaga, a água cai com força total e gira geradores gigantescos. Esse conceito simples transforma o desnível do terreno em uma imensa bateria gravitacional. Na **Usina de Hatta**, as turbinas funcionam em sentido duplo: bombeiam água morro acima quando há sobra solar e operam como geradores na descida. Essa tecnologia se chama usina hidrelétrica reversível e apresenta eficiência global de armazenamento superior a 75% sem degradação química ao longo de décadas. Quais são os números e especificações da usina hidrelétrica de Hatta? Projetada sob responsabilidade da **DEWA**, a estrutura combina geotecnia pesada com engenharia hidráulica avançada para operar de forma contínua no clima árido dos Emirados Árabes Unidos. Potência nominal instalada: entrega 250 MW por meio de duas unidades geradoras de 125 MW acopladas a turbinas reversíveis tipo Francis. - Capacidade de armazenamento operacional: totaliza 1.500 MWh de energia garantida, o equivalente a seis horas ininterruptas de geração em carga máxima. - Volume do reservatório superior: comporta 5,3 milhões de m³ de água contidos por duas barragens de **concreto compactado com rolo**. - Extensão do túnel subterrâneo: possui cerca de 1,2 km de comprimento com diâmetro de 7 metros escavados no maciço rochoso. - Velocidade de resposta operacional: atinge acionamento total em até 90 segundos para estabilizar flutuações repentinas na rede elétrica nacional. O que acontece na prática quando a cidade de Dubai precisa de energia urgente? Quando ar-condicionado e indústrias elevam o consumo elétrico no pico da noite, válvulas de grande porte se abrem no reservatório superior. A água despenca sob altíssima pressão pelo túnel subterrâneo de 1,2 km de extensão, ganhando aceleração antes de atingir a casa de força escavada na rocha. Ao chegar às turbinas, o fluxo hídrico faz girar os eixos em alta rotação, gerando eletricidade imediata antes de desembocar na represa inferior. Durante as horas de sol alto, o ciclo se inverte usando energia do **Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park** para mandar a água de volta ao topo. Como a engenharia escavou mais de um quilômetro de rocha nas montanhas Hajar? Construir uma usina hidráulica em ambiente desértico exigiu perfurações com explosivos e tuneladoras de alta precisão para criar condutos capazes de suportar pressões hídricas extremas sem vazamentos no solo. O registro audiovisual detalha o avanço das escavações subterrâneas e a montagem das estruturas de concreto que sustentam o complexo energético de Dubai. Abaixo, um vídeo do canal The National News que aprofunda o tema: Quais normas de engenharia garantem a segurança de usinas hidráulicas reversíveis? Projetos de usinas reversíveis seguem diretrizes internacionais rígidas, como a norma **IEC 60041** para testes de aceitação de turbinas hidráulicas e a **IEEE 1010** para controle e proteção de centrais hidrelétricas. No Brasil, requisitos similares de estanqueidade e segurança de barragens são regidos pela **NBR 11502** e pela Lei de Segurança de Barragens. Esses padrões estabelecem limites rígidos para tolerância de vibração em turbinas e estipulam fatores de segurança em maciços rochosos, prevenindo rupturas estruturais ou perdas de água por infiltração profunda no solo. Quando é necessário contratar um engenheiro hidráulico e geotécnico? Dimensionar reservatórios, contenções de solo ou sistemas de bombeamento de grande vazão exige estudos geológicos aprofundados e modelagem computacional de fluidos. Qualquer intervenção em barragens ou condutos forçados requer a assinatura técnica de um **engenheiro geotécnico** ou **engenheiro hidráulico** qualificado. Tentativas manuais de contenção de água ou escavação não profissional podem provocar erosão acelerada, colapso de taludes e alagamentos catastróficos nas áreas a montante e a jusante. Contexto importante: Este artigo é informativo. Para projetos estruturais locais similares, recomenda-se avaliação de engenheiro geotécnico ou hidráulico, especialmente em contextos de risco de vazamento, infiltração, impacto ambiental ou comprometimento estrutural.

artigo.texto: Jupiter Wagons shares hit a day high of Rs 226.99 on 5 October, up 1%, after the firm won a Rs 100 crore battery storage order in Uttarakhand. The company told exchanges about the win at around 13:30 pm. Jupiter Wagons, better known for building railway wagons, landed the job through JEM Energy, its clean energy arm. Madhav Infra Projects Limited is its partner on the project. The customer is Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited (UPCL). The project is essentially a giant battery. It stores electricity when demand is low and sends it back to the grid when demand peaks. The system is rated at 41 MW and can hold 102.5 MWh of energy. Jupiter and its partner will supply and set it up, and the work is worth about Rs 100 crore. The two firms won by quoting the lowest price in a competitive bidding round run by UPCL. It is JEM Energy’s first project in Uttarakhand. This is not the only recent win. In August 2026, the company also received a formal award letter from West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited. That job is a 50 MW/200 MWh battery project at the Jeerat substation in North 24 Parganas. Managing Director Vivek Lohia called both wins important steps in turning JEM Energy into a bigger business. Jupiter Wagons still aims to build a battery storage order book of about Rs 1,000 crore by FY27. Lohia also said the electric mobility arm, Jupiter Electric Mobility, should start making an operating profit in the October to December quarter of FY27. He expects it to turn profitable overall by FY28. The orders follow the Union Cabinet’s approval of Green Energy Corridor Phase-III, which includes 50 GWh of battery storage. The early rally did not hold. Jupiter Wagons closed at Rs 223.44 on the NSE, down 0.22%, after swinging between a low of Rs 218.61 and its high of Rs 226.99. artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA atNorth planeja o Data Center FIN05 em Salo, Finlândia, com caminho para 230 MW Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google O operador nórdico de data centers atNorth, em 5 de outubro de 2026, anunciou planos para desenvolver o FIN05, um novo data center em Salo, Finlândia. A empresa espera investir aproximadamente €2 bilhões no site de 28,6 hectares, onde a energia para a primeira fase planejada de 75 MW está garantida, com um caminho para até 230 MW para o desenvolvimento mais amplo. Especificações do Site e Planos de Investimento A atNorth afirmou que Salo oferece uma localização forte para infraestrutura crítica que atende clientes com exigentes requisitos de conectividade e resiliência. A empresa citou a proximidade da cidade com Helsinque e o pool de talentos digitais da Finlândia como fatores adicionais que sustentam o desenvolvimento, e posicionou o FIN05 como parte de seu objetivo contínuo de atender à demanda por infraestrutura digital de alto desempenho de maneira responsável. O site será conectado por meio de uma subestação da Fingrid. O investimento esperado de €2 bilhões da empresa não inclui servidores de propriedade dos clientes ou sua instalação, o que a atNorth estima que pode representar um investimento adicional de até €10 bilhões. A empresa planeja celebrar acordos de compra de energia de longo prazo com fornecedores locais para apoiar a produção de energia na região, juntamente com soluções de flexibilidade que, segundo ela, podem apoiar a operação eficiente da rede de transmissão da Fingrid. A atNorth também trabalhará com partes interessadas locais para explorar oportunidades de uso do calor gerado pelo data center, que a empresa afirma ter como objetivo gerar valor além da própria instalação. Esse esforço baseia‑se em colaborações existentes de reutilização de calor com a Kesko Corporation na Finlândia, a Stockholm Exergi na Suécia, e a Vestforbrænding e a Selected Group na Dinamarca. Declarações da atNorth e Parceiros Locais “O FIN05 é uma oportunidade de desenvolver infraestrutura digital crítica enquanto trabalhamos com a região para criar valor local duradouro”, disse Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson, CEO da atNorth. Ele afirmou que a empresa está explorando como parcerias energéticas locais, soluções de flexibilidade e reutilização de calor podem contribuir para o sistema energético mais amplo e para a comunidade, e espera trabalhar com Salo e parceiros regionais à medida que o projeto avança. Anna‑Kristiina Korhonen, prefeita de Salo, disse estar encantada em receber o investimento na região. Ela afirmou que o novo data center criará oportunidades de emprego valiosas tanto durante a construção quanto nas operações contínuas, gerando benefícios econômicos mais amplos para os negócios locais, acrescentando que o desenvolvimento reforça a posição de Salo como um destino atraente para indústrias inovadoras e apoia o crescimento sustentável de longo prazo da comunidade. Matti‑Juho Ervasti, sócio da Regant Oy, afirmou que o projeto demonstra o potencial de Salo como local para investimentos significativos em infraestrutura digital. Ele disse que a Regant trabalhou de perto com a atNorth e a municipalidade para oferecer um site pronto para desenvolvimento, com a escala, prontidão de planejamento e roteiro energético necessários para grandes projetos de data center. Cadeia de Valor Nórdica e Histórico de Propriedade A atNorth descreveu o FIN05 como parte de seu investimento contínuo nos países nórdicos, juntamente com desenvolvimentos em Estocolmo e Sollefteå, na Suécia, Haugaland, na Noruega, Ølgod, na Dinamarca e Kouvola, na Finlândia. O projeto de Kouvola, FIN04, foi anunciado em dezembro de 2023 como um mega site em um terreno de 21 hectares, a 139 km a nordeste de Helsinque e a 52 km da cidade de Hamina, atendendo tanto clientes de colocation quanto projetos build‑to‑suit. A atNorth disse na época que o FIN04 teria um fornecimento de energia imediato de 60 MW, uma primeira fase pronta para operação no segundo semestre de 2025, e um caminho para potência de várias centenas de megawatts quando totalmente construído, descrevendo‑o como o décimo data center da empresa nos países nórdicos e seu quarto campus na Finlândia. Trabalhando com a cidade de Kouvola e o parceiro energético KSS Energia, o site foi projetado com capacidades de reutilização de calor, permitindo que o excesso de calor do data center fosse reciclado para possível reutilização na comunidade local. O projeto de Salo também segue uma mudança na propriedade da atNorth. A CPP Investments e a Equinix concluíram a aquisição de US$4 bilhões da atNorth em 2 de setembro de 2026, com a CPP Investments detendo uma participação controladora de cerca de 51 % com um compromisso de US$1,3 bilhão, a Equinix detendo cerca de 34 % com um compromisso de US$895 milhões, e a Partners Group detendo cerca de 10 % com um compromisso de US$260 milhões. O restante está nas mãos dos acionistas internos da atNorth, que mantiveram uma parte substancial de sua participação acionária. A transação envolveu um pacote de financiamento de US$4,1 bilhões (€3,6 bilhões) garantido por um grupo de credores europeus e canadenses, e a atNorth continua a operar de forma independente sob sua marca existente.

artigo.texto: The two battery energy storage facilities in East Hampton Town, jointly owned by NextEra Energy and National Grid, have been temporarily shut down. The move comes after the town board passed a resolution at Thursday’s meeting to hire Rigano L.L.C., an environmental law firm, and authorized up to $50,000 for a lawsuit against NextEra Energy that would compel it to do the same. In a statement, Supervisor Kathee Burke-Gonzalez took a victory lap. “Less than 24 hours after the town board unanimously authorized litigation to shut down the East Hampton and Montauk battery storage facilities, NextEra has temporarily shut both facilities down,” she wrote. Those facilities are on Cove Hollow Road in East Hampton and North Shore Road in Montauk. “This is the action we demanded, and I am pleased that NextEra responded swiftly to my Sept. 29 letter and the town board’s action.” Gary Morris, the vice president of the East Hampton Storage Center and the Montauk Storage Center, had, as recently as Thursday, been defiant and unmoved by a series of demands made by the supervisor in a string of letters dating back to July 31. Her most recent letter, dated Sept. 30, had asked that the facilities cease operations by Friday unless it removed Novec 1230, a chemical that the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation has blamed for contaminating nearby drinking water wells after its use in a May 2023 fire at the 3 Cove Hollow Road energy storage center. “The town’s September 29, 2026, letter identifies no basis for its request that the facilities cease operations by October 2, 2026, and we are aware of none,” wrote Mr. Morris, in an Oct. 1 response to the supervisor, adding that he intended to continue operations there. Newsday reported that Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine had also been negotiating with NextEra, apparently threatening a county lawsuit, before the energy supplier decided to change course and suspend operations while it manages the Novec 1230. East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen had also been calling for the facilities to be shut. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

US Solar Financing Three US solar and battery deals raise $1.26B CleanChoice, Maxwell and Lydian close new funding Projects target 2027 operations and 6GW build-out Stock video by K via Pexels Oct 5, 2026 US Solar and Battery Storage Financing: $1.26B Across Three Deals US solar and battery storage financing activity has produced a trio of transactions spanning the Northeast and the consumer and small commercial segment, according to a round-up published by pv-tech.org. CleanChoice Energy has secured more than US$166 million in financing for two solar photovoltaic projects in the US Northeast, the Dolan project in New York at roughly 27MW and the Kylertown project in Pennsylvania at roughly 28MW. The package included a US$105 million construction loan from Investec Bank, which acted as lead arranger, green loan structuring agent and collateral agent. BHI, the US branch of Bank Hapoalim, BM and Stifel Bank served as coordinating lead arrangers. Advantage Capital supplied a US$61 million tax equity commitment for the portfolio. Both projects are expected to reach commercial operations in 2027. Separately, distributed energy company Maxwell Power has closed an US$800 million investment from private equity firm Fairtide Partners to acquire battery storage and solar PV power projects. The deal follows investments of US$250 million and US$750 million in 2024 and June 2026, lifting Fairtide's total commitment to US$1.8 billion for projects developed by Maxwell. Maxwell said it has helped its consumer and small commercial customers achieve US$100 million in future energy savings so far this year. The company also relocated its headquarters from San Diego, California, to Salt Lake City, Utah, a move it described as fulfilling a promise to Utah Senator John Curtis. In a third transaction, independent power producer Lydian Energy and infrastructure asset manager Infranity agreed on a US$300 million holding company credit facility intended to support expansion of Lydian's 6GW portfolio of solar PV and utility-scale battery energy storage systems. The bespoke facility is based on Lydian Energy's existing operating and construction-ready assets and is designed to give the company added flexibility to accelerate build-out of its business pipeline. Lydian said the financing will help it advance projects from development through construction and retain ownership of operating assets. Lydian Energy is backed by Exelsior Energy Capital. Sacha Kamp, global head of debt investment at Infranity, characterized the transaction as resting on a portfolio of high-quality contracted projects and a strong pipeline of energy infrastructure assets developed and owned by Lydian, adding that the support of an experienced and committed sponsor provides a foundation for long-term growth. artigo.texto: Amazon Commits $1 Billion to US Data Center Communities Amid AI Backlash - Amazon will invest more than $1 billion over five years in US communities hosting its data centers, targeting education, workforce training, energy affordability and water preservation. - AWS says it is 75% of the way toward its 2030 water-positive goal, as scrutiny grows over the electricity and water demands of AI infrastructure. - More than 100 data center moratoriums are under consideration across the US, raising political and investment risks as technology companies accelerate AI infrastructure spending. Amazon is committing more than $1 billion over five years to communities hosting its US data centers. The investment comes as the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure faces growing resistance over energy costs, water consumption and local impacts. Amazon Web Services will direct the funding through its new Built Together framework. It will support education, job training, energy affordability, water preservation and other community priorities. The initiative adds a community investment component to one of the largest private infrastructure expansions underway in the United States. Amazon said it invested $276 billion in data centers between 2011 and 2025. Large projects or expansions are now underway across several states, including Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Virginia and Mississippi. AI growth collides with local infrastructure concerns Data centers provide the computing capacity required to train and operate AI models. Their rapid expansion has also intensified questions about who bears the infrastructure costs. Communities across the US have raised concerns about electricity demand, utility bills, water use and pressure on local infrastructure. More than 100 data center moratoriums are currently being considered nationwide, according to Amazon. That opposition creates a growing governance challenge for technology companies and policymakers. It also adds a political dimension ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. AWS CEO Matt Garman framed continued construction as an economic and national security priority. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it,” Garman said. Amazon compared the current expansion of digital infrastructure with the construction of the US interstate highway system. However, the company stressed one major difference. Private companies, rather than taxpayers, are financing much of today’s infrastructure buildout. AI infrastructure is increasingly tied to healthcare, education, financial services, cybersecurity, defense and scientific research. That broadening role has strengthened the case for investment while increasing scrutiny of its environmental footprint. RELATED ARTICLE: Amazon Adds 50+ Mercedes Electric Trucks in Germany Water and energy move higher on the agenda Amazon’s investment framework seeks to address some of the most contentious environmental issues surrounding data centers. AWS has committed to becoming water positive across its data center operations by 2030. The company said it is now 75% of the way toward that goal. Water positive means returning more water to communities than its operations consume. The commitment has become increasingly relevant as new data centers expand into regions facing competing demands for water and electricity. Energy affordability is another focus of the $1 billion program. Rising data center demand has prompted questions about grid investment and whether households could face higher costs as utilities build infrastructure to serve large technology customers. For Amazon, addressing those concerns has become part of maintaining community support for continued expansion. Community acceptance becomes an investment risk The scale of proposed data center development means community relations are moving from corporate philanthropy into core infrastructure strategy. Moratoriums, permitting disputes and public opposition can delay projects and raise development costs. They can also complicate the long-term power procurement and grid planning needed to support AI investment. Amazon’s Built Together framework gives communities a role in determining how funds are allocated. That approach could help companies align investments with local concerns rather than applying a uniform national model. For executives and investors, the broader issue extends beyond Amazon. AI growth depends on physical infrastructure that requires land, power, water and political approval. The next phase of the AI investment cycle will therefore depend on more than access to capital and computing technology. Developers will need credible plans for resource use, community benefits and energy affordability. As governments compete for leadership in AI, those local constraints are becoming part of the global race for digital infrastructure. The companies that manage them effectively may gain an advantage in securing the permits, power and public support required for continued expansion. artigo.texto: MONTEZUMA COUNTY, Colo., Oct. 5, 2026 (SEND2PRESS NEWSWIRE) — NoValleyRange, a neighborhood group located near Mesa Verde (a UNESCO World Heritage site and National Park), are fighting a Texas developer proposing a $240 million dollar solar and lithium battery development. The proposed project consists of 900 acres of solar panels and 8 acres of lithium battery storage at the base of Colorado’s only UNESCO world heritage site. This project is comparable in size to the 500,000-panel Cleve Hill Solar Park, the largest solar field in the UK. The neighbors are fighting the project for the same reasons that many other rural communities across the US are fighting similar projects. Namely, that the solar field and BESS facility will degrade property values, harm tourism, and put small businesses out of business. However, the Valley Range Energy Park presents unique problems. It will dominate the views from the northside overlooks from Mesa Verde National Park and degrade the park visitor experience. Mesa Verde is not only a cultural treasure, but also the economic tourism engine that supports the entire community. Even more alarming is the potential for a catastrophic battery fire. According to Lillian Wakeley, Board Director at Mesa Verde Association, in a recent social media comment, “The solar array will overwhelm the views from every overlook on the north escarpment in Mesa Verde National Park. Large battery storage means fire risk and also huge security lights. One of Mesa Verde’s major drawing points is the dark night sky, and ranger programs with new night-scopes are hugely popular. Please think about the impact on our tourist industry if we encroach on our national park with overwhelming lights, noise, and nearly a thousand acres of solar panels.” Mesa Verde National Park is also a huge driver of the local economy. According to a National Park Service report, in 2023 505,000 visitors came to Mesa Verde National Park and spent $59.5 million in communities near the park. That spending in the local area had a cumulative benefit to the local economy of $75.6 million (*see note 1). Park visitation was directly responsible for approximately 8% of total employment in Montezuma County (*2). The Valley Range solar project also includes 8 acres of lithium battery storage commonly referred to as a BESS. BESS facilities are new technology with a dismal safety record. Most of the BESS systems in the US have been installed since 2020 (*3) Unlike conventional fires, BESS fires produce their own oxygen and are nearly impossible to extinguish (*4). BESS fires also produce poisonous gasses including hydrogen cyanide and hydrogen fluoride. Most troubling, is the ability of a BESS fire to produce carcinogenic fallout in the form of aerosolized exotic metals (*5). In the 2025 Moss Landing battery fire, 55,000 pounds of carcinogenic metals were aerosolized into the neighboring tourist town and surrounding marshes (*6). BESS installations present unique economic problems when located near a major tourist attraction, such as Mesa Verde National Park. According to KAZU News, the 2025 lithium-ion battery fire in the popular tourist town of Moss Landing California (and the accompanying repeated evacuation orders and national news coverage) devastated the local tourism industry (*7). According to neighboring business owner, Bryan Davis, “Anything negatively effecting Mesa Verde National Park is a critical economic issue here. This community relies on the National Park for a huge percentage of the local economy.” In recent weeks the Valley Range project has become a local political issue in Montezuma County with Republican commissioner candidate Rodney Cox saying “There is a solar farm being proposed now, and I’m against everything about that.” Rodney Cox’s opponent Democrat Rebecca Busic has said she supports the solar project and lithium battery installation (*8). ABOUT NOVALLEYRANGE: NoValleyRange is a local community activism group made up of two neighborhoods located near Mesa Verde National Park. We are sheep farmers, chocolate shop owners, campground owners, retirees and ordinary folks. NoValleyRange is not a partisan group, our members span the political spectrum. However, we are united in our effort to stop this project. Sign the petition and learn more at https://www.novalleyrange.com/. artigo.texto: 5 de out, 2026 Neste episódio do POWER, Adriano Pires conversa com Alexandre Americano, CEO da Mercurio Partners, sobre um paradoxo cada vez mais visível no setor elétrico brasileiro: o País tem sobra de energia em alguns momentos, uma das tarifas mais caras do mundo e, ainda assim, risco de apagão. A Mercurio começou como uma plataforma de serviços financeiros e regulatórios que, ao longo dos anos, avançou para comercialização, varejo, e desenvolvimento de projetos próprios. O principal deles é a UTE Pilar, uma térmica a gás natural de 270 megawatts em desenvolvimento em Alagoas. A empresa também recontratou a UTE Paulínia Verde, que começou com biometano e agora entra em um novo ciclo também com gás natural. Pires também aborda o papel crescente das baterias. A Mercurio inscreveu um projeto para o leilão da tecnologia, mas Americano avalia que a disputa tende a favorecer algumas empresas. “Vai ser um leilão para quem tem custo de capital muito baixo, para quem já tem alguma outra sinergia,” afirma. Também disponível no Spotify.
