artigo.texto: Tesla produced 464,391 vehicles and delivered 486,532 vehicles during the third quarter of 2026, while deploying 13.7 GWh of energy storage products across its energy business. The quarterly figures show that Tesla delivered about 22,000 more vehicles than it produced, indicating that deliveries came partly from vehicles manufactured in previous quarters, in addition to third-quarter production. Model 3 and Model Y continued to account for the overwhelming majority of Tesla’s automotive activity. Tesla produced 457,387 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles during the quarter and delivered 478,237 of the two models. That means Model 3 and Model Y represented approximately 98% of Tesla’s total vehicle deliveries during the period. Deliveries of Model 3 and Model Y exceeded production by 20,850 vehicles, contributing most of the difference between companywide production and deliveries. Approximately 1% of Model 3 and Model Y deliveries were subject to operating lease accounting. Tesla does not break out Model 3 and Model Y results separately in its quarterly production and delivery announcement, instead reporting the vehicles as a combined category. The company’s Other Models category accounted for a much smaller portion of automotive volumes. Tesla produced 7,004 Other Models vehicles during the third quarter and delivered 8,295. Approximately 4% of Other Models deliveries were subject to operating lease accounting. The category includes Tesla vehicles outside the Model 3 and Model Y group, although the company’s production and delivery announcement did not provide individual results for each vehicle within the category. Across the company’s complete vehicle portfolio, deliveries exceeded production by 22,141 vehicles. The difference is notable because production and deliveries do not necessarily move in parallel from quarter to quarter. Vehicles produced near the end of a reporting period may not be delivered until the following quarter, while vehicles produced during earlier periods can contribute to current-quarter deliveries. Transportation timing, geographic distribution and customer handoffs can also create differences between the two figures. Tesla’s third-quarter release provides an early indication of operating activity but does not include enough information to determine the profitability of those deliveries. The company did not disclose quarterly automotive revenue, average selling prices, gross profit, operating income, net income or free cash flow in the production and delivery announcement. Tesla will report those figures as part of its complete third-quarter financial results. Tesla specifically cautioned investors that vehicle deliveries and energy storage deployments represent only two measures of company performance and should not be relied upon independently to estimate quarterly financial results. Several factors can significantly affect the financial contribution associated with any given level of vehicle deliveries. Average selling prices are one major variable. Changes in vehicle pricing, product mix, geographic mix and incentives can cause automotive revenue to rise or fall even when the number of vehicles delivered remains relatively stable. The mix between Model 3 and Model Y and Tesla’s higher-priced vehicles can also affect revenue and margins. Cost of sales is another important factor. Vehicle profitability depends on manufacturing costs, raw materials, factory utilization, logistics expenses and other costs associated with producing and delivering vehicles. As a result, higher delivery volumes do not necessarily translate directly into higher earnings. Foreign exchange movements can also influence Tesla’s reported results because the company sells vehicles and other products across multiple international markets. Currency changes can affect the dollar value of international revenue and expenses when Tesla translates them into its reporting currency. Investors will therefore need to wait for the company’s full earnings report to assess how the third-quarter operating volumes translated into revenue, margins, and cash generation. Tesla’s energy business also accounted for a significant share of the quarter’s operating activity. The company deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage products during the third quarter. Tesla’s energy storage business includes systems that store electricity for later use, helping customers manage energy supply and demand and integrate power from different generation sources. Energy storage has become an increasingly important part of Tesla’s business alongside electric vehicles. Utilities, power producers, and other customers can use large-scale battery storage to store electricity and release it when grid demand is higher or when generation from other sources is lower. The third-quarter deployment figure measures the storage capacity Tesla delivered during the period, but as with vehicle deliveries, it does not reveal the financial contribution from those deployments. Revenue and profitability from energy storage can vary depending on product mix, pricing, project timing and associated costs. Tesla will provide greater visibility into those factors when it reports complete quarterly results. The combination of 486,532 vehicle deliveries and 13.7 GWh of energy storage deployments highlights the company’s two major physical-product businesses ahead of the earnings report. Automotive activity remains substantially larger in unit volume, but energy storage gives Tesla another business tied to electrification and energy infrastructure. The third-quarter vehicle figures also give investors insight into the relationship between production and customer deliveries. artigo.texto: Data centers are preventing a US recession, NMSU economist says Despite a weak housing market, data center growth has buoyed the US economy, New Mexico State University economics professor Chris Erickson tells KOAT. Data centers are preventing the U.S. from falling into a recession, a New Mexico State University economic expert told KOAT on Saturday. "Data centers are keeping the economy growing at this point; they are the main drivers of the economy," said Chris Erickson, a professor of economics at NMSU. RELATED: Data centers become key issue in New Mexico governor’s race "Its investment in data centers has kept the economy buoyed up. The housing sector has been quite weak for a while. Usually when the housing sector is that weak, you can expect either slowdown or even a recession to follow that because construction is such an important source of jobs. But because the data centers have taken up all the slack in construction, that hasn't happened," Erickson explained. Data center growth in New Mexico is not uncontroversial, and Erickson said he believes there could be a slowdown in new data center development. The controversy surrounding them might make it difficult for companies to secure funding for new projects, he said. Three New Mexico counties have placed moratoriums on data center development, and a fourth is currently considering one. Democratic lawmakers in Santa Fe are proposing a statewide moratorium for the 2027 legislative session. Opponents are wary of the environmental impacts and financial costs of data centers. Still, there are major data centers currently operating or in development across the state, including an operational Meta data center in Valencia County and a major Oracle data center under construction in Doña Ana County. Google is also exploring a potential site in Lea County.

artigo.texto: Wisconsin Policy Forum Data centers can deliver multi-billion-dollar investments and large numbers of jobs to Wisconsin communities. But key issues around their development remain unresolved, including how to ensure residents are spared from increases to transmission rates or property taxes. Far from being a hub of data center construction, a new Wisconsin Policy Forum report finds Wisconsin lags states such as Virginia and Ohio in both the number and size of its data centers. Still, three major hyperscale data centers are being built in Wisconsin in recent years, with more being proposed and often facing significant opposition. A Microsoft data center is up and running in Mount Pleasant, while centers are under construction in Port Washington and Beaver Dam. Recent technological advancements in artificial intelligence are driving a national data center boom. A broader examination of the impacts of this technology — an understandably salient issue for many — is beyond the scope of this report. Instead, our report seeks to ground discussions in facts about how they affect local government finances, the regional economy, the energy grid, and more. For example, due in large part to these centers, the latest state projections show peak power demand in Wisconsin is expected to increase by more than 5 gigawatts between 2024 and 2030. This raises the question of who will pay for the added capacity to serve these centers. Electricity arguably represents the single biggest challenge for large data centers– and the single biggest issue for policymakers, our report finds. In considering data center proposals, elected officials have a difficult balance to strike. An August Marquette University Law School poll found 78% of registered voters in Wisconsin felt the costs of large data centers outweigh their benefits, while only 21% felt their benefits outweighed their costs. Some Wisconsin communities have recently blocked construction of large data centers, either by rejecting a specific proposal or approving a blanket moratorium. One of the implications of this is that local officials may have leverage in negotiating data center deals with developers, since there is a credible risk that these proposals will be rejected. The Forum reviewed deals between data center developers and the communities of Mount Pleasant, Port Washington, and Beaver Dam, as well as in two communities where centers were proposed but later canceled: Janesville and DeForest. In general, we found communities were striking reasonable deals that included fiscal safeguards. However, state law makes it challenging for local officials to protect existing taxpayers in the case of data center developments that require significant tax increment finance (TIF) spending on infrastructure or developer incentives. Under current law, there could be initial tax increases on existing property owners — despite the possibility that once the TIF district closes, residents’ taxes could decline to what they were prior to the data center or even less. In addition, most states offer a state sales tax exemption to data centers, as Wisconsin does. While other industries such as manufacturing receive similar treatment here, the cost of these forgone tax revenues is significant. Our report concludes by offering a menu of options for state and local policymakers to consider in response to issues highlighted in our report. Click here to read the full report and learn more. artigo.texto: 43 proposed power plants needed to fuel data centers listed across NEPA PHILADELPHIA (WOLF) — A new environmental report warning about Pennsylvania’s expected growth in natural-gas power generation comes as proposed power plants are already listed across much of northeastern and central Pennsylvania. PennEnvironment Research & Policy Center and Frontier Group project Pennsylvania could add 4.4 gigawatts of natural-gas capacity by the end of 2030, an increase of nearly 15% over the state’s existing gas footprint. The groups say growing demand from data centers is a major driver behind the proposed expansion. A separate Track Data Centers listing provided to FOX56 identifies 43 proposed power plants across the station’s coverage area. Lackawanna County has the largest number, with 15 proposals and 4.8 gigawatts of listed capacity. Luzerne County has nine proposals and 4.3 gigawatts of listed capacity. Three plants are listed in each of Carbon, Northampton and Schuylkill counties. Carbon County’s listed capacity is 350 megawatts, while Northampton and Schuylkill counties each have 1.2 gigawatts listed. Bradford, Monroe and Union counties each have two proposed plants. Listed capacity is 248 megawatts in Bradford County and 300 megawatts in Union County; no capacity figure was listed for Monroe County. One proposed plant is listed in each of Columbia, Lycoming, Montour and Wayne counties. The listed capacity figures total nearly 12.4 gigawatts in the counties where capacity was provided. The database listings may cover projects with different timelines and scopes than the statewide projections cited in PennEnvironment’s report. PennEnvironment says new gas plants can operate for 25 to 30 years and has called for a moratorium on new data centers, arguing that the projects could increase air pollution and long-term greenhouse-gas emissions. The organization’s conclusions and policy recommendations reflect its environmental advocacy position.

artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: Japão: país se prepara para investir em data centers (AFP/AFP) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 2 de outubro de 2026 às 13h01. Uma parceria entre JERA, Dell e RHAELM prevê um data center de mais de US$ 15 bilhões em Chiba. Segundo o Financial Times, a expansão pode alcançar US$ 140 bilhões. O primeiro projeto deve começar a operar em 2028. Uma expansão de data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) no Japão pode mobilizar até US$ 140 bilhões, segundo reportagem do Financial Times. O primeiro passo é uma parceria entre a geradora japonesa JERA, a Dell Technologies e a desenvolvedora britânica RHAELM, anunciada nesta quinta-feira, 1º. O projeto inicial será instalado em Chiba, perto de Tóquio, com capacidade elétrica de até 400 megawatts (MW) e investimento previsto superior a US$ 15 bilhões ao longo de todas as fases. A proposta é reunir geração de energia e computação no mesmo local para acelerar a implantação. O valor da expansão não consta no comunicado oficial e não corresponde a uma verba pública anunciada. A parceria foi formalizada por um memorando de entendimentos. O complexo ficará junto à usina térmica de Chiba, da JERA. A alimentação elétrica será feita diretamente a partir do ativo de geração, em uma configuração conhecida como behind-the-meter. A intenção é reduzir a dependência dos prazos de conexão convencional à rede. “Podemos entregar uma instalação de 400 MW anos antes do cronograma de uma conexão convencional à rede”, afirmou Bradd Lewis, CEO da RHAELM, no comunicado da parceria. A estratégia responde a um gargalo de energia que acompanha a expansão da IA. Na projeção atualizada em 2026, a Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) estima que os data centers consumam 950 terawatts-hora de eletricidade em 2030, ante 485 em 2025. Os números medem o consumo anual mundial, enquanto os 400 MW de Chiba representam capacidade de potência. São medidas diferentes: uma indica a quantidade de energia utilizada ao longo do tempo; a outra, a capacidade elétrica prevista para atender o projeto. A JERA entra com o terreno e a energia; a Dell fornece infraestrutura de computação organizada em conjuntos de servidores; e a RHAELM lidera o desenvolvimento do empreendimento. A Apollo Global Management pretende atuar como parceira de investimento e financiamento da RHAELM. O orçamento de Chiba abrange terreno, infraestrutura elétrica, construção e equipamentos de IA. Portanto, os mais de US$ 15 bilhões não se destinam apenas ao edifício que abrigará os computadores. As empresas querem padronizar a integração de energia, refrigeração e computação para reduzir o tempo de implantação dos próximos projetos. A JERA e a RHAELM pretendem explorar outros locais da geradora, com a ambição de alcançar vários gigawatts de infraestrutura no Japão na década de 2030. Segundo a Reuters, Chiba deverá iniciar a operação por etapas em 2028 e atingir plena capacidade em 2029. Não. O valor se refere à possível expansão empresarial descrita pelo Financial Times, não a uma verba pública anunciada. JERA, Dell Technologies e RHAELM assinaram a parceria. A Apollo pretende atuar como parceira de investimento e financiamento da RHAELM. A proposta é fornecer eletricidade diretamente a partir da geração da JERA e encurtar o prazo necessário para disponibilizar energia ao data center. O início está previsto para 2028. Segundo a Reuters, a operação será gradual, com plena capacidade esperada em 2029.

artigo.texto: Springfield, IL-(Effingham Radio)- As more Illinois municipalities weigh moratoriums on data center construction, Gov. J.B. Pritzker is pressing state lawmakers to pass uniform regulations – despite light pushback from some who view the proposed rules as potentially misguided. The Illinois General Assembly failed to pass legislation to further regulate data centers statewide through the POWER Act before the end of the spring session on June 1. Pritzker said recently he’s not concerned about getting short-term solutions passed sooner than when state lawmakers return to Springfield. Pritzker noted there isn’t always transparency for communities when a data center project is being pitched in a locality. State Rep. Jeff Keicher, R-Sycamore, said data center non-disclosure agreements aren’t much different from privacy measures put in place when others buy a property, but there should be transparency after that. He also said there’s been benefits in his district including significant decreases to the property tax levy – though he acknowledged there are bad actors in the space. Lawmakers are set to return to Springfield for a six-day veto session from Nov. 17-19, and Dec. 1-3. The legislature is expected to return to bills that didn’t pass in May, such as the Power Act. Story from Illinois Radio Network

artigo.texto: Ceará Segundo data center da Angola Cables no Ceará pode ganhar estrutura de hiperescala A Angola Cables está reformulando o projeto de seu segundo data center no Ceará e avalia ampliar a estrutura para um modelo de hiperescala, voltado principalmente ao crescimento da demanda por processamento de dados, inteligência artificial, redes sociais e jogos. A informação foi confirmada pelo CEO da empresa na Europa, Samuel Carvalho, durante uma conferência sobre infraestrutura digital realizada em Lisboa. A companhia já mantém um data center em funcionamento na Praia do Futuro, em Fortaleza, desde 2019. Em 2022, a empresa havia firmado parceria com o Governo do Ceará para a construção de uma segunda unidade, com previsão inicial de investimento de US$ 40 milhões. O novo planejamento, porém, passou por mudanças diante do aumento da demanda do mercado. Segundo a empresa, o Ceará apresenta vantagens pela estrutura de conectividade internacional. A Angola Cables opera uma rede de aproximadamente 33 mil quilômetros de cabos submarinos, com sistemas que chegam ao hub de Fortaleza, permitindo conexões de baixa latência com regiões como Europa e África. O projeto ainda não tem previsão de formalização. A empresa avalia possíveis locais para a nova estrutura tanto na Praia do Futuro quanto na região do Pecém. A possibilidade de um empreendimento de hiperescala também está relacionada à busca por grandes clientes de tecnologia e inteligência artificial. Além do novo data center, a Angola Cables pretende ampliar a infraestrutura de cabos submarinos na Praia do Futuro. artigo.texto: Demand for artificial intelligence data centers will continue to push shares of Vertiv higher, according to BMO Capital Markets. The firm initiated coverage of the stock on Sunday with an outperform rating and $329 price target, which implies roughly 30% upside from Friday's close. The company provinces digital infrastructure and hardware for data centers and other facilities, with data centers making up about 85% of its revenue, said analyst Daniel DiCicco. He called Vertiv a "premium data center play" that has already run up more than 900% in the last five years. Shares have pulled back from their peak in May and now offer an attractive entry point, he said. "Vertiv is well positioned as data centers are increasing in scale and intensity (more power to the rack) and demand for resilience and speed to deployment continues to increase," DiCicco wrote in a note to clients. VRT YTD mountain Vertiv year to date There are more than 4,700 data centers in the United States — and the number is growing . Some $6 billion was spent on land purchases in the U.S. for future data centers in the first half of 2026, according to commercial real estate firm Avison Young. That's a 79% increase from last year, the firm found. Vertiv's management has estimated that its $75 billion total addressable market is increasing 16% to 18% a year, with data centers growing 18% to 20% annually, DiCicco said. However, the company's long-term growth forecasts could be conservative, he noted. Plus, Vertiv has a full suite of offerings. The current rate for data center content is $3.25 to $3.75 per megawatt, but innovation, standardization, service growth and integrated systems can all push that higher, DiCicco pointed out. "VRT has positioned itself as one of the few providers capable of delivering a fully integrated power and thermal management solution across the entire data center," he said. Shares of Vertiv are up nearly 56% year to date. — CNBC's Tobias Burns contributed reporting.

artigo.texto: Silicon has long been the tantalizing prize of lithium-ion battery research. Theoretically, it can hold roughly ten times more lithium than the graphite that dominates today’s anodes, promising batteries that last dramatically longer on a single charge. Yet silicon has a fatal flaw that has kept it out of most commercial cells: when lithium floods into the material during charging, it swells by hundreds of percent, cracking particles, fracturing electrodes, and destroying the delicate interfaces that make a battery work. A team of researchers in Qinghai, China, now reports a practical route around this problem, combining a metal-processing technique borrowed from metallurgy with a carefully tuned dose of ordinary graphite. The study, published in the journal Ionics by Zhanshou Yang, Fa-Feng Xu, and colleagues at the Qinghai Institute of Salt Lakes of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, centers on a process called dealloying. In dealloying, one element is selectively dissolved out of an alloy, leaving behind a sponge-like scaffold of the remaining element riddled with pores at the nanometer scale. The technique has a pedigree in materials science, having been used to create nanoporous gold and other architectures, and it has increasingly attracted attention as a scalable way to fabricate porous electrode materials for rechargeable batteries. Applied to silicon-bearing alloys, it produces porous silicon structures whose internal voids act as built-in expansion chambers. That architectural trick addresses the core failure mode of silicon anodes. In a dense silicon particle, the volume change that accompanies lithiation generates enormous mechanical stress. Particles pulverize, fresh surfaces are repeatedly exposed to the electrolyte, and a thick, unstable solid electrolyte interphase layer grows and rebuilds with every cycle, consuming lithium and raising the cell’s internal resistance. A porous particle, by contrast, can expand into its own empty space. The pores absorb much of the strain, the particle’s outer dimensions stay comparatively stable, and the electrode’s conductive network and binder matrix survive far longer. Porosity alone, however, does not solve every problem. Silicon is a semiconductor with modest intrinsic conductivity, and the tortuous pathways through a porous structure can slow both electrons and lithium ions. The Qinghai team therefore wrapped the porous silicon in a carbon coating, producing a composite they designate Si@C. The carbon shell serves a dual role: it provides an electron-conducting highway that connects the silicon to the current collector, and it acts as a mechanical and chemical skin that stabilizes the electrode structure and limits parasitic reactions with the electrolyte. Carbon coatings of this kind have become a standard strategy in silicon anode research, but their effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of the underlying silicon architecture and on how the composite is formulated. The second half of the team’s strategy is arguably the more pragmatic one: blending the carbon-coated porous silicon with graphite. Graphite remains the workhorse anode of the lithium-ion industry, prized for its low cost, flat voltage profile, and remarkable structural stability over thousands of cycles. By mixing silicon with graphite, researchers can trade some of silicon’s enormous capacity for graphite’s reliability, while the graphite matrix helps buffer swelling and maintains electronic contact throughout the electrode. The ratio matters enormously. Too little silicon and the energy-density gain is marginal; too much and the electrode’s mechanical integrity collapses within a few hundred cycles. Yang and colleagues systematically optimized this ratio, testing different proportions of porous silicon to graphite before settling on a mass ratio of 1:2. At that composition, the composite delivered the best combination of capacity, stability, and rate performance in their experiments. The finding underscores a broader lesson in battery engineering: the performance of a composite electrode is not simply the weighted average of its components, but emerges from how those components interact mechanically and electrochemically during cycling. The graphite appears to function not merely as a diluent but as an active structural partner for the swelling silicon. The electrochemical results reported in the paper are striking. After 500 charge-discharge cycles, the optimized Si@C anode retained a reversible capacity of 688.5 milliampere-hours per gram, corresponding to a capacity retention of 63.6 percent. For context, conventional graphite anodes typically deliver around 350 to 370 milliampere-hours per gram, so even after substantial degradation the composite still stores nearly twice as much charge per unit mass. Equally important is the coulombic efficiency, which the team reports at 99.9 percent. This figure measures how many lithium ions that enter the anode during charging come back out during discharge, and values approaching 100 percent indicate that parasitic side reactions, which slowly poison a cell, have been largely suppressed. The authors state that these results surpass previously reported data for comparable silicon-based anodes in both cycling stability and rate performance, the latter describing the electrode’s ability to deliver capacity at high charging speeds. Rate capability is often the quiet casualty of silicon anode designs, because the same structural features that buffer swelling can impede ion transport. The combination of porous silicon, a conductive carbon coating, and a graphite matrix appears to keep those transport pathways open even as the electrode ages, allowing the material to sustain fast charging without catastrophic capacity loss. The work also carries a regional and industrial dimension. artigo.texto: A Posição de Byron Donalds sobre Data Centers Entra em Choque com a Reação dos Eleitores da Flórida Byron Donalds transformou os data centers em uma prioridade econômica, apesar de uma pesquisa na Flórida apontar 79% de oposição à construção de instalações de IA no estado. Esse conflito tornou a posição de Byron Donalds sobre data centers um teste decisivo para sua campanha ao governo. Donalds argumenta que a Flórida pode receber grandes campi de computação sem transferir seus custos de eletricidade e água para os moradores. Ele apoia o controle local e proteções ao consumidor, mas rejeita uma paralisação estadual de novos empreendimentos. Seu adversário democrata, David Jolly, escolheu uma linha divisória mais clara. Jolly apoia uma moratória, enquanto Donalds afirma que construções cuidadosamente reguladas devem continuar. Essa diferença oferece aos eleitores uma escolha incomumente direta sobre quem deve arcar com os custos da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. A disputa deixou de ser um debate abstrato sobre a tecnologia do futuro. Condados e cidades da Flórida já estão suspendendo projetos enquanto estudam a demanda por eletricidade, o consumo de água, o ruído, o uso do solo e o financiamento dos serviços públicos. Para Donalds, o problema político é maior do que defender uma única política. Ele precisa convencer moradores céticos de que as proteções funcionarão, enquanto interesses ligados a data centers investem pesadamente nas eleições do estado. A Posição de Byron Donalds sobre Data Centers Enfrenta uma Revolta Local Donalds avançou em direção a salvaguardas mais fortes, mas não se juntou à campanha crescente para interromper a construção em escala hyperscale. Em um evento de campanha em julho, em Clearwater, Donalds disse que era favorável a desacelerar o desenvolvimento quando as comunidades precisassem de proteções mais robustas. No entanto, ele se opôs a uma moratória estadual que suspenderia todos os projetos qualificados. Ele também prometeu respeitar as decisões dos governos locais. Se um condado ou cidade rejeitar um data center, disse Donalds, o estado não deveria forçar essa comunidade a aceitá-lo. Essa posição o coloca entre defensores da indústria e eleitores que exigem uma pausa abrangente. Ela reconhece a oposição local sem aceitar a política central proposta por Jolly e por vários governos de condados. A distinção importa porque os projetos em debate não são simples salas de servidores. Instalações hyperscale são campi de computação concebidos para operar enormes frotas de servidores para serviços em nuvem e inteligência artificial. Suas necessidades contínuas de eletricidade podem se equiparar às de grandes operações industriais. Os equipamentos de refrigeração também podem aumentar a pressão sobre os sistemas de água, dependendo do projeto e das condições operacionais da instalação. A Flórida já tem mais de 100 data centers em operação, segundo reportagens citadas por organizações de notícias estaduais. As disputas mais intensas envolvem locais hyperscale propostos, e não todos os prédios existentes que armazenam ou processam dados. Condados em todo o estado adotaram ou consideraram moratórias temporárias. Leon, Nassau, Pasco, Sarasota e outros governos locais avaliaram pausas enquanto autoridades desenvolvem regras de zoneamento e infraestrutura. O Condado de Nassau, por exemplo, publicou uma moratória temporária que abrange o recebimento, a análise e a aprovação de pedidos para data centers. Autoridades de Pasco também consideraram uma pausa de um ano devido a preocupações com infraestrutura e recursos naturais. Essas ações revelam um movimento político de baixo para cima. Autoridades locais estão respondendo a moradores que temem custos mais altos de serviços públicos, esgotamento dos recursos hídricos, ruído persistente de geradores e construções industriais perto de suas casas. As objeções também refletem incerteza. As comunidades muitas vezes não dispõem de informações públicas suficientes sobre a demanda final de energia de uma instalação proposta, seu método de refrigeração, geração de reserva, incentivos fiscais ou empregos de longo prazo. Essa lacuna de informação oferece aos defensores da moratória uma mensagem direta. Eles argumentam que os governos devem estabelecer as regras antes de aprovar empreendimentos que podem remodelar o planejamento dos serviços públicos por décadas. Donalds propõe uma sequência diferente. Ele quer proteções aplicáveis, tomada de decisão local e continuidade das construções onde as comunidades concederem aprovação. Sua posição pressupõe que a Flórida consegue avaliar os projetos individualmente. A oposição argumenta que decisões fragmentadas deixam os moradores expostos a riscos que ultrapassam as fronteiras dos condados e das concessionárias. Esse desacordo criou a tensão central da campanha. Donalds apresenta o desenvolvimento regulado como um caminho para o crescimento econômico, enquanto críticos veem a mesma política como um subsídio público evitável. A disputa se intensificou à medida que desenvolvedores de data centers e organizações aliadas ampliaram sua atividade política. Reportagens compiladas a partir de registros estaduais de campanha estimaram seus gastos na Flórida em mais de US$ 22 milhões durante o ciclo eleitoral. Mais de US$ 5 milhões teriam apoiado Donalds ou iniciativas alinhadas à sua candidatura. Esses gastos não comprovam que doadores controlem sua política, mas intensificam o escrutínio público sobre cada promessa que ele faz. Para os eleitores, portanto, a questão central não é se Donalds reconhece as preocupações locais. É se suas salvaguardas propostas conseguem superar as pressões financeiras e técnicas criadas por projetos de dimensão sem precedentes. As Contas de Energia se Tornaram a Promessa Mais Difícil da Campanha Donalds afirma que os data centers devem pagar seus próprios custos, mas a lei da Flórida não garante que as contas das famílias permanecerão inalteradas. artigo.texto: Physical AI’s bottleneck shifts from what robots can do to whether factories trust them AI is moving beyond the data centers where models are trained and onto factory floors where machines must handle constant change. But traditional industrial robots work behind a cage, repeat a single task and were never designed for the complexities of today’s market. Manufacturers now want general-purpose machines that can switch tasks and improve as processes evolve. The hard part is deploying it, according to Adrien Gaidon (pictured, right), co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics Inc. “If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon said. “What we do is we do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.” Gaidon and John Mancuso (left), vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc., spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante at Fully Connected, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how cloud infrastructure, simulation and human assistance help robots learn and adapt on factory floors. (* Disclosure below.) Physical AI moves from data centers to the factory floor Walden spun out of Toyota Research Institute in January 2026 and launched with $300 million in July to put general-purpose robots to work in manufacturing. Its robots have worked full production shifts alongside people since May. They handle machine tending, parts kitting, and subassembly, tasks manufacturers had either failed to automate or never tried, Gaidon explained. “There’s half a million open positions for machinists in the U.S. because it’s a hard job and it requires skills,” Gaidon said. “But part of that job does not require the craft or the human creativity.” Getting a robot to that point takes serious compute long before it reaches a production line. CoreWeave, which has been betting on physical AI, also brings mechanical engineers and robotics experts into customer engagements alongside its infrastructure, Mancuso explained. “In the end, before a model is ever going to do something in the physical world, it’s going to have a tremendous amount of simulation that happens in the virtual world,” Mancuso said. “We’re providing the infrastructure.” But while simulation in data centers can make a robot useful, but it can’t make it perfect. Walden pairs autonomous robots with remote human assistants. The setup is comparable to automated looms of 120 years ago, when one person oversaw 40 machines, Gaidon noted. “Our robots are autonomous, but they know how to call for help,” Gaidon said. “They know when they need some assistance – and that assistance feeds the most valuable data to improve over time.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of Fully Connected: (* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Fully Connected 2026 event. artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr. e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA A análise do ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico), em nota técnica, sobre a margem de escoamento disponível no SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional) para conexão de sistemas de baterias que participarão do leilão de dezembro indica que o espaço na rede é superior à necessidade de potência estimada, afirmou a Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia). A entidade identificou cerca de 56 GW (gigawatts) de capacidade, ante uma potência necessária de 4,5 GW a 10 GW entre 2028 e 2030, ou seja, pelo menos mais cinco vezes a necessidade. Para as áreas em que haverá bonificação no leilão – locais prioritários onde o preço de classificação terá bônus de 10% – foi identificada margem disponível de 13,7 GW, também acima da demanda de potência do SIN. Por isso, segundo o diretor-executivo da Absae, Fabio Lima, os lances do certame devem se concentrar nas áreas bonificadas, que estão localizadas nas regiões Norte e Nordeste e no norte de Minas Gerais. “Vamos ter um quadro melhor quando tivermos o resultado da inscrição efetiva dos projetos, depois da habilitação técnica. Mas o fato é que tem margem nos pontos bonificados, então, boa parte dos projetos deve se concentrar por lá”, afirmou. De acordo com a associação, 93 das 129 localidades bonificadas têm margem de escoamento. As áreas estão no Nordeste, principalmente nos estados da Bahia, Piauí e Ceará, e no norte de Minas Gerais. A bonificação considera pontos da rede onde, além de potência, a bateria tende a contribuir também para aumentar a robustez elétrica, ou seja, em locais onde há menos capacidade de manter a tensão estável. Contrafluxo Fontes explicam que a metodologia do ONS para análise do acesso de baterias ao SIN é diferente da que é utilizada para demais empreendimentos de geração ou de carga. Isso porque é considerado o perfil diferente do armazenamento, que atua no contrafluxo na maioria das horas, descarregando no horário de pico – quando não há geração solar – e carregando no horário em que há maior oferta de energia na rede. O presidente da Thymos Energia, João Carlos Mello, chama atenção para algumas restrições na rede indicadas pelo ONS no norte de Minas Gerais, no sul da Bahia e no Ceará, áreas que sofrem com o curtailment. Ainda assim, ele aponta que a maior parte dos barramentos com bonificação têm margem. “É natural ter prevalência desses locais no leilão, que foi desenhado com um critério locacional justamente para isso”, afirmou. Mello projeta que a demanda final do certame deve ficar próxima a 3 GW, conforme cálculos da Thymos. Assim, ele avalia, a margem indicada pelo ONS será suficiente para acomodar os projetos, inclusive nas regiões que contam com alguma restrição. O diretor de Novos Negócios da Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), Marcello Cabral, chama atenção para o fato de a nota apontar que o fluxo de recarga da bateria limitou a conexão em diversos pontos. “É importante avaliar se os cenários adotados capturam adequadamente a possibilidade de carregar as baterias nos horários de excedente eólico e solar, respeitando as condições da rede”, disse. Conclusão esperada Para Cabral, a publicação da margem de escoamento disponível é um avanço importante para o leilão, já que dá “mais transparência às condições de conexão e permite que os empreendedores avaliem a localização e o dimensionamento dos seus projetos”. Além disso, segundo ele, a existência de margem em diversos pontos deve contribuir para a competitividade do certame. De acordo com o diretor-executivo da Absae, a nota técnica do ONS é positiva e veio na linha esperada pelos agentes que cadastraram projetos, que já estruturaram os empreendimentos considerando a metodologia de acesso à margem. Por isso, segundo ele, não deve haver grande número de projetos inabilitados por falta de espaço na rede. Na etapa de cadastros, quase 300 GW de projetos foram enviados à EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética). “Como foram identificados poucos barramentos onde você não tem margem dentre os barramentos bonificados, por exemplo, isso não deve ser um fator que exclua um percentual elevado de projetos”, afirmou o diretor da Absae. Por isso, ele afirma que mesmo após a habilitação o número de empreendimentos deve continuar elevado, o que deve favorecer a competição por preços menores.

artigo.texto: Hawaii County considers curbing AI data centers HILO — Two Hawaii County commissions are considering a bill aimed at prohibiting artificial intelligence data centers on the Big Island through the creation of a new definition in the county code. The Windward Planning Commission discussed the bill at its meeting on Thursday after previously deferring on Sept. 3. Introduced by Hamakua Councilperson Heather Kimball, Bill 170 distinguishes between “data processing facilities” and “data centers.” Data processing facilities are defined as places where records and other digital information are stored and are currently a permitted use under the county code in certain zoning districts, while data centers refer to the large-scale facilities being built to house the infrastructure needed to power AI. These data centers, which use significant amounts of energy, water and other resources, have drawn concern and pushback from communities across the country where they have been built or proposed. The Leeward Planning Commission will also evaluate the bill and make a recommendation to the Council. The Leeward commission’s next meeting is scheduled for Oct. 15. Kimball told the Hawaii Tribune-Herald that her goal in introducing the bill was to close a potential loophole that could allow such centers to be constructed on the island. “I think we have to preemptively prepare for an interest in developing data centers in Hawaii,” she said. “The purpose of this bill is very simple, very straightforward, from the standpoint that it defines what data centers are, and therefore, because it defines them and then does not put them anywhere in Chapter 25 (of the county code) as a permitted use, they become prohibited through that absence.” The bill defines a data center as “a facility used for the industrial-scale operation of computer systems and associated equipment for the processing, computing, transmission, or dissemination of digital data, and that requires supporting infrastructure beyond that typically accessory or incidental to office, commercial, or public institutional uses.” Kimball said this definition came from the National Association of Counties. While commissioners expressed support for the intent of the bill at the Thursday’s meeting, they voted 5-1 to send an unfavorable recommendation to the County Council, due primarily to concerns that the definition was not specific enough. “They need to come up with something better that involves expertise, opinions, and it needs to be done in a way that’s separated and in a clean way so that there’s no loopholes left,” said Commissioner JoNelle Fukushima. “That’s the biggest issue here, is that if we do this too quickly, and we don’t take our time in understanding what the definition is, we may leave with unintended consequences, pathways to them being able to come in and do the data centers.” Windward Planning Commission Vice Chair Chantel Perrin, who was the sole vote in favor of the bill, said there would be future opportunities for additions and clarifications to be made to the bill once it returns to Council. She suggested that instead of submitting an unfavorable recommendation for Bill 170, the commission instead indicate support for the intent of the bill and submit a list of the changes they would like to see made to the definition. “Bill 170 needs to happen. It needs a definition,” she said. “Nonetheless, we may not agree with what’s being written, but it doesn’t mean it’s done there. We can tell them, that’s why we can suggest recommendations as to how we want it worded.” Several members of the public who provided testimony during the meeting, expressed strong opposition to data centers and support for the bill’s goal, but also asked for additional, more specific language to be included. “Bill 170’s intent is what our hopes and dreams are as a community,” said Hilo resident Cristina Holt. “However, the only thing that we are doing with Bill 170 is creating a definition. As I’m sure you guys have seen in your own research and the testimony that has come your way, there’s a lot of confusion about what we’re even talking about, so, setting a clear definition for what we are talking about is literally the very first step.” There was also confusion surrounding recommendations submitted by the county Planning Department in response to the bill which included potential permitting regulations, which Kimball and Deputy County Corporation Counsel Jean Campbell noted are beyond the scope of this bill and would acquire additional legislation. “(The Council) would not be able to amend this particular bill in the ways that are being recommended,” Campbell said. “However, they have other options. They could withdraw this bill and introduce one that’s broader. They could pass this bill and then introduce something else that would address your recommendations.”

artigo.texto: HiTHIUM, a leading global green energy technology company,has showed its next-generation sodium-ion energy storage solution at its “Powered Day, Day in and Day out” launch event. The company introduced the ∞Power N4.0MWh system, built around the ∞Cell N785Ah sodium-ion battery, with full-scale production and delivery planned for 2027. The system is designed for a 30-year service life, while the battery supports 20,000 cycles and 2- to 8-hour storage durations. artigo.texto: Depois do fim das bets, Vila Nova fecha patrocínio com a BYD Clube afirmou que acordo representa o “maior patrocínio da história do Tigrão” O clube goiano Vila Nova anunciou nesta 6ª feira (2.out.2026) uma nova parceria fechada com a montadora de carros chinesa BYD. O acordo de patrocínio foi confirmado pelo clube em sua conta oficial no Instagram. Nenhum valor foi revelado ainda, mas o anúncio nas redes sociais afirmou que este é o “maior patrocínio da história do Tigrão”. “O espaço mais nobre do nosso Manto agora carrega uma das maiores marcas do mundo. O Vila Nova Futebol Clube tem o prazer de anunciar a BYD Saga como sua nova patrocinadora master, em um acordo que marca um novo capítulo na história do clube. […] esta parceria representa um momento histórico para o Vila Nova. É o maior patrocínio da história do Tigrão!”, escreveu o clube. O Vila Nova é atualmente o líder da Série B do Brasileirão. Até a proibição das bets, tinha como patrocinador master a marca Bet da Sorte. O setor de bets era responsável por até 10% da receita dos clubes, segundo o ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan. O novo patrocínio foi fechado em menos de 96 horas sob um acordo de confiança mútua e garante ao clube um montante mensal superior ao contrato anterior, assegurando a estabilidade financeira e o pagamento de salários do elenco até o término do Campeonato Brasileiro da Série B. Válida inicialmente até o fim da temporada, a parceria estampa a marca no uniforme e visa a ações de expansão, como a instalação de pontos de recarga para veículos elétricos no CT do clube e o fornecimento de frota para a diretoria e comissão técnica. Embora os valores exatos sigam sob confidencialidade contratual, o acordo já deixa caminhos alinhados para uma possível renovação de longo prazo entre as partes para as próximas temporadas, independentemente da divisão em que o clube disputar.

artigo.texto: Wartsila Launches Valo Joint Venture with RCT Solutions for Energy Storage According to ESS News, Finnish technology group Wartsila has shifted its worldwide energy storage operations into Valo, a joint venture it co-owns on an equal basis with German engineering firm RCT Solutions. The company anticipates that the new entity will post losses during 2026 before returning to profitability near the close of 2027. Valo, characterized as a utility-scale battery energy storage system integrator encompassing Wartsila's Energy Storage operations, commenced on Oct. 1 following the completion of the joint venture between the two owners. Valo starts with over 20 GWh spanning more than 130 projects globally. Peter Fath, who formerly served as chief executive of RCT Solutions, heads the new venture as chief executive, while Luke Witmer holds the position of chief technology officer. Wartsila disclosed the transaction on June 15, stating it would hand over net assets amounting to under 5% of its total net assets. Finalization hinged on regulatory clearances and securing a financing package. Additional investors could enter at a later stage, possibly reducing the stakes of the two founding shareholders, and the joint venture will gain from project guarantees Wartsila has already provided on ongoing projects, according to the Helsinki-based group. Wartsila further indicated that the joint venture would operate at a loss in 2026 owing to weak recent order intake and transformation expenses, primarily a write-down of capitalized research and development. It projected the effect on its full-year 2026 operating result at EUR40 million to EUR50 million, or $45.2 million, contingent on when closing occurs. The company expressed expectations that the joint venture would deliver positive results near the end of 2027, and its Oct. 1 closing release restated the anticipated 2026 loss. Wartsila noted that the energy storage business represented its smallest segment, employing roughly 480 people. It recorded net sales of EUR694 million in 2025 with an operating margin of 3.3%, finishing the year with an order book valued at EUR719 million. Wartsila stated that RCT Solutions, established in 2012, has overseen the engineering and creation of multiple battery and solar manufacturing plants across the globe, and that one RCT entity has served as a crucial supplier to Wartsila Energy Storage for several years. It added that RCT also offers a chance for vertical integration via an existing integrated battery energy storage system manufacturing effort in the United States in the near term. Neither company has disclosed the project's name. Wartsila initiated a strategic review of the business in October 2023 and concluded it in March 2025 by separating storage into a distinct reporting segment with its own financial objectives. Following the joint venture agreement, it reclassified the unit as discontinued operations, and it will now report its stake as a share of result in associated companies. At the time it began the review, Wartsila reported net sales of EUR983 million for the business on a 12-month rolling basis through the end of the third quarter of 2023. The targets established in March 2025, low double-digit annual organic growth and an operating margin of 3% to 5%, are no longer applicable after the joint venture agreement. - 1. artigo.texto: One third of the way there: is the CATL dream lost in translation? The Orbán government had expected the transition to electric mobility to happen more quickly, but the revolution in the automotive industry was delayed. The Hungarian economy was intended to serve as a link between German premium manufacturers and Asian suppliers of key components. To that end, an extremely large amount of funding was made available — at CATL in Debrecen, roughly one in every seven forints of the investment was subsidised — in the hope of achieving economic growth, technology transfer, and job creation. CATL, the global market leader in battery technology, began producing modules at the Debrecen site in 2024, while the battery plant in the immediate vicinity of the BMW New Class factory was still under construction. Since then, BMW has been assembling the cells delivered by its partner into battery packs at its own plant, as has Mercedes at its separate battery final assembly facility in Kecskemét. CATL plant director Qin Lang, speaking during a factory tour ahead of the weekend, said that more than 500,000 modules had been built in just under two years across three production lines in the temporary facility. According to him, the company’s revenues have since totalled 100 billion forints. Both NCM and LFP batteries are manufactured in Debrecen. Nickel technology delivers greater range thanks to its higher energy density, while batteries made from lithium iron phosphate are extremely long-lasting and free of expensive raw materials such as cobalt. On 22 September, a trial run for battery cell production began at the new plant, initially on two production lines. Two further production lines are still being prepared technically for the start of operations. The battery cell plant’s capacity of 40 GWh has long been fully committed by its clients. The original site plan envisaged a total capacity of 100 GWh across three construction phases, for which CATL intended to invest a total of 7.5 billion euros. With the Tisza government taking office, however, the plant expansion appears to be under threat, as the environmental lobby is said to have strong backing within the new political movement. This would freeze the large Chinese investment at one third of its originally planned volume, amounting to a maximum of 4,000 jobs. CATL has not yet abandoned all hope of reaching an agreement with the government on the terms for the plant expansion — an expansion that involves a total of 9,000 jobs, which by 2030 would be filled to around 90% by domestic workers. artigo.texto: How much are AI data centers adding to your electricity bill? Americans are worried AI data centers will raise their electricity bills. Congress has come up with a plan to protect ratepayers, but there's no easy way to find out what AI is costing them. ELISSA NADWORNY, HOST: The construction of huge, new AI data centers has become a political lightning rod. Communities near proposed projects are raising questions about their impact, including on electricity costs. One big question is who will end up paying for expensive new infrastructure needed to power these massive facilities. NPR's Scott Neuman has been looking into that question, and he joins me now. Hi, Scott. SCOTT NEUMAN, BYLINE: Hi, Elissa. NADWORNY: So, Scott, most of us know by now that these hyperscale AI centers require a lot of power and upgrades to the electrical grid. Who is paying for all that? NEUMAN: Well, the simple answer is everybody who buys electricity. That means people who are building and using these data centers for sure, but also local businesses and homeowners and renters, even if they don't think they're using AI. During my reporting this past week, I spoke with Ari Peskoe. He's the director of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative. He says that, ultimately, everyone is shouldering the burden for the billions of dollars in new upgrades to the electrical grid. ARI PESKOE: Everyone pays those costs. They're spread across the region to every business and resident that has an electricity meter. NEUMAN: Now, in many cases, the pace and scale of the demand is coming at - it's really breakneck speed, and that makes all of this unpredictable. The demand for new transmission lines, substations and other infrastructure is ramping up faster than the utilities can keep up in many cases. And that creates an enormous planning challenge. But, you know, Peskoe brings up another interesting point. He says that the speed that all of this is happening can actually drive up the cost of these improvements. Components, things like transformers, are in short supply, and everybody wants them and wants them now. So there's a scarcity, and that makes everything more expensive. NADWORNY: OK, so we're all paying for the AI upgrades, but how are those costs divided up? NEUMAN: That's a really tough question to answer. Even if an AI data center is - in your area is the reason for these improvements, everyone is going to be getting the use of them. But Peskoe says no one has really figured out how to divvy up the costs in an equitable way. PESKOE: There's no agreement as to what infrastructure is for a data center versus for the public. That itself is a disputed point. NEUMAN: So in 2024, Maryland's Office of People's Counsel, an independent state consumer agency, forecast that new costs due to data centers would run residents as much as $216 a year. But the rapid buildout of these data centers means there's a lot of uncertainty. NADWORNY: Do individual customers get any benefit from all this new grid infrastructure? NEUMAN: Yeah, so the fact that everyone gets the use of these improvements to the grid means everyone gets the benefits too. Lucy Qiu is a professor at the University of Maryland who is looking into all of this. She says that in many places, the upgrades are long overdue. They'll be needed for AI data centers, but they'll also be needed for things like meeting the charging capacity for electric vehicles. LUCY QIU: On the positive side, you can accelerate the upgrade of the grid infrastructure. NEUMAN: Qiu says studies show that people who live near data centers where the grid has been more - made more robust to accommodate them, those residential rate payers have fewer power outages during extreme weather events. NADWORNY: All right, so some positive side too, thank you. That was NPR's Scott Neuman. NEUMAN: Thank you. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. artigo.texto: Rethinking WUE: Data Center Water Strategy Beyond The Facitily As AI reshapes data center cooling, improving water usage effectiveness requires a system-level view. October 5, 2026 Water has always served a strategic role in hydronic applications. It carries thermal energy more efficiently than air, making it well-suited for applications where precise thermal management is critical. Today, that includes AI data centers, where rising computing densities are creating unprecedented cooling demands. But as data center development accelerates, the conversation around water is changing. Water is no longer merely a cooling input – its availability, quality and infrastructure capacity have become important considerations for siting, permitting, resilience and community alignment. That makes water usage effectiveness (WUE) an increasingly important metric, but also one that needs to be considered in context. Water as a strategic resource Liquid-based cooling isn't new. Data centers have used water for decades to absorb and remove heat generated by IT equipment. What is changing is the scale and concentration of that heat. AI and high-performance computing are driving higher rack densities that challenge traditional air-cooling approaches. As a result, direct-to-chip liquid cooling and other liquid-based architectures are moving closer to the heat source, where they can efficiently capture heat from CPUs and GPUs. Closed-loop hydronic systems can also recirculate fluid rather than continuously consuming makeup water. Together, these approaches create opportunities to reduce reliance on evaporation and improve facility-level WUE. But there's an important distinction: Using water more efficiently inside a data center doesn't necessarily tell the whole story. Look beyond WUE alone Every cooling architecture involves trade-offs. A closed-loop system, for example, may significantly reduce on-site water consumption, but the heat still has to go somewhere. Depending on the heat rejection strategy, reducing water use can increase electrical demand. Conversely, evaporative cooling can reduce cooling energy under the right conditions while consuming more water. That’s why WUE shouldn't be considered separately from power usage effectiveness (PUE). Water and energy use are closely connected, and the electricity powering a data center can carry its own water footprint depending on the regional generation mix. A cooling strategy that reduces water consumption on-site but requires more electricity may simply shift some of that water demand upstream rather than eliminate it. Liquid cooling adds another factor. Moving liquid closer to high-density computing equipment provides an effective way to manage concentrated heat loads, but liquid cooling alone doesn't determine overall water consumption. Operators and designers still need to consider the complete thermal chain, including pumping, heat exchange, heat rejection and the energy required to operate the system. The objective isn't simply to drive one metric lower. It's to find the appropriate water-energy balance for the site. That balance will look different from one data center to another. Climate, water availability and quality, workload, rack density, grid characteristics, utility capacity and local infrastructure can all influence the appropriate cooling strategy. A data center in a water-stressed region with available electrical capacity may require a different approach than a facility where water is abundant but the grid is constrained. That's where system-level thinking comes in. Instead of starting with a specific cooling technology, project teams should consider the outcomes the facility needs to achieve and consider the complete water cycle: - Where will water come from? - What quality is required? - How will it be treated and moved? - How efficiently can it be reused? - How will heat be rejected? - What happens to the water before it leaves the facility? Advanced treatment technologies can expand opportunities to use reclaimed or alternative water sources while maintaining the quality required for reliable cooling, while digital monitoring can provide visibility into water quality, flow, equipment condition and changing system performance. Meanwhile, heat recovery may create opportunities to put captured thermal energy to beneficial use rather than simply rejecting it. Collaboration outside the facility matters, too. Early coordination with water and wastewater utilities can help data center developers understand local constraints, evaluate reuse opportunities and identify infrastructure investments that strengthen long-term water resilience. Design WUE into the system As AI infrastructure scales, water strategy can no longer be something addressed after the cooling architecture is already established. While WUE provides an important measure of progress, the bigger opportunity is understanding what sits behind the metric. Water source, treatment, hydronics, cooling, monitoring, reuse, discharge and even community infrastructure are all interconnected. The goal isn't simply to use less water. It's to manage water and energy together in a way that supports thermal performance, uptime and responsible growth. For the next generation of data centers, that broader view may be the most effective way to make every drop – and every watt – count. About the Author: Steven Lucente is a business development manager for Xylem’s Applied Water business, where he leads data center business development and turns customer infrastructure challenges into scalable growth strategies and win-ready solutions.

artigo.texto: The Lansing Town Board decided to draft a ban on the construction of new data centers in the town at a special meeting on Tuesday night. The meeting was packed with over 200 concerned citizens, who voiced opposition to data center development during a public comment period. The approval process for a proposed data center on Cayuga Lake was paused in July when Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-N.Y.) signed Executive Order 62, enacting a one year moratorium on state permitting for data centers exceeding a 50 megawatt capacity. The board met to navigate uncertainty with how the state moratorium applies to the town — they were met with a crowd of frustrated residents who expressed concern for the future of their hometown in the event of data center construction. The event was lively, with loud reactions from the crowd throughout the evening, met with multiple requests for quiet from the town board. Many of the speakers and audience members wore red, signifying a “stop” to data center development and support of a data center ban. Of the over 30 people who spoke, all but one called for a data center ban in Lansing — the one dissenter being a TeraWulf employee. The draft of the ban will be presented to the public by the town’s attorney at a future meeting. If developed and passed, Lansing will join Dryden and Danby in being some of the first New York towns to ban data centers of any size. Background In August 2025, data center developer TeraWulf secured an 80 year lease to the former Milliken Station powerplant, located in Lansing, and approval for the construction of a data center with up to 400 megawatts of industrial capacity. The project, known as Lake Hawkeye Data, has been met with protest from groups such as No Data Center FLX and Cayuga Lake Environmental Action Now!. The groups sued Lansing’s Zoning Board of Appeals and TeraWulf in January 2026, challenging the zoning board’s classification of the center as a “general processing facility” — an undefined term in the code which makes it easier for development to proceed. The lawsuit is ongoing in spite of the moratorium, the lead attorney for the environmental groups told The Sun in July, because the zoning board’s decision remains in effect. No Data Center FLX has collected almost 23,000 signatures for their petition rejecting the project and has organized protests throughout the approval process. During the moratorium, the Department of Environmental Conservation is prohibited from issuing discretionary permits, which are a necessary step in the data center approval process. The moratorium, however, “does not directly impact local reviews and approval,” according to the board’s statement to open the public comment period. Therefore, it is unclear the exact impact of the moratorium on TeraWulf’s plans for the data center. Public Comments Over 200 people filled the Lansing Middle School auditorium to voice their concerns at the special meeting. This showing came after previous board meetings about the data center did not allow an open public comment period. Commenters were widely in agreement, raising concerns around noise from the proposed data center and stress on the electrical grid, along with potential costly litigation in the event TeraWulf breaches any agreements. However, most did not directly address the state’s moratorium, instead raising concerns about the data center itself. At the midpoint, the agenda called to shift from hearing comments from Lansing residents to non-Lansing residents, which was met with boos from the crowd. The board decided to allow a mix of Lansing and non-Lansing speakers to come forward, and many of the latter abdicated their allotted two minutes of speaking time to Lansing residents. The single voice in favor of the development was Pace Ralli, TeraWulf’s vice president of project development. He said he has worked in clean energy for over 20 years and “care[s] deeply about our environment and natural resources.” Ralli sees the Lake Hawkeye project as an opportunity for economic development and repurposing old industrial land. He described TeraWulf’s work with the town as “constructive and collaborative” and said TeraWulf has made “meaningful changes to the site plan in response” to local concerns. Ralli asked Lansing residents to keep an open mind and “evaluate the project on the facts.” Board Discussion After hearing public comments, some board members were split between a desire for economic development and opposition from the community. Council member Judy Drake, who expressed concern for Lansing’s economic development, said the town has a reputation as “not interested in business.” She said she wanted to explore the option of a “highly regulated data center” as a means to promote the economy. Regulations on project size “make an ugly project seem not quite as ugly,” Wetmore said. He added that supporting the data center as a means of economic development may push away other businesses. Town Supervisor Ruth Groff described the prospective data center as a “fiscal nightmare” that is “open[ing] the door for more problems,” noting that allowing data centers of any size into Lansing could be risky as the only way to hold these companies accountable in the event they breach contract is expensive litigation. The board discussed a town level moratorium due to uncertainty in how Hochul’s executive order would affect local governments, and expressed hope that the state would provide further frameworks or regulation to guide the local government through the evaluation and approval process. Drake said he does not “trust the state when it comes to deciding what happens in our town.” Within the final minutes of the meeting, board members decided to draft an all-out ban. Despite the complexity of regulations and the details to weigh, the sentiment in the room was voiced by Lansing resident Lisa Peter: “This is my happy place, don’t eff it up.” Lila Davis is a member of the Class of 2029 in the College of Agriculture and Life

artigo.texto: On Oct. 1, SB 484 required each of Florida’s investor-owned utilities to file a tariff for its largest customers. The law’s core is two sentences. The rules must reasonably ensure that each large-load customer, defined as one drawing 50 megawatts or more, bears its own full cost of service. And the risk that such a customer doesn’t pay may not be borne by everyone else. I published a rubric for reading those filings on Sept. 15, before any existed, and finished amending it before the first one arrived. Each filing gets one of three results: it clears, it has a shortfall to defend, or it misses a required test. Three utilities made Oct. 1 filings. Two filed new large-load tariffs, and FPL asked the Commission to deem its existing one compliant. Duke filed nothing new and relies on a petition pending since April. The scorecards are below. Tampa Electric put real numbers on the page: stated charges, a 20-year minimum term, and, in its customer contract, a termination fee covering the remaining generation, transmission, fuel transportation, and purchased-power charges for the rest of the term. Only two required tests are partly met. The tariff reaches only new or incremental load, and security for an investment-grade customer is 50% of $2.0 million multiplied by its contracted megawatts, against roughly $2.7 million per megawatt of committed plant and transmission, by my arithmetic from the company’s exhibits. The open question is year 20: a customer giving notice can leave owing nothing more, while the company’s own exhibits show about $1.07 billion of generation net plant still on the books in 2047. TECO says that plant would then serve its other customers. That may prove true; no one has agreed to pay for it if it does not. Florida Power & Light filed no new large-load tariff. It asked the Commission to find that the tariffs approved in January as part of its rate settlement, before SB 484 took effect, already comply. Those tariffs carry a 20-year term, two years’ notice, and an exit fee covering the remaining generation charges. The miss is coverage: they apply only to a customer with a projected new or incremental load of 50 megawatts or more and a projected load factor of 85% or more. A load factor can lawfully set a price; here it decides who is covered. The statute defines the customer by peak demand alone. That may describe few customers today. The rubric reads the text, not the current queue. Florida Public Utilities says it has no qualifying customers and no inquiries, and leaves every rate to customer-specific agreements the Commission must approve before service starts. That is reasonable for a small utility. But the filing states no rate, and under the rubric’s first test, a filing with no stated rate misses. Duke Energy Florida filed nothing new by Oct. 1. It relies on a petition filed in April, heard in August and briefed in September. Its president, Melissa Seixas, made the case in these pages on Oct. 2: “Floridians should never be asked to finance someone else’s business decision.” That is the right standard. The filing falls short on one required test. Duke’s policy measures the 50-megawatt threshold over 30 minutes; the statute says 15. And it reaches only firm load, so a new customer that takes interruptible service falls outside it. Duke says such customers need less capacity built for them; the statute’s definition makes no such exception. Until a large-load rate arrives in 2028, which Duke committed to in its brief, qualifying customers pay existing general-service rates, backed by a 20-year term and an exit fee. Two points for anyone following these cases. First, the statute requires the outcome and only permits the tools. The Commission may approve exit fees and minimum terms, but the full-cost result is mandatory either way. Second, FPL asked for proposed agency action, so the Commission can rule without a hearing unless an affected party asks for one. And one number belongs in every conversation about this law. SB 484 does not reach municipal utilities or rural electric cooperatives. By the Commission’s own statistics, that is about 25% of the state’s customer accounts. These are readings of the filed words, not Commission findings. Every citation is collected with the rubric. They show a promise written in mandatory terms, met unevenly. ___ Dr. Mark McNees is director of the MS in Social and Sustainable Enterprises at Florida State University’s Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship. He writes on energy cost policy.

artigo.texto: Nearly a year after they received their first data center proposal, Ransom Twp. officials are poised to adopt an ordinance regulating the facilities’ development. Supervisors will vote Monday on an ordinance updating the township’s zoning laws to include requirements for data centers’ development, according to public notices and the agenda for the meeting. The vote comes as the township is involved in litigation over its rejection earlier this year of a proposal by Scranton Materials LLC to construct a data center campus on the company’s Newton Road property. The company in November filed for a curative amendment, challenging the validity of the township’s zoning ordinance, that would have allowed the construction of six data centers — each with a 156,648-square-foot footprint — at its 251-acre quarry at 819 Newton Road. The board voted in January to dismiss the proposed changes due to lack of testimony and evidence from Scranton Materials. Under state law, municipalities are required to allow every type of lawful land use within their borders, or else face legal challenges over exclusionary zoning. The law is the focus of several legal challenges related to the supervisors’ January dismissal of the zoning change. The developer appealed the decision and filed a second lawsuit seeking a declaratory judgment against the board earlier this year. The second lawsuit is ongoing. A Lackawanna County judge ruled in July that a Scranton woman can legally oppose the plans despite not living in Ransom Twp. Officials have not said how the new ordinance would affect the litigation with Scranton Materials. Efforts to reach township Solicitor William Rinaldi about whether the ordinance would render the lawsuits moot were unsuccessful Friday. The Pennsylvania Municipal Planning Code states that no zoning changes or other governing ordinance may adversely affect an existing land development application. More recently, Mudiita Land Venture LLC, a Carbon County-based firm with a parent company in New Jersey, purchased 528.6 acres south of Ransom Road and west of South Keyser Avenue in the township to build a hyperscale data center campus. There have been no other data centers proposed in the township, officials have said. At public meetings on the ordinance, people have been receptive to the proposed law but worry about future development. The ordinance says data centers would be allowed only in the township’s general commercial/manufacturing and heavy manufacturing districts — along the southeastern part of the municipality at the Taylor border and in the southwestern part along the Susquehanna River, respectively — as a conditional use. As a conditional use, the developer would need to meet specific criteria outlined in the ordinance and receive township approval. The board of supervisors would be required to render a written decision on the application within 45 days after the final hearing. Under state law, if a governing body fails to hold a public hearing within 60 days of the application being received, the decision is deemed in favor of the applicant. The ordinance stipulates that data centers have a maximum height of 40 feet and lot area of 8 acres. Other requirements address buffering, fencing, wastewater management, air quality, odor, glare and emissions, battery and fuel storage, parking, noise and vibration, and lighting.

artigo.texto: A 1ª emissão do Plano de Outorgas de Transmissão de Energia Elétrica (POTEE) de 2026 estabelece a implantação de sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) no Acre, com investimento estimado em R$ 249 milhões. O Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) publicou, em edição extra do Diário Oficial da União (DOU) da quinta-feira (1º/10), o documento com ampliações e reforços no sistema de transmissão que devem ser implantados até 2033. Essa edição do POTEE traz 45 novas obras de expansão do sistema de transmissão, localizadas em 17 unidades da federação, nas cinco regiões do país. O objetivo da implantação do BESS é aumentar a confiabilidade do suprimento a Cruzeiro do Sul e a Feijó. A cidade de Cruzeiro do Sul só foi incluída no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) em dezembro de 2024. O plano também determina a instalação de duas linhas de transmissão, com investimento total estimado em R$ 717 milhões. O POTEE estabelece ainda um conjunto de instalações associado ao Bipolo Nordeste II para ampliar a capacidade de exportação de energia da região Nordeste e de importação do Sul. O investimento estimado para esse conjunto de obras é de mais de R$ 24 bilhões, e a data de necessidade é em janeiro de 2033. Outra determinação do documento é a implantação de tecnologia para calcular em tempo real a capacidade de transmissão da linha Mogi Guaçu I – São João da Boa Vista II, em São Paulo, a partir das condições ambientais e operacionais. Com investimento estimado em R$ 2,1 milhões, a solução permitirá postergar a reconstrução da linha, estimada em cerca de R$ 140 milhões.
